arxiv_record.abstract:
Adversarial attacks present a significant challenge to the dependable
deployment of machine learning models, with patch-based attacks being
particularly potent. These attacks introduce adversarial perturbations in
localized regions of an image, deceiving even well-trained models. In this
paper, we propose Outlier Detection and Dimension Reduction (ODDR), a
comprehensive defense strategy engineered to counteract patch-based adversarial
attacks through advanced statistical methodologies. Our approach is based on
the observation that input features corresponding to adversarial
patches-whether naturalistic or synthetic-deviate from the intrinsic
distribution of the remaining image data and can thus be identified as
outliers. ODDR operates through a robust three-stage pipeline: Fragmentation,
Segregation, and Neutralization. This model-agnostic framework is versatile,
offering protection across various tasks, including image classification,
object detection, and depth estimation, and is proved effective in both
CNN-based and Transformer-based architectures. In the Fragmentation stage,
image samples are divided into smaller segments, preparing them for the
Segregation stage, where advanced outlier detection techniques isolate
anomalous features linked to adversarial perturbations. The Neutralization
stage then applies dimension reduction techniques to these outliers,
effectively neutralizing the adversarial impact while preserving critical
information for the machine learning task. Extensive evaluation on benchmark
datasets against state-of-the-art adversarial patches underscores the efficacy
of ODDR. Our method enhances model accuracy from 39.26% to 79.1% under the
GoogleAp attack, outperforming leading defenses such as LGS (53.86%), Jujutsu
(60%), and Jedi (64.34%).

C1.justification: V2 explicitly extends the main contribution to monocular depth estimation and demonstrated effectiveness on Transformer architectures. Its abstract replaces v1's broad claims of performance within 1–3% or 3–5% of clean baselines with a specific GoogleAP comparison. The introduction also adds a depth-error reduction claim.

C2.justification: V2 introduces a substantive adaptive-attack interpretation: matching clean-image distributions makes patches harder to isolate but allegedly weakens their attack effectiveness. It also attributes gains over DR to outlier detection and interprets parameter sensitivity and CPU timings as supporting practical deployment. V1 lacks these analyses of mechanism and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies a 1,000-image classification test sample, additional hyperparameter ranges and minPts values, CPU hardware and processing times, and adaptive-attack constraints. Appendices describe a sample-folder structure and disclose that the code is proprietary and cannot be openly shared. These are substantial documentation additions, although the conflicting tree counts limit reproducibility and the described folders are not included in the supplied PDFs.

E1.justification: V2 adds KITTI monocular depth estimation under SSAP attacks, dynamic and deformable classification attacks through GDPA and Shape Matters, multiple-patch detection examples, and a defense-aware adaptive-attack scenario. The original classification and detection datasets and naturalistic-patch evaluations remain.

E2.justification: V2 adds DR, identified as DefensiveDR, as an evaluated defense in Table 4 and supplies LGS/Jedi comparisons for LAVAN beyond v1's reported GoogleAP comparison. This is a limited expansion of the comparator set. Jujutsu, De-randomized Smoothing and PatchGuard disappear from the comparison table but their original comparison scores remain in Section 4.3.

E3.justification: V2 adds Inception-v3, ViT and Swin classification settings, a Faster-RCNN evaluation on an INRIA subset, and MIMdepth evaluation using depth error, affected-region ratio and MSE against clean predictions. It also introduces parameter-sweep and adaptive-attack protocols. Section 5.4 states 100 isolation trees while Section 4.2 retains v1's 500, so the actual revised tree budget is unresolved.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's naturalistic-patch and Grad-CAM analyses, v2 adds Isolation Forest versus DBSCAN localization comparisons, neutralization alternatives, comparison with dimension reduction alone, hyperparameter sensitivity curves, computational-cost measurements, and adaptive-attack distribution diagnostics. Sections 5.1–5.6 and 7.5–7.6 substantially expand investigation of component effectiveness and robustness.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. V2's Gaussian fits and Mahalanobis plots characterize image-fragment distributions; they do not introduce uncertainty reporting for the reported performance results.

E6.justification: Most matched original classification and detection scores are retained. V2 adds extensive results, including 83.1% ViT accuracy under GoogleAP, KITTI depth error decreasing from 0.59 to 0.11 with ODDR, and larger-patch results in Tables 7–10. These are additional settings, not demonstrated improvements over v1 under identical conditions. ResNet-152/GoogleAP adversarial accuracy is inconsistently reported as 39.3 in v2's main tables versus 39.9 in v1 and v2's appendix.

M1.justification: V1's Algorithm 1 selects the largest outlier cluster and neutralizes one mask. V2 selects all clusters meeting a new minPts threshold and applies SVD to a mask around each cluster. This substantively extends the procedure to multiple suspicious regions while retaining the fragmentation, Isolation Forest and SVD components.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, contributions and experimental discussion. Related work is integrated into the introduction, the standalone Key Findings subsection is removed, and the discussion is reorganized into six subsections. Isolation-tree material and retained clean-sample results move into a substantial appendix.

P2.justification: V2 consolidates classification results into a larger table and merges the separate INRIA/CASIA comparison tables. It relocates the overview diagram, redraws the detailed pipeline in the appendix, removes v1's patch gallery, and adds depth/detection examples, sensitivity plots and distribution plots. Appendix tables expand the original patch-size displays; Table 11 repeats Table 4 rather than providing another experiment.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands its research context through DefensiveDR, GDPA, Shape Matters, SSAP, monocular depth estimation, Transformer architectures and distribution-analysis literature. The explicit comparison with DefensiveDR also positions outlier detection as the source of additional benefit over dimension reduction alone. Moving the retained empirical-versus-certified defense discussion into the introduction is a separate presentation change.

T1.justification: The Isolation Forest scoring equations and truncated-SVD mathematics are retained. V2 adds computational-complexity claims in Section 5.3 and formal Gaussian moment constraints for the adaptive attack, supported by Mahalanobis-distance analysis in Section 7.6. These are limited mathematical extensions; no new theorem or proof is provided.

improvement.justification: V1 offered little direct empirical scrutiny of component choices, parameter sensitivity or defense-aware attacks. V2's ablations, sensitivity curves and adaptive-attack diagnostics substantially improve assessment of the mechanism and its limits, while depth-estimation and Transformer experiments meaningfully test broader applicability. Conflicting 100/500-tree settings and 39.3/39.9 GoogleAP values weaken reproducibility, but the added scrutiny and supporting evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ODDR research and have readable text, equations, tables and figures. V2 includes Section 7 appendices; the supplied v1 ends with references. Results absent from v1's PDF are assessed as newly documented, without assuming the underlying experiments were newly performed.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds depth-estimation results, additional model and attack evaluations, ablations, sensitivity analyses and an adaptive-attack evaluation.

before.justification: V1 reports original classification and object-detection experiments on ImageNet, Caltech-101, INRIA and CASIA, including defense comparisons and Grad-CAM examples.

arxiv_record.abstract: Information Pursuit (IP) is an explainable prediction algorithm that greedily selects a sequence of interpretable queries about the data in order of information gain, updating its posterior at each step based on observed query-answer pairs. The standard paradigm uses hand-crafted dictionaries of potential data queries curated by a domain expert or a large language model after a human prompt. However, in practice, hand-crafted dictionaries are limited by the expertise of the curator and the heuristics of prompt engineering. This paper introduces a novel approach: learning a dictionary of interpretable queries directly from the dataset. Our query dictionary learning problem is formulated as an optimization problem by augmenting IP's variational formulation with learnable dictionary parameters. To formulate learnable and interpretable queries, we leverage the latent space of large vision and language models like CLIP. To solve the optimization problem, we propose a new query dictionary learning algorithm inspired by classical sparse dictionary learning. Our experiments demonstrate that learned dictionaries significantly outperform hand-crafted dictionaries generated with large language models.
arxiv_record.authors: Stefan Kolek, Aditya Chattopadhyay, Kwan Ho Ryan Chan, Hector Andrade-Loarca, Gitta Kutyniok, R\'ene Vidal
arxiv_record.title: Learning Interpretable Queries for Explainable Image Classification with Information Pursuit

native_poster_event.abstract: Building image classification models that are both highly accurate and interpretable remains a challenge in computer vision. Information Pursuit (IP) is an information-theoretic framework for interpretable-by-design sequential prediction. Given a set of task-relevant and semantic data queries, IP selects a sequence of queries in order of information gain and updates the posterior at each step based on the gathered query-answer pairs. To carry out IP, previous methods construct hand-crafted dictionaries of potential data queries, curated either by a domain expert or by prompting large language models. However, in practice, such hand-crafted dictionaries are limited by the expertise of the curator and the heuristics of prompt engineering, resulting in a gap between the predictive performance of IP versus non-interpretable black-box predictors. In this work, we propose to parameterize the IP queries as a learnable dictionary defined in the latent space of vision-language models such as CLIP. Drawing inspiration from sparse dictionary learning, we propose an alternating optimization algorithm that iterates between solving IP's optimization problem for a fixed query dictionary and optimizing the dictionary to maximize classification accuracy. Empirically, our experiments show that our method learns a query dictionary that reduces the accuracy gap between explainable image classification with IP and black-box methods, while preserving interpretability.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains learning interpretable, task-adapted IP dictionaries through an augmented V-IP objective and alternating optimization. v2 broadens the introduction's comparison claim to other interpretable ML methods and explicitly emphasizes reducing the black-box accuracy gap in its abstract and conclusion; v1 principally emphasized outperforming GPT-3 dictionaries.

C2.justification: v1 acknowledges that learned hyperplanes require manual semantic interpretation. v2 replaces that limitation with direct text-concept identification and discusses noisy CLIP answers, illustrated by incorrectly affirming 'anemone' for a jellyfish. It adds an explicit interpretation-versus-accuracy tradeoff from quantization and a more detailed explanation of how dictionary updates disrupt the querier's indexed-query semantics.

D1.justification: v2 documents the approximately 300,000-query universe, LLaMA/COCO construction procedure, full prompt, update ratio, and validation-AUC checkpoint selection. Training specifications are substantially rewritten. Conversely, v1's explicit batch sizes, 10% validation split, temperature-annealing schedule, and direct concept-set repository link are no longer supplied. Architecture and masking details are retained; omitted settings do not establish changed underlying settings.

E1.justification: v2 retains CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, removes Tiny ImageNet, and evaluates RIVAL-10, ImageNet-100, CUB-200, and Stanford-Cars. These introduce different image populations and fine-grained classification coverage. ImageNet-100 is not merely a renamed Tiny ImageNet: v1 explicitly used 200 classes at 64-by-64 resolution. COCO captions additionally supply candidate concepts for query-universe construction.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 adds comparisons against PCBM, LaBo, Label-free, and Res-CBM, using CBM results from the literature. v1 only compared learned dictionaries with GPT-3 soft/hard dictionaries and a black-box baseline. The primary comparison in v2 Figure 3 retains K-LLM and black-box comparators but no longer separately includes the soft-answer GPT-3 baseline.

E3.justification: Training changes from dataset-specific schedules to 800 random-sampling plus 800 biased-sampling epochs for K-Learned and 1500 plus 1500 for K-LLM, with Adam learning rate 1e-5. CIFAR-100 evaluation extends from 15 to 50 queries. The black-box control changes from v1's deeper MLP to a stated two-layer MLP. The added CBM comparison uses RN50 and soft answers.

E4.justification: v1's warm-up, BatchNorm, dictionary-size, and backbone ablations disappear. Initialization analysis expands to include K-Medoids and query-evolution examples; alternating-versus-joint optimization is reevaluated across six datasets. v2 Table 4 examines both answer quantization and the newly introduced query quantization. The deer/dog interpretation cases are replaced by a jellyfish explanation with explicit natural-language queries.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies repeated-run counts or random seeds, reports confidence intervals or error bars, or performs significance tests. The additional results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: v2 replaces benchmark curves and adds CBM, quantization, and query-evolution results. Its RN50/soft-answer comparison reports 88.55% and 68.02% for K-Learned on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. Whereas v1 Figure 11 favors phased optimization on CIFAR-100, v2 Table 1 reports 75.20% for alternating versus 75.67% for joint optimization. Changed methods and budgets prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: v1 learns BatchNorm-parameterized hyperplanes with learned thresholds. v2 instead projects learnable embeddings onto text concepts in a query universe and thresholds min-max-normalized CLIP scores. Algorithm 1 also replaces warm-up and prolonged training phases with alternating updates, using four network updates per dictionary update and freezing both networks during dictionary updates; v1 continued updating the classifier.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and method exposition are extensively rewritten. The method is renamed K-Learned, experiments are integrated into Section 4, and the discussion becomes a focused limitations section. Appendices are reorganized into proof, architecture, history representation, training, and query-universe construction sections.

P2.justification: v2 adds IP workflow and optimization-flow diagrams, replaces the three-panel benchmark plot with six panels, and replaces the deer/dog heatmaps with a jellyfish explanation. Several ablation plots are replaced by tables. The architecture diagram is retained and relocated, while typography and appendix layout are substantially redesigned.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning against concept-discovery CBMs and CLIP-based interpretable representations, discussing residual CBMs, learned bottleneck concepts, SPliCE, text-based CLIP decomposition, and STAIR. It further distinguishes sequential IP explanations from static CBM explanations and adds the foundation-model V-IP precursor. These are substantive positioning changes beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The previously qualitative sparse-dictionary connection gains Proposition 1 and an Appendix A proof relating dictionary optimization to summed posterior KL losses along IP explanations. v2 also introduces formal explanation strategies and the epsilon-sufficiency formulation, and explicitly qualifies V-IP/IP equivalence through infinite network capacity and a unique maximizing query.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses a central deficiency acknowledged in v1: learned queries required manual translation into concepts. Mapping queries directly to text embeddings makes the explainability contribution more concrete. The new formal analysis, broader evaluations, and quantization studies substantially strengthen its support. Some reproducibility details are lost, and Table 1 qualifies the prose's claimed optimization advantage, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the central interpretability advance and stronger evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial methodological and experimental revisions.

after.justification: v2 Section 4.4 and the appendices report original K-Learned classification results across six datasets, optimization and quantization ablations, and qualitative query analyses.

before.justification: v1 Section 5 and Appendix B report original classification accuracies, algorithm ablations, and example predictions on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large Vision Language Models have achieved fine-grained object perception, but the limitation of image resolution remains a significant obstacle to surpassing the performance of task-specific experts in complex and dense scenarios. Such limitation further restricts the model's potential to achieve nuanced visual and language referring in domains such as GUI Agents, counting, \textit{etc}. To address this issue, we introduce a unified high-resolution generalist model, Griffon v2, enabling flexible object referring with visual and textual prompts. To efficiently scale up image resolution, we design a simple and lightweight down-sampling projector to overcome the input tokens constraint in Large Language Models. This design inherently preserves the complete contexts and fine details and significantly improves multimodal perception ability, especially for small objects. Building upon this, we further equip the model with visual-language co-referring capabilities through a plug-and-play visual tokenizer. It enables user-friendly interaction with flexible target images, free-form texts, and even coordinates. Experiments demonstrate that Griffon v2 can localize objects of interest with visual and textual referring, achieve state-of-the-art performance on REC and phrase grounding, and outperform expert models in object detection, object counting, and REG. Data and codes are released at https://github.com/jefferyZhan/Griffon.
arxiv_record.authors: Yufei Zhan, Shurong Zheng, Yousong Zhu, Hongyin Zhao, Fan Yang, Ming Tang, Jinqiao Wang
arxiv_record.comments: Accepted by ICCV 2025. Codes and datasets are released at https://github.com/jefferyZhan/Griffon
arxiv_record.title: Griffon v2: Advancing Multimodal Perception with High-Resolution Scaling and Visual-Language Co-Referring

C1.justification: v2 adds an introductory claim of competitive general-VQA performance. Its conclusion changes the REC/REG/phrase-grounding claim from state-of-the-art to competitive, although state-of-the-art wording remains elsewhere. The central high-resolution and visual-language co-referring contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning rare-category generalization, global-context preservation in VQA and partitioning as an explanation for Qwen2.5-VL's detection difficulties. It removes v1's qualification about ambiguous RefCOCO+ annotations and the interpretation of encoder unfreezing. The underlying resolution-and-context explanation remains.

D1.justification: Supplementary Sections 1–4 newly disclose dataset quantities, filtering and sampling, prompt construction, projector dimensions, training hyperparameters and A800 training time. The grounding-only qualification accompanying v1's REC results is lost. The abstract changes promised code/data release to claimed availability, but future-release statements persist elsewhere, leaving availability internally inconsistent.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluations across 13 ODinW domains and on VQAv2, ChartQA, MME and POPE (Tables 4 and 6), substantially extending domain and task coverage. The original COCO, FSCD-LVIS, RefCOCO/+/g and Flickr30K evaluations remain, including those relocated to the supplement.

E2.justification: v2 adds Lumen, Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL2.5 to relevant comparisons, evaluates LLaVA-NeXt and Monkey against its resolution design, and adds qualitative comparisons with T-Rex. The REC comparator set is substantially revised, dropping methods including CogVLM, UNINEXT-L and OFA-L; some other removed REC comparators remain in different tasks.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include ODinW mAP testing and comparisons using the same training data as LLaVA-NeXt for VQA and Monkey for COCO detection (Section 4.4). New counting baselines are queried for target counts. These extend the evaluation protocol; supplementary hyperparameters document existing training rather than establish changes to it.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct-versus-partitioned high-resolution comparisons (Table 6) and expert-comparison case studies examining detection errors, grounding and counting (Figures 8–10). It removes v1's frozen-versus-trainable encoder ablation (Table 9). The visual-encoder and resampler ablations remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The added experiments retain single-value reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds ODinW results, including 42.0 average mAP, VQA scores and newer baseline results. Detection, counting, phrase-grounding and REG scores are retained. Splitwise REC and encoder-freezing results disappear. The reported REC average of 90.0 equals the mean of v1's grounding-only row; its unspecified configuration prevents interpreting it as a generalist performance gain.

M1.justification: The high-resolution encoder, convolutional down-sampling projector, visual-reference tokenizer, Llama2-13B backbone and three-stage training procedure remain unchanged. The supplement documents existing representations and implementation details without establishing a revised method.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative now prioritizes detection and counting, substantially rewrites the grounding discussion, and moves REG and phrase-grounding sections into the supplement. Related-work passages are revised and extensive data, representation and implementation explanations are added, producing substantial structural reorganization.

P2.justification: The paper changes from single-column to two-column layout. v1's architecture and conversation figures are merged into v2 Figure 2, other figures are redesigned, and the detailed REC table becomes a combined ODinW/REC summary. New comparison tables, dataset displays, hyperparameter tables and qualitative figures substantially change presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL2.5, Lumen and grounded language-image pre-training, while removing several earlier references. Related work sharpens the distinction between class-level visual referring and individual-object/VQA-oriented systems. The foundational positioning around direct high-resolution processing and co-referring remains.

T1.justification: Equation 1 and the reasoning relating visual-token count to resolution and convolution stride are unchanged. Neither version supplies additional formal assumptions, theorems or proofs; the supplementary representation details do not introduce new mathematical results.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in the supplied v1 through evaluated partition-based comparisons (Table 6) and substantial data-processing and training documentation (Supplementary Sections 1–4). ODinW testing and newer baselines further strengthen validation. Removing the freezing ablation and detailed REC results, especially the grounding-only qualification behind the matching 90.0 average, reduces transparency; nevertheless, the gains in design validation and reproducibility constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Griffon v2 work, with readable text, equations, tables and figures. v1 ends with references; v2 includes supplementary material, which was also inspected. Retained content can be matched across the substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds ODinW evaluations, VQA comparisons and supplementary qualitative comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original detection, counting, referring-expression and phrase-grounding experiments, architectural ablations and qualitative results.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Imposing key anatomical features, such as the number of organs, their shapes
and relative positions, is crucial for building a robust multi-organ
segmentation model. Current attempts to incorporate anatomical features include
broadening the effective receptive field (ERF) size with data-intensive
modules, or introducing anatomical constraints that scales poorly to
multi-organ segmentation. We introduce a novel architecture called the
Anatomy-Informed Cascaded Segmentation Network (AIC-Net). AIC-Net incorporates
a learnable input termed "Anatomical Prior", which can be adapted to
patient-specific anatomy using a differentiable spatial deformation. The
deformed prior later guides decoder layers towards more anatomy-informed
predictions. We repeat this process at a local patch level to enhance the
representation of intricate objects, resulting in a cascaded network structure.
AIC-Net is a general method that enhances any existing segmentation models to
be more anatomy-aware. We have validated the performance of AIC-Net, with
various backbones, on two multi-organ segmentation tasks: abdominal organs and
vertebrae. For each respective task, our benchmarks demonstrate improved dice
score and Hausdorff distance.
arxiv_record.authors: Young Seok Jeon, Hongfei Yang, Huazhu Fu, Mengling Feng
arxiv_record.title:
Teaching AI the Anatomy Behind the Scan: Addressing Anatomical Flaws in
  Medical Image Segmentation with Learnable Prior

native_poster_event.abstract: Imposing key anatomical features, such as the number of organs, their shapes and relative positions, is crucial for building a robust multi-organ segmentation model. Current attempts to incorporate anatomical features include broadening the effective receptive field (ERF) size with data-intensive modules, or introducing anatomical constraints that scales poorly to multi-organ segmentation. We introduce a novel architecture called the Anatomy-Informed Cascaded Segmentation Network (AIC-Net). AIC-Net incorporates a learnable input termed "Anatomical Prior", which can be adapted to patient-specific anatomy using a differentiable spatial deformation. The deformed prior later guides decoder layers towards more anatomy-informed predictions. We repeat this process at a local patch level to enhance the representation of intricate objects, resulting in a cascaded network structure. AIC-Net is a general method that enhances any existing segmentation models to be more anatomy-aware. We have validated the performance of AIC-Net, with various backbones, on three multi-organ segmentation tasks: abdominal organs, vertebrae, and ribs. For each respective task, our benchmarks demonstrate improved dice score and Hausdorff distance.

C1.justification: The anatomical-prior and global-local contributions remain, but v2 replaces the advertised activation-maximization contribution with a novel centroid-loss contribution and explicitly includes affine-plus-TPS alignment. Its abstract and introduction assert performance improvements across multiple backbones and two tasks. The general applicability claim itself already existed in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds an explanation of flat deformation-loss regions and how centroid alignment addresses them, interprets HD95 as an anatomical-accuracy indicator, and discusses vertebral-label guidance. It newly acknowledges doubled model size and memory consumption, limited fine-detail deformation, and failure to predict kidney cyst classes. These substantially extend v1's optimization hypothesis and brief future-work discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds implementation information about affine/TPS prediction heads, trilinear resampling, fixed target points and precomputed TPS inversion, the padded volume size, and sliding-window inference. These are documentation additions where v1 did not specify the corresponding details. Conversely, v1's code-availability statement and URL disappear; the PDFs do not establish whether the repository itself became unavailable.

E1.justification: The WORD evaluation covering 16 abdominal structures is replaced by TotalSegmentator organ and vertebra tasks. The later evaluation includes vertebral identity prediction and additional structures such as lung lobes, thyroid and prostate, with varied scan coverage. WORD results are not retained.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates UNet and cascaded UNet comparators. v2 retains the vanilla/cascaded comparison structure and adds evaluated DeepLabV3+, UNETR and UNETR-Swin comparators, each in vanilla and cascaded forms, as shown in Table 1.

E3.justification: The stated training budget changes from 350 epochs of 200 iterations to 200,000 iterations, and TPS regularization weights change from 1e-8 to 1e-5. v2 specifies centroid-loss weights of 0.5 and a vertebra intensity window of [-250, 1100]. Its new dataset uses a 1082/57/65 training/validation/test split instead of WORD's 100/20/30. Dice, NSD and HD95 remain the evaluation metrics.

E4.justification: v2 adds a with/without-centroid-loss analysis of malformed vertebral priors under different scan coverage (Figure 4), and measures local-prior accuracy before and after deformation across backbones and tasks (Table 2). The earlier femur and gallbladder cases are replaced by vertebral-label, spleen and adrenal cases. These provide new component and failure analyses.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates only. v2 adds mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting throughout appendix Tables 3–10. This is a descriptive reporting addition; neither version documents repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests, and v2 does not clearly specify the standard-deviation aggregation procedure.

E6.justification: The WORD results are replaced by TotalSegmentator aggregate and class-level results, with additional component findings. For example, v2 Table 1 reports vertebra HD95 of 12.6 versus 52.2 for AIC-Net versus vanilla UNETR, but vertebra Dice of 89.3 versus 90.2 for AIC-Net versus vanilla UNETR-Swin. These are new-setting comparisons, not v1-to-v2 performance gains. Table 7's organ mean row also conflicts with Table 1 and repeats the vertebra means.

M1.justification: The global-local cascade and alternating prior optimization remain, but v2 adds per-organ affine translations before TPS, centroid alignment loss, and residual SE fusion with layer normalization. The documented objective changes from combined Soft-Dice and cross-entropy with TPS regularization to Soft-Dice, centroid loss and regularization. These change the procedure beyond renaming.

P1.justification: Beyond the new title and AIC-Net terminology, v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, related work and conclusion. It reorganizes the method into more detailed component and loss subsections and develops a Results and Discussion narrative. This is substantial rewriting alongside the scientific additions.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column to a two-column layout. The architecture and deformation diagrams are redrawn and combined, a separate SE-res diagram and centroid-loss figure are added, and qualitative displays are replaced or expanded. The compact WORD table is replaced by a multi-backbone summary, a deformation table and eight appendix result tables.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around template and atlas methods, multiclass topology losses, and limitations of transformers with limited data. Added references include TETRIS, Bayesian atlas approaches, Mamba/Mamba-UNet and recent validation studies. The earlier GNN discussion and its citations are removed, changing the surrounding research context.

T1.justification: v2 introduces formal centroid and centroid-loss definitions and a revised composite objective. The appendix also substantively corrects TPS interpolation: its kernel and polynomial matrices use target control points, while the right-hand side uses source coordinates; v1 used source coordinates in both. This changes the mathematical construction rather than merely its notation.

improvement.justification: The four-backbone, two-task evaluation and direct centroid/deformation analyses substantially strengthen validation beyond v1's single-backbone WORD study. The corrected TPS construction and explicit resource and failure limitations also improve technical clarity. These gains outweigh material reporting weaknesses: the code pointer disappears, Table 1 contradicts blanket superiority claims, and Table 7's organ means repeat vertebra results. Those flaws qualify the conclusions but do not erase the substantial improvement in evidence and explanation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same anatomical-prior segmentation work, renamed from AIC-UNet to AIC-Net. The complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original TotalSegmentator organ and vertebra experiments across four backbones, component analyses, and class-level results in appendix Tables 3–10.

before.justification: v1 reports original WORD segmentation experiments comparing AIC-UNet, CUNet and UNet in Table 1, alongside learned-prior visualizations and qualitative predictions.

arxiv_record.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has emerged as a powerful and popular technique for personalization, enabling efficient adaptation of pre-trained image generation models for specific tasks without comprehensive retraining. While employing individual pre-trained LoRA models excels at representing single concepts, such as those representing a specific dog or a cat, utilizing multiple LoRA models to capture a variety of concepts in a single image still poses a significant challenge. Existing methods often fall short, primarily because the attention mechanisms within different LoRA models overlap, leading to scenarios where one concept may be completely ignored (e.g., omitting the dog) or where concepts are incorrectly combined (e.g., producing an image of two cats instead of one cat and one dog). We introduce CLoRA, a training-free approach that addresses these limitations by updating the attention maps of multiple LoRA models at test-time, and leveraging the attention maps to create semantic masks for fusing latent representations. This enables the generation of composite images that accurately reflect the characteristics of each LoRA. Our comprehensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations demonstrate that CLoRA significantly outperforms existing methods in multi-concept image generation using LoRAs.
arxiv_record.authors: Tuna Han Salih Meral, Enis Simsar, Federico Tombari, Pinar Yanardag
arxiv_record.title: Contrastive Test-Time Composition of Multiple LoRA Models for Image Generation

C1.justification: Training-free composition of community LoRAs remains the central contribution. V2 drops the explicit 'first comprehensive attempt' assertion and the conclusion's claim to introduce a DINO-based metric, while making memory efficiency and scalability explicit contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of same-class separation, selective styling, and competitors' dependence on segmentation or supplied controls. It interprets larger compositions as achieving comparable fidelity without auxiliary conditioning and reframes computational scaling as a measured practical tradeoff. V1's explicit limitation that composition depends on input LoRA quality disappears, although ethical concerns remain.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents 200 prompts, 48 images per user-study participant, randomized presentation, explicit baseline conditioning choices, and detailed H100 runtime/VRAM information. These improve disclosure without establishing changes to retained experiments. Conversely, v1's statement that its main DINO evaluation used six LoRA models is removed.

E1.justification: V2 adds targeted same-class identity separation, multi-person compositions, interacting-object scenes, and selective styling scenarios in Appendices C, D, and G. These substantially extend tested composition requirements. The underlying CustomConcept101/custom-character sources and reported 131-LoRA collection already appear in v1's appendix; they are not newly added coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated comparisons with OMG, LoRA-Composer, and Orthogonal Adaptation, including Figures 12, 14, and 15 and Table 2. The original Table 1 comparator set remains in Table 1a. LoRACLR is discussed as related work but is not an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: V2 introduces CLIP-I/CLIP-T metrics, SEEM-based instance evaluation on 700 images per method, 100 compositions with 3–5 input LoRAs and conditioned baselines, H100 resource benchmarking, and a same-seed with/without-box LoRA-Composer comparison. These are new evaluation protocols; the retained SD1.5, 50-step generation setup does not establish a rerun or changed original protocol.

E4.justification: The original latent-update/masking ablation is retained as v2 Figure 6. V2 adds attention-map analysis of style localization, resource scaling with LoRA count, same-class and interaction stress cases, and examinations of bounding-box dependence and OMG failure cases.

E5.justification: V1 reports point estimates, whereas v2 adds ± quantities throughout the retained DINO/user-study results and new quantitative tables. Both retain ten generation seeds per prompt; additional runs are not established. V2 does not define whether ± represents standard deviation, standard error, or another quantity.

E6.justification: Original DINO and user-study means are retained up to rounding. V2 adds CLIP, instance-level, scalability, and runtime outcomes: Table 3 reports CLoRA average DINO similarity of 57.3%, while Table 2 shows mixed rankings, including average DINO of 0.347 versus Mix-of-Show's 0.351. The book/cup qualitative comparison in v1 Figures 7 and 33 is omitted. New H100 timings do not establish a same-setting speedup over v1.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same prompt variants, token-based attention groups, InfoNCE objective, latent updates, and thresholded union masks for fusion. V2 explains style-application modes and same-class token pairing more explicitly, without establishing a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites and condenses the abstract, introduction, related work, and methodological explanation. It changes the title, separates Background from Methodology, folds the ablation discussion into Experiments, and reorganizes supplementary material into Appendices A–J.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the method overview, consolidates v1 Figures 5, 8, and 9 into Figure 5, and restructures the main qualitative comparisons. It adds tables, runtime plots, attention visualizations, and comparison figures. Many retained appendix panels are enlarged from six to two per page, substantially changing visual presentation.

R1.justification: Related work substantially updates the positioning against OMG, LoRA-Composer, Orthogonal Adaptation, and LoRACLR, emphasizing differences in conditioning, training, segmentation, and community-LoRA compatibility. It also adds bounding-box attention methods and other relevant references while trimming older background citations.

T1.justification: V2 corrects the background cross-attention definition: text embeddings supply keys/values and UNet features supply queries, reversing v1's query/key assignment. The substantive CLoRA loss, latent-update, and masking equations remain equivalent; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V1's broad composition claims rely mainly on whole-image DINO scores and qualitative examples. V2 substantially strengthens validation through instance-level evaluation, harder multi-person tests with conditioned baselines, additional similarity metrics, and measured resource scaling. These additions make identity preservation and practical applicability easier to assess. Undefined ± quantities, inconsistent LoRA-Composer memory figures between Table 1b and Appendix F, and removal of the LoRA-quality caveat weaken reporting, but do not outweigh the substantial evaluation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CLoRA, with matching authors, core methodology, and retained experiments despite the changed title. All 20 pages of v1 and 26 pages of v2, including appendices, provide readable text and visual evidence for comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds CLIP measurements, instance-level evaluation, multi-subject comparisons, and runtime/scalability results in Tables 1–3 and Figure 7.

before.justification: V1 reports original image-generation comparisons, DINO scores in Table 1, a 50-participant user study, and latent-update/masking ablations in Figure 10.

arxiv_record.abstract:
The Transformer architecture has achieved remarkable success in natural
language processing and high-level vision tasks over the past few years.
However, the inherent complexity of self-attention is quadratic to the size of
the image, leading to unaffordable computational costs for high-resolution
vision tasks. In this paper, we introduce Concertormer, featuring a novel
Concerto Self-Attention (CSA) mechanism designed for image deblurring. The
proposed CSA divides self-attention into two distinct components: one
emphasizes generally global and another concentrates on specifically local
correspondence. By retaining partial information in additional dimensions
independent from the self-attention calculations, our method effectively
captures global contextual representations with complexity linear to the image
size. To effectively leverage the additional dimensions, we present a
Cross-Dimensional Communication module, which linearly combines attention maps
and thus enhances expressiveness. Moreover, we amalgamate the two-staged
Transformer design into a single stage using the proposed gated-dconv MLP
architecture. While our primary objective is single-image motion deblurring,
extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that our
approach performs favorably against the state-of-the-art methods in other
tasks, such as deraining and deblurring with JPEG artifacts. The source codes
and trained models will be made available to the public.
arxiv_record.authors: Pin-Hung Kuo, Jinshan Pan, Shao-Yi Chien, Ming-Hsuan Yang

C1.justification: V2 makes CDC a separate central contribution and claims CSA can improve existing restoration backbones, including Restormer. It retains linear-complexity local/global modeling and single-stage gdMLP. V1's concluding claim of state-of-the-art denoising performance is removed, with denoising described as comparable in the supplement.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations linking shared attention and CDC to receptive-field expansion and discussing why concatenation and omission of the global mean help (Section 6.2). V1 attributes marginal SIDD gains to small images limiting useful global context and suggests convolutions may be preferable. V2 replaces that explanation with a limitation concerning careful backbone design for different restoration tasks.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies block size, head allocation and multi-scale spatial/frequency-domain L1 losses. Its supplement supplies SIDD and deraining training schedules, REDS configuration instructions and the alternative denoising model's block allocation. V1 refers to supplementary settings without including them in the supplied PDF. These disclosures do not establish that previously unspecified settings changed; code release remains a future promise.

E1.justification: Test1200 is removed from deraining evaluation. The other restoration tasks and principal datasets remain, including SIDD in v2's supplement. RealBlur testing was already stated in v1, so its newly supplied results do not establish newly added evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds DeepRFT+, Uformer, MPRNet-local and DiffIR to the quantitative GoPro/HIDE comparison; Uformer already appeared in v1's figures. The newly reported RealBlur comparison includes BANet and FMIMO-UNet+ among its comparators. Qualitative comparisons also add DiffIR and, for deraining, DIDMDN.

E3.justification: The 600,000-iteration GoPro curriculum changes from 200k/300k/100k iterations at 128/256/384-pixel patches to 200k per stage at 128/256/320 pixels. AdamW beta2 changes from 0.999 to 0.9, and rotations are added. Ablations switch from 128- to 256-pixel patches, RealBlur uses fine-tuning rather than GoPro-only training, and new analyses introduce diffusion-index measurements and a Restormer comparison.

E4.justification: V2 substantially revises the component ablations and adds tests of the CSA prototype, concatenation, CDC and retaining versus omitting the global mean (Tables 5–6). Figure 8 examines receptive fields through local attribution maps, and Table 7 tests transfer to Restormer. V1's separate cross-attention, shifted-window and multi-head ablations are no longer reported.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. V2's diffusion-index analysis does not introduce statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: GoPro results change from 34.27/34.33 dB for Mansformer-E/P to 34.18/34.42 for Concertormer-lite/full. V2 adds RealBlur-R/J results of 40.78/33.51 dB, new analytical results and supplementary visual comparisons. REDS and deraining scores change; SIDD reports two configurations at 40.28/40.32 versus v1's single 40.32. Models and training differ, and deraining averages exclude Test1200, so these are not unchanged-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: V2 adds Cross-Dimensional Communication projections and convolutions across attention maps before softmax (Section 4.1, Equations 8–9), extending v1's independently computed attention branches. It also revises block allocations and implements CSA within Restormer. The multi-scale U-Net, four spatial/channel branches and gdMLP remain recognizable.

P1.justification: The manuscript is extensively rewritten around Concertormer and Concertino/Ripieno terminology. V2 adds a separate self-attention background section and an Analysis and Discussion section, reorganizes applications, and moves denoising and limitations into the supplement. The changes substantially alter the narrative beyond renaming.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main layout, transposes the main benchmark table, redraws the architecture and self-attention diagrams, and adds attention-map and attribution visualizations. Figure 1 becomes a single HIDE plot with a logarithmic FLOPs axis, dropping the deraining panel. Qualitative figures are reformatted into compact crop grids, and the supplement adds Figures 9–20.

R1.justification: The broad positioning against CNN/U-Net restoration and efficient Transformers remains. V2 adds Talking-heads Attention and local attribution maps to support CDC and analysis, plus references for newer comparators such as DiffIR, DeepRFT and BANet. Several background references disappear, including those supporting the removed SVM analogy.

T1.justification: V2 Section 4.1 introduces a formal shared-mean and residual decomposition and derives the prototype, tensorized CSA and CDC formulations. It adds assumptions concerning projected concatenation and absorbing or replacing the mean. V1 directly defines the four attention operations; its explicit per-branch and total complexity expressions are omitted in v2.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens mechanism evidence and reproducibility through the targeted analyses in Tables 6–7 and Figure 8, reported RealBlur comparisons, and newly supplied task-specific training details. These gains outweigh reduced Test1200 coverage and the loss of explicit complexity formulas. A retained ranking claim becomes inaccurate: Table 1 places Concertormer-lite at 34.18 dB on GoPro, below FFTformer's 34.21, despite claiming the proposed models occupy the top two positions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, renamed from Mansformer to Concertormer with substantial revisions. Their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. V1 ends with references; v2 includes readable supplementary material.

after.justification: V2 reports original restoration results, component and receptive-field analyses, a Restormer adaptation experiment, and supplementary denoising results and visual comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original deblurring, deraining and SIDD denoising results, qualitative comparisons and component ablations in Tables 1–5 and Figures 4–6.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Text animation serves as an expressive medium, transforming static
communication into dynamic experiences by infusing words with motion to evoke
emotions, emphasize meanings, and construct compelling narratives. Crafting
animations that are semantically aware poses significant challenges, demanding
expertise in graphic design and animation. We present an automated text
animation scheme, termed "Dynamic Typography", which combines two challenging
tasks. It deforms letters to convey semantic meaning and infuses them with
vibrant movements based on user prompts. Our technique harnesses vector
graphics representations and an end-to-end optimization-based framework. This
framework employs neural displacement fields to convert letters into base
shapes and applies per-frame motion, encouraging coherence with the intended
textual concept. Shape preservation techniques and perceptual loss
regularization are employed to maintain legibility and structural integrity
throughout the animation process. We demonstrate the generalizability of our
approach across various text-to-video models and highlight the superiority of
our end-to-end methodology over baseline methods, which might comprise separate
tasks. Through quantitative and qualitative evaluations, we demonstrate the
effectiveness of our framework in generating coherent text animations that
faithfully interpret user prompts while maintaining readability. Our code is
available at: https://animate-your-word.github.io/demo/.

Zichen Liu, Yihao Meng, Hao Ouyang, Yue Yu, Bolin Zhao, Daniel
  Cohen-Or, Huamin Qu

native_oral_events.abstract: Text animation serves as an expressive medium, transforming static communication into dynamic experiences by infusing words with motion to evoke emotions, emphasize meanings, and construct compelling narratives. Crafting animations that are semantically aware poses significant challenges, demanding expertise in graphic design and animation. We present an automated text animation scheme, termed "Dynamic Typography", which deforms letters to convey semantic meaning and infuses them with vibrant movements based on user prompts. The animation is represented by a canonical field that aggregates the semantic content in a canonical shape and a deformation field that applies per-frame motion to deform the canonical shape.  Two fields are jointly optimized by the priors from a large pretrained text-to-video diffusion model using score-distillation loss with designed regularization, encouraging the video coherence with the intended textual concept while maintaining legibility and structural integrity throughout the animation process. We demonstrate the generalizability of our approach across various text-to-video models and highlight the superiority of our methodology over baselines. Through quantitative and qualitative evaluations, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in generating coherent text animations that faithfully interpret user prompts while maintaining readability.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains prompt-driven, legible vector animation through jointly optimized base and motion fields. v3's conclusion explicitly extends its generalizability claim to different fonts, prompts and languages, whereas v1 emphasizes arbitrary words, motion patterns and video backbones.

C2.justification: v3 explains that excessive control points promote self-intersections and that strong legibility regularization applied too early can suppress semantic deformation. Its rocket failure case makes the existing legibility–semantic-alignment limitation concrete, and Appendix G proposes shape-compatible input selection as mitigation. The underlying backbone and shape-mismatch limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly specifies Adam, separate learning rates, affine-motion scales, regularization weights, interleaved updates and gradual legibility weighting. Sections 3.1 and 5.1 add subdivision and rendering details. These substantially improve implementation disclosure without establishing changed experimental execution. Conversely, v1's explicit gradient-detachment instruction is omitted. The backbone, optimization budget, hardware/runtime and project link are retained.

E1.justification: The main 33-sample alphabet dataset is retained. Appendix D adds Chinese and Japanese character examples and tests with Segoe Print and Roboto-Bold alongside KaushanScript-Regular (Figures 13–15). These provide limited qualitative extensions of the existing task to additional scripts and font conditions.

E2.justification: Gen-2, DynamiCrafter and LiveSketch remain the comparison methods in Table 1 and Figure 8. The added user study uses the same comparator set. Word-as-Image remains an input-generation component, while GPT-4V is evaluated as a design assistant rather than a competing animation baseline.

E3.justification: Appendix E introduces a four-way human preference evaluation, with eight randomly sampled questions per user and 62 reported responses, considering legibility, semantic alignment and temporal consistency. New controlled experiments vary control-point counts between 75, 204 and 420 and compare regularization strengths. The newly stated frame count and rendering resolution document the retained comparison; they do not establish a changed protocol or rerun.

E4.justification: v3 substantially expands analysis through control-point sensitivity, same-letter font and prompt variations, an explicit legibility-versus-semantic-deformation failure case, and GPT-4V-assisted design examples. The frequency-encoding ablation moves to Appendix B and gains a butterfly example, but its quantitative Table 2 row is removed. The other component ablations and backbone comparison remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new user-study sample count and preference percentages add evaluation information and results, without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the retained Table 2 rows have identical scores. New Figure 16 reports preferences of 44.76% for Ours, 21.57% for LiveSketch, 19.96% for DynamiCrafter and 13.71% for Gen-2, alongside substantial new qualitative findings. v1's No Freq. results—0.02222 warping error, 0.5377 PIC and 20.8280 alignment—disappear. Consequently, the full model becomes the highest-PIC remaining ablation without any score improvement.

M1.justification: Appendix G adds an optional GPT-4V procedure for selecting shape-compatible words, letters and prompts before animation. The core base-field/motion-field algorithm, SDS guidance, regularizers and frequency annealing remain. Newly disclosed optimization details do not establish that the earlier implementation changed.

P1.justification: v3 retitles the paper, substantially condenses and rewrites Related Work, reorganizes the method requirements, and edits explanations throughout. Frequency encoding and its ablation discussion move from the main text to Appendix B, while implementation material is organized in Appendix A. These constitute substantial editorial restructuring beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v3 changes the document typography, author block and layout, revises the framework diagram, restructures Figure 9 and Table 2, and changes score highlighting. Figures 11–18 add or reorganize ablation imagery, sensitivity comparisons, font/script examples, the user-study pie chart, failure cases and GPT-4V-assisted outputs. Some earlier imagery is reused rather than newly generated.

R1.justification: v3 adds references including VBench, HyperNeRF, D-NeRF, Creating Emordle and GPT-4, and removes the SVG specification reference. These support additional context and experiments; the central positioning against static typography, existing kinetic typography and LiveSketch remains.

T1.justification: The written structure-loss definition in Equation 8 changes from an unweighted sum to separately weighted base-to-letter and inter-frame terms; Appendix A supplies unequal weights. This is a limited formal revision. The SDS and frequency-annealing mathematics are retained, and neither version adds theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens reproducibility through missing optimizer and regularization details, and complements v1's automated metrics with direct human preference evidence. New sensitivity and failure analyses also make applicability easier to assess. These gains outweigh the removed numerical frequency ablation and omitted gradient-detachment instruction, although the user study still lacks uncertainty reporting. The improvement comes from stronger documentation and validation, not higher main comparison scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Dynamic Typography framework, with corresponding methods, experiments, figures and tables despite the revised title. All supplied pages are readable. v1 ends with references; v3 additionally contains Appendices A–G, which are included in this comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds a user preference study, control-point sensitivity results, font and language demonstrations, failure cases and GPT-4V-assisted examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original animation experiments on 33 samples, quantitative baseline comparisons and component ablations in Tables 1–2, and qualitative comparisons across video backbones.

arxiv_record.abstract: Denoising diffusion models have emerged as powerful tools for image manipulation, yet interactive, localized editing workflows remain underdeveloped. We introduce Layered Diffusion Brushes (LDB), a novel training-free framework that enables interactive, layer-based editing using standard diffusion models. LDB defines each "layer" as a self-contained set of parameters guiding the generative process, enabling independent, non-destructive, and fine-grained prompt-guided edits, even in overlapping regions. LDB leverages a unique intermediate latent caching approach to reduce each edit to only a few denoising steps, achieving 140~ms per edit on consumer GPUs. An editor implementing LDB, incorporating familiar layer concepts, was evaluated via user study and quantitative metrics. Results demonstrate LDB's superior speed alongside comparable or improved image quality, background preservation, and edit fidelity relative to state-of-the-art methods across various sequential image manipulation tasks. The findings highlight LDB's ability to significantly enhance creative workflows by providing an intuitive and efficient approach to diffusion-based image editing and its potential for expansion into related subdomains, such as video editing.
arxiv_record.authors: Peyman Gholami, Robert Xiao

native_poster_event.abstract: Denoising diffusion models have emerged as powerful tools for image manipulation, yet interactive, localized editing workflows remain underdeveloped. We introduce Layered Diffusion Brushes (LDB), a novel framework that facilitates real-time and iterative image editing with fine-grained, region-specific control. LDB leverages a unique approach that caches intermediate latent states within the diffusion process, enabling users to apply prompt-guided edits via masks in a non-destructive, layered manner. Key innovations include latent caching for significant speed enhancements (achieving edits in under 140ms on consumer GPUs) and redefining layering for diffusion models with an order-agnostic system that allows for independent manipulation and stacking of edits, even in overlapping regions. An editor implementing LDB, incorporating familiar layer concepts, was evaluated through user study and quantitative metrics. Results demonstrate LDB's superior speed alongside comparable or improved image quality, background preservation, and edit fidelity relative to existing state-of-the-art techniques across various sequential image manipulation tasks. The findings highlight LDB's potential to significantly enhance creative workflows by providing an intuitive and efficient approach to diffusion-based image editing and its potential for expansion into related subdomains, such as video editing.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Multimodal sensing has proven valuable for visual tracking, as different
sensor types offer unique strengths in handling one specific challenging scene
where object appearance varies. While a generalist model capable of leveraging
all modalities would be ideal, development is hindered by data sparsity,
typically in practice, only one modality is available at a time. Therefore, it
is crucial to ensure and achieve that knowledge gained from multimodal sensing
-- such as identifying relevant features and regions -- is effectively shared,
even when certain modalities are unavailable at inference. We venture with a
simple assumption: similar samples across different modalities have more
knowledge to share than otherwise. To implement this, we employ a ``weak"
classifier tasked with distinguishing between modalities. More specifically, if
the classifier ``fails" to accurately identify the modality of the given
sample, this signals an opportunity for cross-modal knowledge sharing.
Intuitively, knowledge transfer is facilitated whenever a sample from one
modality is sufficiently close and aligned with another. Technically, we
achieve this by routing samples from one modality to the expert of the others,
within a mixture-of-experts framework designed for multimodal video object
tracking. During the inference, the expert of the respective modality is
chosen, which we show to benefit from the multimodal knowledge available during
training, thanks to the proposed method. Through the exhaustive experiments
that use only paired RGB-E, RGB-D, and RGB-T during training, we showcase the
benefit of the proposed method for RGB-X tracker during inference, with an
average +3\% precision improvement over the current SOTA. Our source code is
publicly available at https://github.com/supertyd/XTrack/tree/main.

native_poster_event.abstract: Multimodal sensing has proven valuable for visual tracking, as different sensor types offer unique strengths in handling one specific challenging scene where object appearance varies.  While a generalist model capable of leveraging all modalities would be ideal, development is hindered by data sparsity, typically in practice, only one modality is available at a time. Therefore, it is crucial to ensure and achieve that knowledge gained from multimodal sensing -- such as identifying relevant features and regions -- is effectively shared, even when certain modalities are unavailable at inference.  We venture with a simple assumption: similar samples across different modalities have more knowledge to share than otherwise. To implement this, we employ a classifier with weak loss tasked with distinguishing between modalities. More specifically, if the classifier "fails" to accurately identify the modality of the given sample, this signals an opportunity for cross-modal knowledge sharing. Intuitively, knowledge transfer is facilitated whenever a sample from one modality is sufficiently close and aligned with another. Technically, we achieve this by routing samples from one modality to the expert of the others, within a mixture-of-experts framework designed for multimodal video object tracking. During the inference,  the expert of the respective modality is chosen, which we show to benefit from the multimodal knowledge available during training, thanks to the proposed method. Through the exhaustive experiments that use only paired RGB-E, RGB-D, and RGB-T during training, we showcase the benefit of the proposed method for RGB-X tracker during inference, with an average +3\% precision improvement over the current SOTA. Our source code will be released.

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from a generalist, modality-blind tracker positioned toward AGI to cross-modal knowledge sharing through deliberately weak classification. V2 foregrounds a claimed first systematic transfer approach and an average three-point precision advantage over SOTA, replacing v1's emphasis on competitive specialist-level performance with small tuning overhead.

C2.justification: V1 treats accurate modality assignment as evidence of successful specialization; v2 interprets classification confusion as an opportunity for knowledge transfer. V2 adds explanations of event-to-thermal versus event-to-depth transfer and scene-dependent expert selection. Its limitations emphasize identical expert designs and adaptive computation, while dropping v1's explicit qualifications about known training modalities, specialist inferiority, and data requirements.

D1.justification: V2 explicitly reports top-k = 2, a 0.001 loss proportion, and backbone sources for its two variants. It removes v1's approximate 100M total and 8M additional parameter counts. The availability statement changes from a promised code/model release to stated public source-code availability; that availability was not independently checked.

E1.justification: The same five datasets and three auxiliary modalities remain. V2 Table 6 adds a limited but distinct scenario: zero-shot tracking on modalities absent from training, including depth and thermal evaluation after event-only training. V1's cross-dataset evaluations retained training exposure to the tested modality.

E2.justification: V2 substantially expands the evaluated comparators, including OSTrack, OneTracker, and SDSTrack across the benchmark tables, plus additional specialist trackers. OneTracker and SDSTrack were cited but not evaluated in v1. Some comparisons disappear: Stark_d is absent from VOT-RGBD2022, and DAFNet/MaCNet no longer have LasHeR results despite remaining in the RGBT234 comparison.

E3.justification: The reported batch size changes from 64 to 32, training from 60 to 90 epochs, and learning-rate decay from epoch 48 to 78. V2 evaluates OSTrack-based XTrack-B and an additional DropMAE-based XTrack-L. It also introduces training-modality subsets and rigid/soft routing comparisons. These are substantive reported setting changes, not merely additional implementation disclosure.

E4.justification: V2 extends shared/specialized-expert and expert-count ablations from DepthTrack to all three training benchmarks. It adds joint-training and zero-shot analyses, routing-strength comparisons, and three scene-specific routing case studies. V1's appendix-wide event-routing histogram and RGBT234 attribute radar analysis are absent rather than simply relocated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests for its experimental results. V2 retains point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: V2 replaces the original XTrack results and adds B/L results: DepthTrack F-score is 59.7 in v1 versus 61.5/64.8; LasHeR precision is 65.5 versus 69.1/73.1; VisEvent precision is 75.6 versus 77.5/80.5. These are results under revised training/model settings, not controlled same-setting gains. Ablation results also change, new transfer/routing results appear, and some retained baseline values change, including DDiMP recall from 46.9 to 56.9.

M1.justification: V1 presents shallow X embedding and deep prompting of an RGB tracker; v2 Section 3.1/Figure 3 specifies bidirectional RGB/X transformer updates with MeME at attention and FFN stages. V2 also deliberately weakens classifier supervision to enable cross-modal expert use, contrasting with the near-exclusive modality assignment validated in v1 Appendix S.1. Shared experts, edge gating, and low-dimensional prompting remain.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work is reframed, an Overall Pipeline subsection is introduced, and experiments are reorganized from within/out-of-distribution sections into depth, thermal, and event sections. Ablations and discussion become a separate major section, and the appendix structure disappears.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column layout, redesigns the motivation and pipeline displays, regroups benchmark tables by modality, and adds training/routing tables and scene visualizations. Core expert diagrams are partly retained. V2 also introduces reporting problems: RGBT234 metric headings are reversed relative to retained baseline values, and Figure 2 labels as AUC values matching Table 6's precision results.

R1.justification: Research positioning substantially shifts from AGI-oriented unification to knowledge transfer across otherwise isolated modality-specific trackers and experts. V2 replaces much of the broad generalist/NLP context with tracking literature and adds works such as DropMAE and LLaMA-MoE. Its novelty argument now centers on cross-modal sharing rather than principally blind, single-parameter-set tracking.

T1.justification: V2 adds mathematical definitions of the coupled attention and FFN residual updates in Equations 1–2, extending v1's formal description of the pipeline. The routing, classification/balance losses, expert fusion, and prompting mathematics are otherwise largely retained with notation changes. Neither version contains theorem or proof contributions.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for cross-modal knowledge sharing: Table 6 directly tests training-modality combinations, Table 7 compares routing alternatives, and component ablations cover all three modalities. These address v1's largely indirect evidence for joint-training benefits, while expanded comparator coverage improves validation. The RGBT234 heading error, Figure 2 metric mismatch, and removal of parameter-count and attribute details weaken reporting, but the direct empirical tests provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe XTrack and its MeME framework. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison. V1's Appendix S.1–S.2 was inspected; the supplied v2 ends with references and contains no appendix.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark results for XTrack-B/L, expanded component ablations, multimodal training and zero-shot transfer experiments, and routing analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original tracking experiments on five benchmarks, component and expert-count ablations, and appendix analyses of routing and tracking attributes.

arxiv_record.abstract: In this paper, we introduce Part-Aware Point Grounded Description (PaPGD), a challenging task aimed at advancing 3D multimodal learning for fine-grained, part-aware segmentation grounding and detailed explanation of 3D objects. Existing 3D datasets largely focus on either vision-only part segmentation or vision-language scene segmentation, lacking the fine-grained multimodal segmentation needed for robotic navigation and interaction in real-world environments. To address this gap, we present the 3DCoMPaT Grounded Instructions (3DCoMPaT-GrIn) Dataset, a comprehensive resource that pairs rich point cloud descriptions with corresponding part-level segmentation masks. This dataset encompasses extensive samples designed for both PaPGD and fine-grained single-part grounding tasks. To tackle the inherent challenges of grounding objects and generating grounded descriptions at the part level, we propose Kestrel, a part-aware 3D multimodal large language model that integrates an advanced language model for nuanced language comprehension with multi-level point feature propagation and query refinement mechanism to enhance spatial reasoning at the part level. The extensive experiments demonstrate that Kestrel effectively bridges the gap between part-aware language understanding and 3D segmentation grounding, paving the way for more robust and interpretable 3D object comprehension that meets the demands of real-world robotic applications. Project page at https://feielysia.github.io/Kestrel.github.io/

Its central claims expand to reasoning segmentation, superiority over competing grounding systems and leading GPT-based compositional scores (abstract, introduction and conclusion).

C2.justification: V1 discusses model-size/LoRA effects and explicitly identifies richer attributes and extension beyond single objects as future work. V2 removes that limitations discussion, adds encoder/refinement/data-mixture explanations, and interprets new examples as evidence of domain-shift, multi-object and real-world generalization. These substantially broaden the applicability arguments.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands implementation and annotation documentation: Mask3D voxel size, point/query counts and pretraining source; segmentation dimensions and learning rates; GPT-4o prompts; response templates; and human-validation instructions/interface (Appendices A and E). Hardware and batch-size disclosures also change. Some details remain inconsistent, including four generation views in Section 3 versus eight in Appendix E.1.

E1.justification: Grounded captioning is retained as grounded description, but v2 adds functionality-based reasoning segmentation, PartNet-Mobility and RPSeg3D evaluation, and qualitative Objaverse, multi-object and ScanObjectNN scenarios. V1's separate material-mask and composition-mask grounding evaluations are not retained.

E2.justification: V1 mainly compares against PointLLM and PointLLM-SG. V2 retains PointLLM, drops PointLLM-SG, evaluates ShapeLLM, PARIS3D and an author-implemented SegPoint, and includes a revised Mask3D-based comparator (Tables 1–3). The added PartNet-Mobility comparison also includes PointNeXt, PartSLIP and PartSTAD.

E3.justification: The reported caption-annotation pipeline changes from InstructBLIP plus ChatGPT/GPT-4 to GPT-4o, and training uses a revised dataset mixture. Separate 3-/10-epoch, 7B/13B experiments become five-epoch 7B training. V2 adds GPT-based 3D-CALC, reports BLEU-4 instead of BLEU-1 in the main table, and introduces RPSeg3D adaptation and zero-/few-shot PartNet-Mobility protocols.

arxiv_record.abstract:
3D reconstruction and simulation, although interrelated, have distinct
objectives: reconstruction requires a flexible 3D representation that can adapt
to diverse scenes, while simulation needs a structured representation to model
motion principles effectively. This paper introduces the Mesh-adsorbed Gaussian
Splatting (MaGS) method to address this challenge. MaGS constrains 3D Gaussians
to roam near the mesh, creating a mutually adsorbed mesh-Gaussian 3D
representation. Such representation harnesses both the rendering flexibility of
3D Gaussians and the structured property of meshes. To achieve this, we
introduce RMD-Net, a network that learns motion priors from video data to
refine mesh deformations, alongside RGD-Net, which models the relative
displacement between the mesh and Gaussians to enhance rendering fidelity under
mesh constraints. To generalize to novel, user-defined deformations beyond
input video without reliance on temporal data, we propose MPE-Net, which
leverages inherent mesh information to bootstrap RMD-Net and RGD-Net. Due to
the universality of meshes, MaGS is compatible with various deformation priors
such as ARAP, SMPL, and soft physics simulation. Extensive experiments on the
D-NeRF, DG-Mesh, and PeopleSnapshot datasets demonstrate that MaGS achieves
state-of-the-art performance in both reconstruction and simulation.
arxiv_record.authors: Shaojie Ma, Yawei Luo, Wei Yang, Yi Yang
arxiv_record.title:
MaGS: Reconstructing and Simulating Dynamic 3D Objects with
  Mesh-adsorbed Gaussian Splatting
