arxiv_record.abstract: Autonomous Graphical User Interface (GUI) navigation agents can enhance user experience in communication, entertainment, and productivity by streamlining workflows and reducing manual intervention. However, prior GUI agents often trained with datasets comprising tasks that can be completed within a single app, leading to poor performance in cross-app navigation. To address this problem, we present GUIOdyssey, a comprehensive dataset for cross-app mobile GUI navigation. GUIOdyssey comprises 8,334 episodes with an average of 15.3 steps per episode, covering 6 mobile devices, 212 distinct apps, and 1,357 app combinations. Each step is enriched with detailed semantic reasoning annotations, which aid the model in building cognitive processes and enhancing its reasoning abilities for complex cross-app tasks. Building on GUIOdyssey, we develop OdysseyAgent, an exploratory multimodal agent for long-step cross-app navigation equipped with a history resampler module that efficiently attends to historical screenshot tokens, balancing performance and inference speed. Extensive experiments conducted in both in-domain and out-of-domain scenarios validate the effectiveness of our approach. Moreover, we demonstrate that historial information involving actions, screenshots and context in our dataset can significantly enhances OdysseyAgent's performance on complex cross-app tasks.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on the cross-app dataset, history-resampling agent, and numerical superiority over existing models. v2 makes semantic reasoning annotations and their benefits central contributions, emphasizes performance versus inference efficiency, and recasts the third contribution around comprehensive historical-information modeling. The original dataset-and-agent contribution remains, but its claimed scope substantially broadens.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking context abstraction to generalization, instruction-granularity gaps to insufficient planning and reasoning, and device-transfer failures to layout and resolution differences. It also removes v1 Appendix A's explicit limitations concerning simulated operations, Google-only devices, alternative valid action sequences, and offline evaluation. These are substantive interpretive additions and lost qualifications, not merely relocated discussion.

D1.justification: v2 documents GPT-4o annotation generation, sequential context construction, high-fidelity image inputs, generation prompts, expanded dataset fields, and semantic-QA training. It also supplies OmniParser evaluation prompts, device resolutions, token counts, and inference measurements; reported training cost changes from 24 to 32 A100 hours. Existing optimizer details are retained and moved to the supplement.

E1.justification: v2 adds step-level instruction following alongside episode-level navigation and introduces AndroidControl training and evaluation for transfer to single-app tasks (Sec. 10.5). GUIOdyssey's app inventory changes from 201 to 212 apps, while the six task categories and six devices remain. Direct AITW evaluation disappears, although AITW remains a training-data source.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds Claude3.5-Sonnet, SphAgent, and OmniParser-assisted comparators, replaces InternVL-1.5 with InternVL2-Pro, and removes GeminiProVision. Conversely, v2's out-of-domain Table 3 reports only OdysseyAgent variants, removing v1's Qwen-VL, GPT-4V, and GeminiProVision comparisons. The appendix also adds a direct multi-image comparator for the history resampler.

E3.justification: The random split changes from 75/25 to 80/20, the task split from 90/10 to approximately 6:1, and the device holdout from Pixel Fold to Pixel Tablet. Closed-model evaluation sampling changes from 500 instances to 200 episodes. v2 additionally accepts clicks within SAM2-derived target regions and introduces instruction-granularity, device-transfer, and controlled training-data-mixture protocols.

E4.justification: v2 expands the history ablation to include screenshots alone, contextual summaries, and combined inputs. It adds semantic-component ablations, resampler-versus-multi-image efficiency analysis, instruction-granularity transfer, six-device holdout analysis, and cross-app-to-single-app transfer. v1's history-length sensitivity, AITW-pretraining ablation, and direct single-app/cross-app difficulty experiment are removed rather than relocated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or run-to-run variability. The expanded experiments continue reporting point estimates; retained corpus-distribution plots do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Results are extensively revised and expanded. Table 2 reports OdysseyAgent AMS of 74.25 in v1 versus 75.79 for high-level instructions without semantic supervision in v2, and 78.24 with it. These are not same-setting gains because the corpus, splits, and scoring change. New results cover semantic supervision, efficiency, and AndroidControl transfer; the earlier pretraining, history-length, and AITW evaluation results disappear.

M1.justification: The Qwen-VL backbone, history resampler, and base action-prediction objective remain. However, v2 adds optional semantic-supervised training using screen descriptions, contextual summaries, and decision rationales as additional QA samples (Sec. 9.2), plus variants using contextual summaries as history inputs (Table 4). These substantially extend the training targets and input configurations beyond v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and method narrative are extensively rewritten. Detailed task descriptions and training settings move into a reorganized numbered supplement, while the main ablation narrative becomes focused on historical information. These changes substantially alter exposition and document structure beyond the accompanying scientific additions.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the collection pipeline to include fine-grained annotation, and restructures results tables around instruction levels and semantic supervision. Dataset statistics move into the main text and add AndroidControl. The existing triangle-task example is reformatted, while new annotation examples, an unsuccessful episode, SAM2 visualizations, and generation-prompt figures expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 substantially refocuses related work around coordinate-based versus accessibility-tree/Set-of-Marks agents and training datasets versus evaluation environments. It acknowledges earlier cross-app evaluations while retaining the cross-app dataset novelty claim. AndroidControl, AMEX, AndroidWorld, OSWorld, OmniParser, and other added works materially broaden the research positioning beyond v1's more general agent survey.

T1.justification: The formal episode definition and next-word prediction objective retain the same mathematical content. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs. The SAM2 addition changes empirical scoring, without introducing a mathematical derivation or formal property.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support and reproducibility. Table 7 directly tests the resampler's efficiency rationale, which v1 asserted without a corresponding comparison; Table 6 systematically tests semantic supervision, and the supplement documents how those annotations are generated and used. Broader baseline and transfer studies further improve assessment of applicability. Removing explicit limitations and out-of-domain baseline comparisons weakens balance, but the gains in controlled evidence and technical transparency outweigh these losses. This judgment does not rely on incomparable headline-score increases.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GUIOdyssey and OdysseyAgent. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material that was renamed, reformatted, or relocated.

after.justification: v2 reports original navigation evaluations and experiments on semantic supervision, inference efficiency, instruction granularity, device generalization, and transfer to AndroidControl.

arxiv_record.abstract: Although deep neural networks are well-known for their outstanding performance in tackling complex tasks, their hunger for computational resources remains a significant hurdle, posing energy-consumption issues and restricting their deployment on resource-constrained devices, preventing their widespread adoption. In this paper, we present an optimal transport-based method to reduce the depth of over-parametrized deep neural networks, alleviating their computational burden. More specifically, we propose a new regularization strategy based on the Max-Sliced Wasserstein distance to minimize the distance between the intermediate feature distributions in the neural network. We show that minimizing this distance enables the complete removal of intermediate layers in the network, achieving better performance/depth trade-off compared to existing techniques. We assess the effectiveness of our method on traditional image classification setups and extend it to generative image models. Our code is available at https://github.com/VGCQ/LaCoOT.
arxiv_record.authors: Victor Qu\'etu, Zhu Liao, Nour Hezbri, Fabio Pizzati, Enzo Tartaglione
arxiv_record.title: LaCoOT: Layer Collapse through Optimal Transport

C2.justification: V2 replaces the blanket dimensionality restriction and proposed zero-padding exploration with a tested workaround and future Gromov-Wasserstein direction. Appendix I also discusses SWD's empirical advantage despite the stated theoretical preference for MSWD.

D1.justification: V1 promises public code upon acceptance; v2 supplies a repository link. V2 documents sorting/backpropagation behavior, the unseeded MSWD default, timing hardware and detailed DiT training/sampling settings, including AdamW, batch size 60, EMA and three L40S GPUs. These substantially expand reproducibility information while retaining the shared classifier settings.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates classification only. V2 retains the seven classification datasets and adds ImageNet image generation using DiT-XL/2 (Section 5.2.2 and Appendices E/J). Although ImageNet already supplied classification pretraining weights, generating images is a substantially different evaluated task.

E2.justification: Layer Folding, EGP, NEPENTHE and EASIER are retained, while IMP disappears from the ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 comparison. V2 adds comparisons against networks trained from scratch at reduced depths (Appendix H) and SWD, l1, l2, MMD and KL regularizers (Appendix I), substantially expanding the comparator types.

E3.justification: V2 adds critical-path-length, latency and training-time evaluations alongside accuracy/MACs. Its new DiT protocol uses 5,000 finetuning steps and FID on 50,000 generated 256×256 images with 250 sampling steps and guidance 1.5. New analyses examine block distances versus performance, mismatched dimensions, critical path versus resource consumption, training shallow networks from scratch, post-pruning retraining, projection seeding/count, batch size and alternative discrepancy metrics. Appendix E also analyzes generated-image failures.

Conversely, the detailed ResNet-18/MobileNetv2 result grids for the five other classification datasets are absent. These are additions and removals, not demonstrated version-to-version performance gains.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) and Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated outstanding performance in various general multimodal applications and have shown increasing promise in specialized domains. However, their potential in the insurance domain-characterized by diverse application scenarios and rich multimodal data-remains largely underexplored. To date, there is no systematic review of multimodal tasks, nor a benchmark specifically designed to assess the capabilities of LVLMs in insurance. This gap hinders the development of LVLMs within the insurance industry. This study systematically reviews and categorizes multimodal tasks for 4 representative types of insurance: auto, property, health, and agricultural. We introduce INS-MMBench, the first hierarchical benchmark tailored for the insurance domain. INS-MMBench encompasses 22 fundamental tasks, 12 meta-tasks and 5 scenario tasks, enabling a comprehensive and progressive assessment from basic capabilities to real-world use cases. We benchmark 11 leading LVLMs, including closed-source models such as GPT-4o and open-source models like LLaVA. Our evaluation validates the effectiveness of INS-MMBench and offers detailed insights into the strengths and limitations of current LVLMs on a variety of insurance-related multimodal tasks. We hope that INS-MMBench will accelerate the integration of LVLMs into the insurance industry and foster interdisciplinary research. Our dataset and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/FDU-INS/INS-MMBench.

native_poster_event.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have demonstrated outstanding performance in various general multimodal applications and have shown promising potential in specialized domains. However, the application potential of LVLMs in the insurance domain—characterized by rich application scenarios and abundant multimodal data—has not been effectively explored. There is no systematic review of multimodal tasks in the insurance domain, nor a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate the capabilities of LVLMs in insurance. This gap hinders the development of LVLMs within the insurance domain. In this paper, we systematically review and distill multimodal tasks for 4 representative types of insurance: auto insurance, property insurance, health insurance, and agricultural insurance. We propose INS-MMBench, the first hierarchical LVLMs benchmark tailored for the insurance domain. INS-MMBench encompasses 22 fundamental tasks, 12 meta-tasks and 5 scenario tasks—enabling a comprehensive and progressive assessment from basic tasks to real-world insurance scenarios. Furthermore, we evaluate multiple representative LVLMs, including closed-source models such as GPT-4o and open-source models like LLaVA. Our evaluation not only validates the effectiveness of our benchmark but also provides an in-depth performance analysis of current LVLMs on various multimodal tasks in the insurance domain. We hope that INS-MMBench will facilitate the further application of LVLMs in the insurance domain and inspire interdisciplinary development. A sample dataset and evaluation code are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/INS-MMBench-Anonymize. The full dataset will be released after the review process.

C1.justification: The central contribution expands from a 2.2K-question benchmark of fundamental capabilities to a three-level benchmark with 10,372 questions and integrated insurance scenarios. The abstract and introduction now claim assessment from basic perception through real-world decision tasks, and add headline findings about human comparisons, multi-step reasoning limitations, and prompt mitigation.

C2.justification: v2 interprets scenario failures as limits on multi-step reasoning and recommends restricting near-term deployment to reliable fundamental tasks. It adds explanations of conflicting-prompt failures and distractor-generator bias, alongside proposals involving reasoning datasets, reinforcement learning, and RAG. The public-data mismatch limitation remains, while v1's fundamental-task-only limitation is replaced by discussion of the expanded evaluation.

D1.justification: v2 documents CSV records containing image paths, accompanying text and labels, expert-guided scenario reference answers, and a structured health-underwriting prompt in Figure 3. Conversely, removing Appendix A eliminates the systematic collection of task-specific prompts, options, correct answers, and responses. v1's explicit assurance of balanced correct-option positions also disappears. The dataset/code access statement remains unchanged.

E1.justification: The original four insurance categories and 22 fundamental tasks remain. v2 additionally evaluates five scenarios covering auto claims, accident liability, property risk management, health underwriting, and agricultural claims. These introduce multi-image and image-plus-document reasoning and insurance decisions, using DADA, Fast Furious and Insured, xBD, IU-XRay, and Precision viticulture data.

E2.justification: The main evaluation removes GeminiProVision, Claude3V_Sonnet, and BLIP-2, and adds Gemini 1.5 Flash, GPT-4o-mini, GLM4V-Plus-0111, and Qwen-2.5-VL-32B. A human baseline replaces the displayed random-guess baseline. These are substantive comparator changes, not merely renamed models.

E3.justification: v1 uses 100 examples per fundamental task; v2 uses varying counts up to 500 and specifies stratified sampling for tasks with fewer than 10 labels. Answer extraction changes from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4o. v2 adds selection of three models for scenario evaluation, stepwise regex and numerical-deviation scoring, a six-person human study on 220 questions, and separate prompt and distractor experimental protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled prompt-enhancement experiments across three tasks and five models, plus a 1,500-question ablation comparing GPT-4o-, Claude 3.5 Haiku-, and DeepSeek-V3-generated distractors. The four-category error analysis remains, with Gemini 1.5 Flash replacing GeminiProVision. Conversely, v1's complete collection of qualitative task cases and model responses in Appendix A is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests. The new human participant count and experimental sample sizes describe evaluation design, not added uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The main accuracy tables are extensively revised: GPT-4o remains first, but its reported overall score changes from 72.91 in v1 Table 2 to 69.70 in v2 Table 4 under revised sampling and scoring. This is not a same-setting performance decline. v2 adds human, scenario, prompt, and distractor results, including GPT-4o's 9.26% responsible-party identification accuracy in Table 5; Appendix A's individual response results disappear.

M1.justification: v2 Section 4.3 introduces inference-time augmentation of prompts with insurance knowledge, whereas v1 only analyzes errors. This is a limited procedural adaptation; no new model architecture or training objective is introduced.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, benchmark-construction description, results discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around the three-level task hierarchy and two-stage evaluation. Sections are renamed and reorganized, error analysis gains mitigation discussion, an ablation section is introduced, and Appendix A is removed.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws Figures 1–3 with a task pyramid and scenario components, expands the dataset table, and adds comparison, scenario, prompt, and ablation tables. v1's radar chart and Appendix Figures 6–27 are removed. The error-distribution chart is retained as a reformatted Figure 4.

R1.justification: The literature categories and insurance-benchmark gap argument largely remain. v2 adds Table 1 comparing six existing benchmarks, including potential data overlap, and references for the five scenario datasets. This extends contextual positioning without substantially replacing the related-work framework.

T1.justification: Neither version presents mathematical propositions, proofs, or substantive formal derivations. The expanded task hierarchy and stepwise evaluation descriptions are operational definitions rather than new mathematical theory.

improvement.justification: The five scenario evaluations substantially address v1's acknowledged limitation to isolated fundamental tasks by testing integrated insurance workflows and their intermediate and final decisions. Human references and prompt/distractor experiments add useful diagnostic evidence. Removing Appendix A reduces transparency, and Table 7 contains 5.6-point drops despite the 'within 5%' summary. These reporting weaknesses temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial improvement in application-level evaluation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe INS-MMBench, with matchable tasks, datasets, and evaluation sections. The material is readable, including v1's Appendix A. The supplied v2 ends with references and contains no appendix.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of 11 LVLMs, a human baseline, scenario-task results, prompt-mitigation experiments, and distractor-generation ablations in Tables 3–7.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 10 LVLMs in Tables 2–3, error analysis in Figure 5, and model-response examples in Appendix A.

arxiv_record.abstract: World models allow autonomous agents to plan and explore by predicting the visual outcomes of different actions. However, for robot manipulation, it is challenging to accurately model the fine-grained robot-object interaction within the visual space using existing methods which overlooks precise alignment between each action and the corresponding frame. In this paper, we present IRASim, a novel world model capable of generating videos with fine-grained robot-object interaction details, conditioned on historical observations and robot action trajectories. We train a diffusion transformer and introduce a novel frame-level action-conditioning module within each transformer block to explicitly model and strengthen the action-frame alignment. Extensive experiments show that: (1) the quality of the videos generated by our method surpasses all the baseline methods and scales effectively with increased model size and computation; (2) policy evaluations using IRASim exhibit a strong correlation with those using the ground-truth simulator, highlighting its potential to accelerate real-world policy evaluation; (3) testing-time scaling through model-based planning with IRASim significantly enhances policy performance, as evidenced by an improvement in the IoU metric on the Push-T benchmark from 0.637 to 0.961; (4) IRASim provides flexible action controllability, allowing virtual robotic arms in datasets to be controlled via a keyboard or VR controller.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. P2.justification: v2 adopts a redesigned template with institutional logos, a boxed abstract, colored headings, and revised table/caption styling. R1.justification: Related work is substantially refocused toward world-model planning and policy evaluation. v2 adds positioning around works such as Cosmos, Genie 2, FLIP, VLMPC, and GPC, expands its treatment of iVideoGPT, and removes several physical-simulator and DAgger references alongside the earlier 7-DoF priority claim.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses a central gap in v1: the proposed usefulness of generated rollouts for evaluating and improving policies was largely untested. The new evidence remains limited by narrow task coverage and absent uncertainty intervals.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe IRASim, with matching core architecture and original experiments despite the changed title and expanded scope. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison.

arxiv_record.abstract: Recent advancements in video diffusion models enable the generation of photorealistic videos with impressive 3D consistency and temporal coherence. However, the extent to which these AI-generated videos simulate the 3D visual world remains underexplored. In this paper, we introduce Learned 3D Evaluation (L3DE), an objective, quantifiable, and interpretable method for assessing AI-generated videos' ability to simulate the real world in terms of 3D visual qualities and consistencies, without requiring manually labeled defects or quality annotations. Instead of relying on 3D reconstruction, which is prone to failure with in-the-wild videos, L3DE employs a 3D convolutional network, trained on monocular 3D cues of motion, depth, and appearance, to distinguish real from synthetic videos. Confidence scores from L3DE quantify the gap between real and synthetic videos in terms of 3D visual coherence, while a gradient-based visualization pinpoints unrealistic regions, improving interpretability. We validate L3DE through extensive experiments, demonstrating strong alignment with 3D reconstruction quality and human judgments. Our evaluations on leading generative models (e.g., Kling, Sora, and MiniMax) reveal persistent simulation gaps and subtle inconsistencies. Beyond generative video assessment, L3DE extends to broader applications: benchmarking video generation models, serving as a deepfake detector, and enhancing video synthesis by inpainting flagged inconsistencies. Project page: https://justin-crchang.github.io/l3de-project-page/

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from detecting generated videos and explaining transferable artifacts to providing an interpretable, quantitative measure of 3D visual coherence. v2 adds core claims of alignment with reconstruction quality and human judgment, generator benchmarking, and synthesis refinement. Fake-video detection becomes a downstream application rather than the principal objective.

C2.justification: v2 interprets classifier confidence as a coherence measure and fusion as capturing more complex inconsistencies. It adds substantive qualifications concerning reconstruction-selection constraints, training-data diversity, and the distinction between visual coherence and comprehensive physical simulation (Appendices M–N). v1 primarily discusses future-generator generalization and limited video length; the latter limitation remains.

D1.justification: v2 supplies substantially fuller reproducibility information: scene-cut processing, cropping and resizing instructions, specific feature-extractor variants, network layers and channel counts, and participant screening and rating rubrics (Appendices I–K; Figure A10). Hardware assignments also change: v1 trains classifiers on 4090 GPUs, whereas v2 reports A100 training and 4090 reconstruction. These disclosures go well beyond v1's brief implementation paragraph.

E1.justification: The Pexels/SVD training sources remain, but evaluation expands substantially. v1 evaluates Sora, Pika, and Runway-Gen2 against real videos including Pixabay. v2 evaluates newer generator coverage including Kling, MiniMax, Vidu, Luma, CogVideoX, and Runway-Gen3, and adds static/dynamic reconstruction datasets, ECTV quality evaluation, and video refinement. Pika, Runway-Gen2, and Pixabay are absent from the revised evaluations.

E2.justification: CNNDetection and DIRE remain detection comparators, with NPR added in Table A6. The new quality-evaluation comparisons actually evaluate selected VBench metrics and EvalCrafter against L3DE (Table 4), with another EvalCrafter comparison on ECTV (Table A9). This substantially broadens the comparison methods beyond v1's two image detectors.

E3.justification: Training grows from 6,946 real and 6,946 synthetic videos to 80,000 of each. v2 introduces matched-prompt generator evaluation, reconstruction protocols using 3D-GS/SC-GS and PSNR, selection for successful pose estimation, and human studies including 15 participants rating 300 videos. Accuracy is supplemented by reconstruction and human-agreement metrics. The stated learning rate and batch size remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 replaces the original pairwise modality-ensemble ablation with contrastive-loss and addition-versus-concatenation experiments (Table A8). It adds controlled training-diversity analyses for motion and indoor/outdoor scenes (Table A7), quantitative validation of localized artifacts against reconstruction errors and human annotations, and refinement examples. Some qualitative failure motifs recur, but the analytical evidence expands substantially.

E5.justification: Beyond v1's accuracy summaries, v2 introduces Spearman rank-correlation estimation for agreement with reconstruction quality, human ratings, and annotated regions (Tables 2–4; Figure 5). This adds statistical association analysis, but neither version reports training-seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 replaces the original detection results and adds extensive validation, ablation, and generator-ranking results. New findings include fusion correlations of 0.7566 with reconstruction quality (Table 2) and 0.6484 with human ratings (Figure 5). Sora detection is reported as 81.33% in v1 Table 3 and 56.31% in v2 Table A6, but changed methods, training data, and test sets prevent interpreting this as a same-setting decline.

M1.justification: v1 combines separately trained classifiers through weighted logit ensembling. v2 introduces a nearest-real-feature contrastive loss and a learned fusion network that concatenates modality features before further convolutional processing (Section 4.2; Appendix J). Appendix H.2 also introduces artifact refinement using localized masks and multiview inpainting. These are procedural changes beyond renaming the framework L3DE.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around L3DE. Data curation, method design, validation, and applications become distinct main sections, while detection, implementation details, and limitations are organized in the supplement. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column presentation to a two-column layout with a new opening overview, reconstruction panels, correlation plots, expanded tables, and detailed architecture diagrams. Qualitative examples are reorganized into reference-frame, artifact-region, and Grad-CAM comparisons in the supplement. Some imagery recurs, but the displays and overall layout are extensively redesigned.

R1.justification: The research positioning shifts from generated-image detection toward video-quality assessment and 3D reconstruction. v2 adds substantive discussion and citations for EvalCrafter, NeRF/Gaussian-splatting reconstruction, and newer generators, while removing the main related-work subsection devoted to generated-image detection. Retained detector citations still support the supplementary detection comparison.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Accurate camera motion estimation is essential for recovering global human
motion in world coordinates from RGB video inputs. SLAM is widely used for
estimating camera trajectory and point cloud, but monocular SLAM does so only
up to an unknown scale factor. Previous works estimate the scale factor through
optimization, but this is unreliable and time-consuming. This paper presents an
optimization-free scale calibration framework, Human as Checkerboard (HAC). HAC
innovatively leverages the human body predicted by human mesh recovery model as
a calibration reference. Specifically, it uses the absolute depth of
human-scene contact joints as references to calibrate the corresponding
relative scene depth from SLAM. HAC benefits from geometric priors encoded in
human mesh recovery models to estimate the SLAM scale and achieves precise
global human motion estimation. Simple yet powerful, our method sets a new
state-of-the-art performance for global human mesh estimation tasks, reducing
motion errors by 50% over prior local-to-global methods while using 100$\times$
less inference time than optimization-based methods. Project page:
https://martayang.github.io/HAC.

While SLAM is widely used for estimating camera trajectory and point cloud, monocular SLAM does so only up to an unknown scale factor. Specifically, it innovatively uses the absolute depth of human-scene contact joints as references to calibrate the corresponding relative scene depth from SLAM. Simple yet powerful, our method sets a new state-of-the-art performance for global human mesh estimation tasks. It reduces motion errors by 50\% over prior local-to-global methods while using 100$\times$ less post-SLAM inference time than optimization-based methods. Our code will be made public.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Diffusion models have emerged as the de facto choice for generating
high-quality visual signals across various domains. However, training a single
model to predict noise across various levels poses significant challenges,
necessitating numerous iterations and incurring significant computational
costs. Various approaches, such as loss weighting strategy design and
architectural refinements, have been introduced to expedite convergence and
improve model performance. In this study, we propose a novel approach to design
the noise schedule for enhancing the training of diffusion models. Our key
insight is that the importance sampling of the logarithm of the Signal-to-Noise
ratio ($\log \text{SNR}$), theoretically equivalent to a modified noise
schedule, is particularly beneficial for training efficiency when increasing
the sample frequency around $\log \text{SNR}=0$. This strategic sampling allows
the model to focus on the critical transition point between signal dominance
and noise dominance, potentially leading to more robust and accurate
predictions.We empirically demonstrate the superiority of our noise schedule
over the standard cosine schedule.Furthermore, we highlight the advantages of
our noise schedule design on the ImageNet benchmark, showing that the designed
schedule consistently benefits different prediction targets. Our findings
contribute to the ongoing efforts to optimize diffusion models, potentially
paving the way for more efficient and effective training paradigms in the field
of generative AI.

arxiv_record.title: Improved Noise Schedule for Diffusion Training

snapshot_arxiv_record.abstract:
Diffusion models have emerged as the de facto choice for generating
high-quality visual signals across various domains. However, training a single
model to predict noise across various levels poses significant challenges,
necessitating numerous iterations and incurring significant computational
costs. Various approaches, such as loss weighting strategy design and
architectural refinements, have been introduced to expedite convergence and
improve model performance. In this study, we propose a novel approach to design
the noise schedule for enhancing the training of diffusion models. Our key
insight is that the importance sampling of the logarithm of the Signal-to-Noise
ratio ($\log \text{SNR}$), theoretically equivalent to a modified noise
schedule, is particularly beneficial for training efficiency when increasing
the sample frequency around $\log \text{SNR}=0$. This strategic sampling allows
the model to focus on the critical transition point between signal dominance
and noise dominance, potentially leading to more robust and accurate
predictions.We empirically demonstrate the superiority of our noise schedule
over the standard cosine schedule.Furthermore, we highlight the advantages of
our noise schedule design on the ImageNet benchmark, showing that the designed
schedule consistently benefits different prediction targets. Our findings
contribute to the ongoing efforts to optimize diffusion models, potentially
paving the way for more efficient and effective training paradigms in the field
of generative AI.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims: noise scheduling corresponds to importance sampling, concentrating computation near log SNR = 0 improves training efficiency, and Laplace benefits ImageNet generation across prediction targets. The new contribution list makes existing claims explicit without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 adds the interpretation that concentration around intermediate noise levels matters more than the precise schedule family, connects logit-normal flow sampling to this principle, and discusses generalization across conditioning regimes. It also explicitly limits the study's objective to fixed-budget efficiency rather than XL-scale or state-of-the-art performance.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies patch size, conditioning details, continuous implementation and γ = 5 for the weighting baselines. It also supplies CelebA architecture and CC12M preprocessing, CLIP-conditioning and training details. The Laplace code is unchanged; the earlier Appendix B sampling instructions are relocated into Section 2.4.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates class-conditional ImageNet generation at two resolutions. v2 additionally evaluates unconditional face generation on CelebA in 64×64 pixel space and text-conditioned generation on CC12M at 256×256, substantially broadening domains, conditioning requirements and data representations.

E2.justification: The comparator membership in Table 3 remains unchanged. New appendix comparisons introduce Cosine-Ply against Laplace and evaluate Cosine-Ply as a loss weight alongside the retained weighting baselines. Logit-normal flow matching receives analytical discussion, not a newly reported empirical baseline evaluation.

E3.justification: Appendix A.5 adds a distinct protocol: train for one million iterations, fine-tune separately within four timestep bins for 140,000 iterations, and selectively substitute checkpoints during inference. A.7 adds a specified CelebA model configuration and a 200,000-iteration CC12M setup. The original ImageNet evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled tests of which timestep intervals benefit from fine-tuning, a direct comparison of the same sampling distribution used as scheduling versus loss weighting, and matched-initial-noise visual case studies across training checkpoints. These substantially extend v1's prediction-target, resolution and schedule-parameter analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, empirical variability or statistical significance tests. The distributional mean and variance derived in A.4 are theoretical properties, not experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 3–7 are numerically unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results. Table 9 reports FID-10K of 7.98 for Cosine-Ply versus 8.88 as a loss weight. New Laplace-versus-cosine results include 6.58359 versus 7.93795 on CelebA at 150,000 iterations and 54.3492 versus 58.3619 on CC12M at 200,000 iterations. Additional convergence, interval and visual findings are also reported.

M1.justification: Appendix A.3 introduces Cosine-Ply, which applies a polynomial timestep-sampling transformation before the cosine schedule; A.6 also evaluates its loss-weighting variant. These extend the existing scheduling framework. The original Laplace implementation remains identical.

P1.justification: The introduction and method explanation undergo extensive rewriting, including an explicit contribution list and expanded probability-based narrative. The ablation discussion is expanded, sampling instructions move into the main text, and the appendix is reorganized into eight subsections. These changes exceed simple renumbering or insertion of results.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 8–11 and Figures 4–8, including density plots, interval comparisons, weighting curves and generated-image grids. Figure 2 expands from one convergence panel to two, Figure 3's legend is rearranged, and Table 1 is reformatted. The visual presentation changes substantially despite retained main-table values.

R1.justification: v2 expands background citations and discussion, including Ernie-ViLG 2.0, additional video/3D diffusion work, and Movie Gen in the logit-normal analysis. It elaborates connections to MM-DiT, HDiT and prior noise schedules while retaining the same central research positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 newly defines the normalized polynomial timestep distribution, its sampling transformation and its induced log-SNR density. A.4 derives that logit-normal timestep sampling in flow matching induces a normal log-SNR distribution with mean -2µ and variance 4σ². These extend the mathematical analysis beyond the retained scheduling identities.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's reliance on ImageNet and indirect comparisons between sampling and weighting. The new CelebA/CC12M evaluations and controlled interval and sampling-versus-weighting tests strengthen generalizability and support for the central argument. Added derivations and implementation disclosures improve assessability. Repeated-run uncertainty remains absent, and Table 8 inconsistently labels the Laplace parameter in its caption, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same noise-scheduling research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original timestep-interval tests, sampling-versus-weighting comparisons, CelebA and CC12M results, and generated-image comparisons.

arxiv_record.abstract: Monocular dynamic reconstruction is a challenging and long-standing vision problem due to the highly ill-posed nature of the task. Existing approaches depend on templates, are effective only in quasi-static scenes, or fail to model 3D motion explicitly. We introduce a method for reconstructing generic dynamic scenes, featuring explicit, persistent 3D motion trajectories in the world coordinate frame, from casually captured monocular videos. We tackle the problem with two key insights: First, we exploit the low-dimensional structure of 3D motion by representing scene motion with a compact set of SE(3) motion bases. Each point's motion is expressed as a linear combination of these bases, facilitating soft decomposition of the scene into multiple rigidly-moving groups. Second, we take advantage of off-the-shelf data-driven priors such as monocular depth maps and long-range 2D tracks, and devise a method to effectively consolidate these noisy supervisory signals, resulting in a globally consistent representation of the dynamic scene. Experiments show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance for both long-range 3D/2D motion estimation and novel view synthesis on dynamic scenes. Project Page: https://shape-of-motion.github.io/

C1.justification: Both versions claim joint persistent 3D tracking and novel-view synthesis through compact SE(3) motion bases and consolidation of learned priors, with state-of-the-art performance. v2 emphasizes world-coordinate trajectories, but that capability was already specified in v1. The main contribution scope is retained.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 adds a three-part explanation of gains over TAPIR+DA involving shared motion, acceleration regularization and persistent geometry. The limitations discussion broadens dependence on external predictions to geometry and motion and discusses newer alternatives. However, v1's explicit inability to handle large viewpoint changes is omitted without evidence that it was resolved.

D1.justification: New appendices substantially document preprocessing, track sampling and filtering, learning rates, loss weights, batching, regularization, metric-scale alignment and the DynMF implementation. These mostly expand documentation of the retained pipeline. A reproducibility inconsistency remains: v2's main text specifies 1000 initialization iterations, whereas Appendix B.1 specifies 2000 steps.

E1.justification: Alongside the retained iPhone and Kubric evaluations, v2 adds novel-view synthesis on seven NVIDIA scenes captured from a static training camera. Appendix E also adds a qualitative multi-object DAVIS school-girl example. This materially broadens the evaluated data and capture conditions.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds DynMF, DELTA (world), and SpatialTracker (world) to the iPhone comparison while retaining the previous comparators. New Table 3 evaluates Dynamic Gaussian Marbles on NVIDIA. DynMF and Dynamic Gaussian Marbles were already cited in v1 but were not evaluated there.

E3.justification: The stated motion-basis count changes from 20 to 10. The new NVIDIA protocol trains on camera 4 and evaluates cameras 3, 5 and 6 at half resolution using covisibility masks (Appendix F). Added frame-space tracking baselines are transformed into world coordinates. These introduce substantive experimental settings; retained numerical results do not establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a Per-Gaussian SE(3) ablation to isolate the contribution of shared motion bases, alongside the 2DGS variant comparison and a qualitative DAVIS case study. Existing ablations remain. The Kubric PCA visualization is relocated to Appendix D, not newly added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. TAPIR uncertainty scores used during optimization concern input confidence, not statistical uncertainty of the reported experimental results.

E6.justification: Original iPhone, Kubric and retained ablation scores are unchanged, but v2 adds substantial result entries. Its 2DGS variant reports EPE 0.097 versus 0.082 for the original model, while LPIPS improves from 0.45 to 0.40. NVIDIA mean PSNR is 23.37 for Ours versus 23.46 for DGM. Reported rendering speed changes from approximately 40 to 140 FPS, without sufficient timing details to establish a controlled speedup.

M1.justification: The shared SE(3) motion-basis representation and trajectory rendering remain. v2 adds an optional 2DGS variant with monocular-normal supervision (Appendix B.2), and introduces MegaSaM initialization followed by joint camera-pose refinement for in-the-wild videos (Section 3.3). These extend the retained reconstruction method.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the method exposition remain. v2 selectively condenses and rewrites the abstract, introduction, baseline descriptions and discussion, makes world-coordinate terminology more explicit, updates authors and affiliations, and organizes additional documentation into appendices.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout, with widespread resizing and repositioning of figures and tables. Figure 1 moves onto the title page, Figure 6 moves to the appendix, Table 1 and the ablation table gain rows, and a NVIDIA results table and DAVIS Figure 7 are added.

R1.justification: v2 substantially updates positioning through classical low-rank reconstruction and newer learned reconstruction and tracking work, including DELTA, SpatialTracker, DUSt3R and MonST3R. It replaces v1's absence-of-generic-3D-trackers rationale with a distinction between frame-space and world-space trajectories, and discusses newer joint reconstruction/tracking and motion-segmentation approaches.

T1.justification: Equation 7 changes the mask-loss target from constant 1 to the input mask M, correcting the formal objective to match the stated supervision. Appendix B.2 introduces normal-supervision loss definitions for the 2DGS variant. No new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens reproducibility and empirical assessment through detailed appendices, relevant additional competitors, a direct shared-basis ablation and a distinct static-camera evaluation. The new results expose useful performance tradeoffs while retaining the original evidence. The conflicting initialization budgets and removal of the large-viewpoint limitation temper these gains, but the improved methodological transparency and stronger comparisons provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Shape of Motion and retain matching methods, experiments and visualizations. The complete text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 additionally includes Appendices A-G.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds NVIDIA results, additional comparator and model-variant results, an ablation, and a DAVIS visualization.

before.justification: v1 reports original iPhone tracking and view-synthesis experiments, Kubric tracking results, and component ablations in Tables 1-3.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Recent efforts in video reasoning segmentation (VRS) integrate large language
models (LLMs) with perception models to localize and track objects via textual
instructions, achieving barely satisfactory results in simple scenarios.
However, they struggled to discriminate and deduce the objects from user
queries in more real-world scenes featured by long durations, multiple objects,
rapid motion, and heavy occlusions. In this work, we analyze the underlying
causes of these limitations, and present ViLLa: Video reasoning segmentation
with Large Language Model. Remarkably, our ViLLa manages to tackle these
challenges through multiple core innovations: (1) a context synthesizer that
dynamically encodes the user intent with video contexts for accurate reasoning,
resolving ambiguities in complex queries, and (2) a hierarchical temporal
synchronizer that disentangles multi-object interactions across complex
temporal scenarios by modelling multi-object interactions at local and global
temporal scales. To enable efficient processing of long videos, ViLLa
incorporates (3) a key segment sampler that adaptively partitions long videos
into shorter but semantically dense segments for less redundancy. What's more,
to promote research in this unexplored area, we construct a VRS benchmark,
VideoReasonSeg, featuring different complex scenarios. Our model also exhibits
impressive state-of-the-art results on VideoReasonSeg, Ref-YouTube-VOS,
Ref-DAVIS17, MeViS, and ReVOS. Both quantitative and qualitative experiments
demonstrate that our method effectively enhances video reasoning segmentation
capabilities for multimodal LLMs. The code and dataset will be available at
https://github.com/rkzheng99/ViLLa.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Event cameras have shown promise in vision applications like optical flow
estimation and stereo matching, with many specialized architectures leveraging
the asynchronous and sparse nature of event data. However, existing works only
focus event data within the confines of task-specific domains, overlooking how
tasks across the temporal and spatial domains can reinforce each other. In this
paper, we reformulate event-based flow estimation and stereo matching as a
unified dense correspondence matching problem, enabling us to solve both tasks
within a single model by directly matching features in a shared representation
space. Specifically, our method utilizes a Temporal Recurrent Network to
aggregate event features across temporal or spatial domains, and a Spatial
Contextual Attention to enhance knowledge transfer across event flows via
temporal or spatial interactions. By utilizing a shared feature similarities
module that integrates knowledge from event streams via temporal or spatial
interactions, our network performs optical flow estimation from temporal event
segment inputs and stereo matching from spatial event segment inputs
simultaneously. We demonstrate that our unified model inherently supports
multi-task fusion and cross-task transfer. Without the need for retraining for
specific task, our model can effectively handle both optical flow and stereo
estimation, achieving state-of-the-art performance on both tasks.

However, existing works only focus event data within the confines of task-specific domains, overlooking the correlations between tasks across the temporal and spatial domains. In this paper, we propose a novel matching-based framework for event cameras to estimate flow and disparity simultaneously in a shared representation space, reformulating them as a unified pixel-wise correspondence matching problem. Specifically, our method utilizes a Temporal Recurrent Network to aggregate asynchronous event features across temporal or spatial domains, and a Spatial Contextual Attention to enhance knowledge transfer across event flows via temporal or spatial interactions. By utilizing a shared pixel-wise feature similarities module, our network performs optical flow estimation from temporal event segments and stereo matching from spatial event segments simultaneously. Our unified model inherently supports multi-task unification and cross-task transfer, which facilitate training and streamline deployment. Without the need for retraining on specific tasks, our model can effectively handle both event-based flow and stereo estimation, achieving state-of-the-art performance on both tasks. Our code will be released upon acceptance.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Unsupervised 3D object detection aims to identify objects of interest from
unlabeled raw data, such as LiDAR points. Recent approaches usually adopt
pseudo 3D bounding boxes (3D bboxes) from clustering algorithm to initialize
the model training. However, pseudo bboxes inevitably contain noise, and such
inaccuracies accumulate to the final model, compromising the performance.
Therefore, in an attempt to mitigate the negative impact of inaccurate pseudo
bboxes, we introduce a new uncertainty-aware framework for unsupervised 3D
object detection, dubbed UA3D. In particular, our method consists of two
phases: uncertainty estimation and uncertainty regularization. (1) In the
uncertainty estimation phase, we incorporate an extra auxiliary detection
branch alongside the original primary detector. The prediction disparity
between the primary and auxiliary detectors could reflect fine-grained
uncertainty at the box coordinate level. (2) Based on the assessed uncertainty,
we adaptively adjust the weight of every 3D bbox coordinate via uncertainty
regularization, refining the training process on pseudo bboxes. For pseudo bbox
coordinate with high uncertainty, we assign a relatively low loss weight.
Extensive experiments verify that the proposed method is robust against the
noisy pseudo bboxes, yielding substantial improvements on nuScenes and Lyft
compared to existing approaches, with increases of +6.9% AP$_{BEV}$ and +2.5%
AP$_{3D}$ on nuScenes, and +4.1% AP$_{BEV}$ and +2.0% AP$_{3D}$ on Lyft.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Meshes are the de facto 3D representation in the industry but are
labor-intensive to produce. Recently, a line of research has focused on
autoregressively generating meshes. This approach processes meshes into a
sequence composed of vertices and then generates them vertex by vertex, similar
to how a language model generates text. These methods have achieved some
success but still struggle to generate complex meshes. One primary reason for
this limitation is their inefficient tokenization methods. To address this
issue, we introduce MeshAnything V2, an advanced mesh generation model designed
to create Artist-Created Meshes that align precisely with specified shapes. A
key innovation behind MeshAnything V2 is our novel Adjacent Mesh Tokenization
(AMT) method. Unlike traditional approaches that represent each face using
three vertices, AMT optimizes this by employing a single vertex wherever
feasible, effectively reducing the token sequence length by about half on
average. This not only streamlines the tokenization process but also results in
more compact and well-structured sequences, enhancing the efficiency of mesh
generation. With these improvements, MeshAnything V2 effectively doubles the
face limit compared to previous models, delivering superior performance without
increasing computational costs. We will make our code and models publicly
available. Project Page: https://buaacyw.github.io/meshanything-v2/

arxiv_record.abstract: Large multimodal models (LMMs) have exhibited proficiencies across many visual tasks. Although numerous well-known benchmarks exist to evaluate model performance, they increasingly have insufficient headroom. As such, there is a pressing need for a new generation of benchmarks challenging enough for the next generation of LMMs. One area that LMMs show potential is graph analysis, specifically, the tasks an analyst might typically perform when interpreting figures such as estimating the mean, intercepts or correlations of functions and data series. In this work, we introduce GRAB, a graph analysis benchmark, fit for current and future frontier LMMs. Our benchmark is predominantly synthetic, ensuring high-quality, noise-free questions. GRAB is comprised of 3284 questions, covering five tasks and 23 graph properties. We evaluate 20 LMMs on GRAB, finding it to be a challenging benchmark, with the highest performing model attaining a score of just 21.0%. Finally, we conduct various ablations to investigate where the models succeed and struggle. We release GRAB and a lightweight GRAB-Lite to encourage progress in this important, growing domain.

arxiv_record.title: GRAB: A Challenging GRaph Analysis Benchmark for Large Multimodal Models

arxiv_record.abstract: Continual Test Time Adaptation (CTTA) has emerged as a critical approach for bridging the domain gap between the controlled training environments and the real-world scenarios, enhancing model adaptability and robustness. Existing CTTA methods, typically categorized into Full-Tuning (FT) and Efficient-Tuning (ET), struggle with effectively addressing domain shifts. To overcome these challenges, we propose Hybrid-TTA, a holistic approach that dynamically selects instance-wise tuning method for optimal adaptation. Our approach introduces the Dynamic Domain Shift Detection (DDSD) strategy, which identifies domain shifts by leveraging temporal correlations in input sequences and dynamically switches between FT and ET to adapt to varying domain shifts effectively. Additionally, the Masked Image Modeling based Adaptation (MIMA) framework is integrated to ensure domain-agnostic robustness with minimal computational overhead. Our Hybrid-TTA achieves a notable 1.6%p improvement in mIoU on the Cityscapes-to-ACDC benchmark dataset, surpassing previous state-of-the-art methods and offering a robust solution for real-world continual adaptation challenges.
arxiv_record.authors: Hyewon Park, Hyejin Park, Jueun Ko, Dongbo Min
arxiv_record.title: Hybrid-TTA: Continual Test-time Adaptation via Dynamic Domain Shift Detection

arxiv_record.abstract: Event cameras, known for their high temporal resolution and ability to capture asynchronous changes, have gained significant attention for their potential in feature tracking, especially in challenging conditions. However, event cameras lack the fine-grained texture information that conventional cameras provide, leading to error accumulation in tracking. To address this, we propose a novel framework, BlinkTrack, which integrates event data with grayscale images for high-frequency feature tracking. Our method extends the traditional Kalman filter into a learning-based framework, utilizing differentiable Kalman filters in both event and image branches. This approach improves single-modality tracking and effectively solves the data association and fusion from asynchronous event and image data. We also introduce new synthetic and augmented datasets to better evaluate our model. Experimental results indicate that BlinkTrack significantly outperforms existing methods, exceeding 80 FPS with multi-modality data and 100 FPS with preprocessed event data. Codes and dataset are available at https://github.com/ColieShen/BlinkTrack.

arxiv_record.abstract: We propose Long-LRM, a feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction model for instant, high-resolution, 360{\deg} wide-coverage, scene-level reconstruction. Specifically, it takes in 32 input images at a resolution of 960x540 and produces the Gaussian reconstruction in just 1 second on a single A100 GPU. To handle the long sequence of 250K tokens brought by the large input size, Long-LRM features a mixture of the recent Mamba2 blocks and the classical transformer blocks, enhanced by a light-weight token merging module and Gaussian pruning steps that balance between quality and efficiency. We evaluate Long-LRM on the large-scale DL3DV benchmark and Tanks&Temples, demonstrating reconstruction quality comparable to the optimization-based methods while achieving an 800x speedup w.r.t. the optimization-based approaches and an input size at least 60x larger than the previous feed-forward approaches. We conduct extensive ablation studies on our model design choices for both rendering quality and computation efficiency. We also explore Long-LRM's compatibility with other Gaussian variants such as 2D GS, which enhances Long-LRM's ability in geometry reconstruction. Project page: https://arthurhero.github.io/projects/llrm

arxiv_record.abstract: We introduce SeaS, a unified industrial generative model for automatically creating diverse anomalies, authentic normal products, and precise anomaly masks. While extensive research exists, most efforts either focus on specific tasks, i.e., anomalies or normal products only, or require separate models for each anomaly type. Consequently, prior methods either offer limited generative capability or depend on a vast array of anomaly-specific models. We demonstrate that U-Net's differentiated learning ability captures the distinct visual traits of slightly-varied normal products and diverse anomalies, enabling us to construct a unified model for all tasks. Specifically, we first introduce an Unbalanced Abnormal (UA) Text Prompt, comprising one normal token and multiple anomaly tokens. More importantly, our Decoupled Anomaly Alignment (DA) loss decouples anomaly attributes and binds them to distinct anomaly tokens of UA, enabling SeaS to create unseen anomalies by recombining these attributes. Furthermore, our Normal-image Alignment (NA) loss aligns the normal token to normal patterns, making generated normal products globally consistent and locally varied. Finally, SeaS produces accurate anomaly masks by fusing discriminative U-Net features with high-resolution VAE features. SeaS sets a new benchmark for industrial generation, significantly enhancing downstream applications, with average improvements of $+8.66\%$ pixel-level AP for synthesis-based AD approaches, $+1.10\%$ image-level AP for unsupervised AD methods, and $+12.79\%$ IoU for supervised segmentation models. Code is available at \href{https://github.com/HUST-SLOW/SeaS}{https://github.com/HUST-SLOW/SeaS}.

native_poster_event.abstract: We introduce SeaS, a unified industrial generative model for automatically creating diverse anomalies, authentic normal products, and precise anomaly masks.  While extensive research exists, most efforts either focus on specific tasks, i.e., anomalies or normal products only, or require separate models for each anomaly type.  Consequently, prior methods either offer limited generative capability or depend on a vast array of anomaly-specific models.  We demonstrate that U-Net's differentiated learning ability captures the distinct visual traits of slightly-varied normal products and diverse anomalies, enabling us to construct a unified model for all tasks.  Specifically, we first introduce an Unbalanced Abnormal (UA) Text Prompt, comprising one normal token and multiple anomaly tokens.  More importantly, our Decoupled Anomaly Alignment (DA) loss decouples anomaly attributes and binds them to distinct anomaly tokens of UA, enabling SeaS to create unseen anomalies by recombining these attributes.  Furthermore, our Normal-image Alignment (NA) loss aligns the normal token to normal patterns, making generated normal products globally consistent and locally varied.  Finally, SeaS produces accurate anomaly masks by fusing discriminative U-Net features with high-resolution VAE features.  SeaS sets a new benchmark for industrial generation, significantly enhancing downstream applications, with average improvements of +8.66% pixel-level AP for synthesis-based AD approaches, +1.10% image-level AP for unsupervised AD methods, and +12.79% IoU for supervised segmentation models.  The code will be released publicly available.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion broaden SeaS from anomaly-image/mask generation supporting segmentation to unified generation of anomalies, normal images and masks. New central claims concern benefits for synthesis-based and unsupervised anomaly detectors, beyond the retained supervised-segmentation claims.

C2.justification: Appendices A.11–A.12 explicitly qualify generation of extremely subtle defects and distinguish unseen instances within known anomaly types from genuinely unseen types. v2 also explains Textual Inversion shortcomings and interprets detector-augmentation benefits. Earlier discussions emphasizing small supervised models outperforming larger unsupervised detectors are removed with their comparisons.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 newly specifies forward-diffusion t=1500 and 25 sampling steps, detector checkpoint sources, GLASS foreground-mask omissions and PatchCore preprocessing. These are additional disclosures rather than demonstrated changes to retained experiments. The per-stage resource/time breakdown is removed, while aggregate timings, core training hyperparameters and the code link remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds VisA's 12 object categories alongside the retained MVTec datasets. Evaluation expands beyond anomaly-image generation and supervised segmentation to normal-image generation, anomaly replacement in synthesis-based detectors, and normal-image augmentation for unsupervised detectors.

E2.justification: v2 newly evaluates GLASS, PatchCore, MambaAD and Textual Inversion, and adds a DRAEM control using real training anomalies. CDC is removed from generation comparisons. DRAEM disappears as a synthesis source for the common segmentation networks but appears in new detector-augmentation comparisons. Earlier direct comparisons with RealNet, Shape-guided and FOD are removed.

E3.justification: v2 adds normal-image KID, anomaly-region IC-LPIPS, detector-augmentation protocols, lighting-specific training subsets and a real-anomaly DRAEM control. The RMP ablation baseline is revised from having no components to retaining coarse-mask supervision (v1 Table 5; v2 Table 6), without establishing a rerun. The principal few-shot split and generation-training budget remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained token, loss, training-strategy and RMP ablations, v2 adds a fixed-prompt ablation, Textual Inversion comparison, lighting/background experiment, small-defect examples and t-SNE analysis of unseen-type generalization. Appendix A.13 adds a substantive control testing whether DRAEM gains exceed those obtained from access to the same real anomalies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run or seed counts, confidence intervals, standard deviations, error bars or significance tests. Both present point estimates; averages across categories or models do not establish repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results, including VisA IS/IC-LPIPS of 1.27/0.26, normal-image KID and detector-augmentation outcomes. Retained MVTec AD generation and per-category segmentation scores are unchanged. Some MVTec 3D AD summaries change: average SeaS image-AUROC becomes 78.38 rather than 78.44, while DFMGAN image-AP changes from 82.83 to 83.83 despite unchanged component rows averaging 82.83.

M1.justification: Section 3.4 adds a normal-image output mode conditioned on the normal token alone, whereas v1 describes inference for abnormal image-mask pairs. The shared U-Net, UA prompts, DA/NA losses, mixed training and RMP architecture remain unchanged; this is a limited extension of the stated inference procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contributions and conclusion are substantially rewritten around unified generation and broader downstream applications. Experimental discussion and appendices are reorganized, with MVTec 3D AD material redistributed and implementation, ablation and qualitative-result sections reordered.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column layout. Tables consolidate datasets and image/pixel metrics; retained qualitative displays are merged, relocated or stripped of removed comparators. Figure 1 is redesigned, and normal-generation, feature-visualization, lighting, small-defect and t-SNE displays are added.

R1.justification: The central positioning shifts from anomaly-only versus complete-image generation to one model serving anomaly, normal-image and mask generation, revising the contrasts with AnomalyDiffusion and DFMGAN. References supporting GLASS, MambaAD, PatchCore and VisA are added; references associated with RealNet, Shape-guided, FOD and FID are removed.

T1.justification: The loss equations, attention formulation and Appendix A.2 multi-head-attention argument are retained. Explicit prompt indexing and added qualitative explanations do not introduce a substantive new mathematical definition, derivation or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation through defect-region diversity measurements, VisA evaluation and detector-augmentation experiments, including the real-anomaly control in Appendix A.13. Appendices A.11–A.12 also meaningfully constrain the generalization claims. These gains outweigh removed comparator/resource detail and limited reporting defects, including Table 4's inconsistent DFMGAN average. Uncertainty across runs remains unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SeaS. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material across substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds VisA evaluations, detector-augmentation experiments, and further diagnostic analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-generation, downstream detection and segmentation, and ablation results on MVTec AD and RGB images from MVTec 3D AD.

arxiv_record.abstract: We present REM, a framework for segmenting a wide range of concepts in video that can be described through natural language. Our method leverages the universal visual-language mapping learned by video diffusion models on Internet-scale data by fine-tuning them on small-scale Referring Object Segmentation datasets. Our key insight is to preserve the entirety of the generative model's architecture by shifting its objective from predicting noise to predicting mask latents. The resulting model can accurately segment rare and unseen objects, despite only being trained on a limited set of categories. Additionally, it can effortlessly generalize to non-object dynamic concepts, such as smoke or raindrops, as demonstrated in our new benchmark for Referring Video Process Segmentation (Ref-VPS). REM performs on par with the state-of-the-art on in-domain datasets, like Ref-DAVIS, while outperforming them by up to 12 IoU points out-of-domain, leveraging the power of generative pre-training. We also show that advancements in video generation directly improve segmentation.
arxiv_record.authors: Anurag Bagchi, Zhipeng Bao, Yu-Xiong Wang, Pavel Tokmakov, Martial Hebert

native_poster_event.abstract: We present REM, a framework for segmenting a wide range of concepts in video that can be described through natural language. Our method unlocks the universal visual-language mapping learned by video diffusion models on Internet-scale data by fine-tuning them on small-scale Referring Object Segmentation datasets. Our key insight is preserving the entirety of the generative model's architecture by shifting its objective from predicting noise to predicting mask latents. The resulting model can accurately segment and track rare and unseen objects, despite only being trained on object masks from a limited set of categories. Additionally, it can effortlessly generalize to non-object dynamic concepts, such as smoke or raindrops, as demonstrated in our newly introduced benchmark for Referring Video Process Segmentation (Ref-VPS). Our experiments show that REM performs on par with state-of-the-art approaches on in-domain datasets, like Ref-DAVIS, while outperforming them by up to 11 points in terms of region similarity out-of-domain, leveraging the power of Internet-scale pre-training.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain preserving generative architectures for open-world referring segmentation and introducing Ref-VPS. v2 explicitly emphasizes benefits from advances in video generation in its abstract and conclusion, but v1 already articulated that relationship in Section 5.3 and discussed interchangeable backbones. The expanded experiments principally strengthen existing claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations connecting two-stage training to spatial priors, image/video balance to generalization, and VAE reconstruction to mask-domain compatibility. It discusses ambiguous ground truth, the limitations of temporal-consistency measurement and misleading consistency from empty predictions. Existing object-centric bias and fast-motion limitations remain in the appendix.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds Wan's 80k-step schedule, batch size and 17-frame clips, model-specific MeViS fine-tuning schedules, and inference-versus-scoring frame rates. Computational-cost sections document measurement hardware and baseline-estimation procedures. However, v1's exhaustive supervision inventory for the original baselines is omitted, and v2's general eight-GPU training statement is not clearly reconciled with its four-GPU ModelScope cost report.

E1.justification: v2 adds training and evaluation on MeViS, substantially extending evaluation toward motion-dependent referring expressions. The earlier training sources and five evaluation benchmarks remain. Ref-VPS's additional clips retain the same 39 concepts and do not independently establish broader task coverage.

E2.justification: The new MeViS comparison includes VISA-13B, DsHmp and GLUS alongside Referformer. GLUS also joins the existing Ref-VPS comparison in v2 Table 4, whereas v1 Table 3 compared only MUTR, UNINEXT and VD-IT. The original in-domain and BURST/VSPW comparator sets remain.

E3.justification: Ref-VPS changes from 141 clips annotated at 24 FPS to 145 clips annotated at 6 FPS, with ambiguous pixels excluded using Ignore labels. The stated default evaluation resolution changes from original resolution to 512×512. v2 also introduces Wan and MeViS training schedules, controlled resolution/supervision experiments and temporal-consistency evaluation. These establish reported protocol changes without proving that every retained result was rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's backbone/CNN ablations, v2 adds latent-versus-pixel supervision, frozen-versus-tuned VAE and MLP-decoder comparisons; training-stage, data-ratio and noise ablations; annotation agreement and VAE reconstruction checks; quantitative failure, temporal-consistency and computational-cost analyses; and ambiguous-scene cases. Earlier backbone, fight-scene, failure-example and concept-coverage analyses are retained or relocated.

E5.justification: Appendix B.3 newly specifies averaging inference measurements over 80 runs, and Appendix A.3 reports inter-annotator agreement. The timing repeats do not establish additional training runs. Neither version reports segmentation-performance seed variability, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds MeViS results of 53.5 and 60.3 J&F for ModelScope and Wan, respectively, plus Wan results and numerous diagnostic outcomes. Matched ModelScope entries change from 40.4 to 37.5 J on BURST and 49.56 to 49.0 on Ref-VPS; several baseline and backbone-ablation values also change. Revised protocols prevent interpreting these as same-setting regressions. Original Table 1 scores are retained with rounding.

M1.justification: v2 adds a principal REM variant using the Wan-14B diffusion transformer alongside the ModelScope model. Its joint spatiotemporal architecture uses single-stage fine-tuning instead of ModelScope's spatial-then-joint training. This substantially extends the implemented model family, while retaining the mask-latent objective, frozen VAE and single-pass decoding.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, benchmark-collection narrative and discussion are extensively rewritten, and terminology changes from 'Referral' to 'Referring'. The appendix is reorganized into dataset, quantitative evaluation, qualitative evaluation and implementation sections. The existing generative-backbone analysis moves from the main text into the supplement.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 becomes a front-page teaser, and existing qualitative comparisons are extensively rearranged. v2 adds an annotation-pipeline diagram, ground-truth/Ignore visualizations and a quantitative failure plot, while expanding and regrouping tables for additional models, comparisons and analyses.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting MeViS, Wan/DiT, GLUS, VISA, DsHmp, reconstruction analysis and annotation-quality evaluation. It extends comparisons to recent language-model-based video segmentation systems. The central positioning against object-centric RVOS and diffusion feature-extractor approaches remains; publication updates and merged duplicate citations are bibliographic changes.

T1.justification: Appendix B.7 adds a formal temporal-consistency metric in Equations (A)-(B), absent from v1. The original diffusion and segmentation Equations (1)-(7) remain substantively unchanged. The new signed IoU-difference definition permits cancellation, limiting its interpretation as temporal stability.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's limited decoder ablation and absence of annotation-agreement measurement, v2 adds controlled supervision/decoder experiments and independent annotation validation, substantially strengthening the central method and benchmark evidence. MeViS and Wan evaluations further test applicability. The flawed signed temporal-consistency definition and inconsistencies in training-cost reporting weaken those particular additions, but the stronger central validation provides a clear substantial net improvement. Revised Ref-VPS scores alone do not establish performance improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ReferEverything, the REM framework and Ref-VPS benchmark. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison. Changed evaluation settings limit direct score comparisons, not identification of the revisions.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Wan and MeViS evaluations, annotation-agreement measurements, computational-cost measurements and extensive supplementary analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original REM evaluations, backbone and decoder ablations, and qualitative analyses on established datasets and the newly collected Ref-VPS benchmark.
