arxiv_record.abstract: Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations have demonstrated remarkable performance in novel view synthesis; further, material-lighting disentanglement on 3DGS warrants relighting capabilities and its adaptability to broader applications. While the general approach to the latter operation lies in integrating differentiable physically-based rendering (PBR) techniques to jointly recover BRDF materials and environment lighting, achieving a precise disentanglement remains an inherently difficult task due to the challenge of accurately modeling light transport. Existing approaches typically approximate Gaussian points' normals, which constitute an implicit geometric constraint. However, they usually suffer from inaccuracies in normal estimation that subsequently degrade light transport, resulting in noisy material decomposition and flawed relighting results. To address this, we propose GeoSplatting, a novel approach that augments 3DGS with explicit geometry guidance for precise light transport modeling. By differentiably constructing a surface-grounded 3DGS from an optimizable mesh, our approach leverages well-defined mesh normals and the opaque mesh surface, and additionally facilitates the use of mesh-based ray tracing techniques for efficient, occlusion-aware light transport calculations. This enhancement ensures precise material decomposition while preserving the efficiency and high-quality rendering capabilities of 3DGS. Comprehensive evaluations across diverse datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of GeoSplatting, highlighting its superior efficiency and state-of-the-art inverse rendering performance. The project page can be found at https://pku-vcl-geometry.github.io/GeoSplatting/.
arxiv_record.authors: Kai Ye, Chong Gao, Guanbin Li, Wenzheng Chen, Baoquan Chen
arxiv_record.title: GeoSplatting: Towards Geometry Guided Gaussian Splatting for Physically-based Inverse Rendering

C1.justification: The shared geometry-guided Gaussian contribution remains, but v3 makes opaque mesh surfaces and efficient occlusion-aware light transport central contributions in its abstract and introduction. Its conclusion emphasizes normal accuracy, material disentanglement and efficiency relative to implicit-field methods, replacing v1's stronger emphasis on NeRF/DTU results and novel-view synthesis.

C2.justification: v1 identifies shadows baked into albedo and leaves ray tracing to future work. v3 explains how occlusion modeling addresses this problem and discusses the remaining indirect-light approximation and path-tracing cost. It adds explanations of deferred shading, coarse-mask applicability, resolution costs and the failure of initial-mesh reconstruction on specular objects, while dropping detailed lighting-inconsistency and underexposure discussions.

D1.justification: v3 supplies implementation details for revised attribute networks and losses, refinement at learning rate 0.001 for 100 steps, and coarse-mask generation using 5,000 3DGS steps. It adds resolution-dependent GPU-memory and runtime information and identifies ReSTIR for path tracing. A project-page link is added, although both conclusions still describe code release as future work.

E1.justification: Synthetic4Relight and TensoIR are retained; TensoIR already appeared in v1 Appendix F.3. v3 adds the Shiny Blender reflective-object suite, Stanford-ORB objects, Garden outdoor captures and scene-level demonstrations using initial meshes. The full NeRF Synthetic NVS evaluation, DTU experiments and dedicated four-scene geometry-recovery suite from v1 are removed.

E2.justification: Within the retained Synthetic4Relight comparison, v3 adds NVdiffrecmc, TensoIR and NeRO. Within TensoIR, it adds NVdiffrecmc, NeRO and GS-Shader. arxiv_record.abstract:
3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has demonstrated remarkable effectiveness in
novel view synthesis (NVS). However, 3DGS tends to overfit when trained with
sparse views, limiting its generalization to novel viewpoints. In this paper,
we address this overfitting issue by introducing Self-Ensembling Gaussian
Splatting (SE-GS). We achieve self-ensembling by incorporating an
uncertainty-aware perturbation strategy during training. A
$\mathbf{\Delta}$-model and a $\mathbf{\Sigma}$-model are jointly trained on
the available images. The $\mathbf{\Delta}$-model is dynamically perturbed
based on rendering uncertainty across training steps, generating diverse
perturbed models with negligible computational overhead. Discrepancies between
the $\mathbf{\Sigma}$-model and these perturbed models are minimized throughout
training, forming a robust ensemble of 3DGS models. This ensemble, represented
by the $\mathbf{\Sigma}$-model, is then used to generate novel-view images
during inference. Experimental results on the LLFF, Mip-NeRF360, DTU, and
MVImgNet datasets demonstrate that our approach enhances NVS quality under
few-shot training conditions, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods.
The code is released at: https://sailor-z.github.io/projects/SEGS.html.
arxiv_record.authors: Chen Zhao, Xuan Wang, Tong Zhang, Saqib Javed, Mathieu Salzmann

arxiv_record.abstract: The recent segmentation foundation model, Segment Anything Model (SAM), exhibits strong zero-shot segmentation capabilities, but it falls short in generating fine-grained precise masks. To address this limitation, we propose a novel zero-shot image matting model, called ZIM, with two key contributions: First, we develop a label converter that transforms segmentation labels into detailed matte labels, constructing the new SA1B-Matte dataset without costly manual annotations. Training SAM with this dataset enables it to generate precise matte masks while maintaining its zero-shot capability. Second, we design the zero-shot matting model equipped with a hierarchical pixel decoder to enhance mask representation, along with a prompt-aware masked attention mechanism to improve performance by enabling the model to focus on regions specified by visual prompts. We evaluate ZIM using the newly introduced MicroMat-3K test set, which contains high-quality micro-level matte labels. Experimental results show that ZIM outperforms existing methods in fine-grained mask generation and zero-shot generalization. Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of ZIM in various downstream tasks requiring precise masks, such as image inpainting and 3D NeRF. Our contributions provide a robust foundation for advancing zero-shot matting and its downstream applications across a wide range of computer vision tasks. The code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/ZIM.

arxiv_record.abstract: Category-agnostic pose estimation (CAPE) has traditionally relied on support images with annotated keypoints, a process that is often cumbersome and may fail to fully capture the necessary correspondences across diverse object categories. Recent efforts have explored the use of text queries, leveraging their enhanced stability and generalization capabilities. However, existing approaches often remain constrained by their reliance on support queries, their failure to fully utilize the rich priors embedded in pre-trained large language models, and the limitations imposed by their parametric distribution assumptions. To address these challenges, we introduce CapeLLM, the first multimodal large language model (MLLM) designed for CAPE. Our method only employs query image and detailed text descriptions as an input to estimate category-agnostic keypoints. Our method encompasses effective training strategies and carefully designed instructions for applying the MLLM to CAPE. C1.justification: v2 expands the main contributions to dynamic-round training, cumulative spatial reasoning and flexible probability-distribution modeling. It also strengthens novelty positioning to the first fully support-free CAPE framework. The claim of outperforming prior five-shot methods was already present in v1 and is not itself a new contribution.

C2.justification: v2 introduces substantive mechanism explanations: dynamic training enables accumulated relational context to help prediction, and decoded distributions can better respect object boundaries than fixed-variance Gaussians. It also interprets new experiments as evidence of robustness to description, resolution and decoding variations. These extend v1's explanations concerning descriptions, backbone tuning and model size.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository hyperlink and decoding parameters such as temperature, top-k and nucleus thresholds. However, it omits v1's explicit split-1 ablation scope, padding rule for incomplete keypoint groups, and some pre-training data and initialization details. Default optimizer, hardware and training-budget disclosures remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: MP-100 and its category coverage remain unchanged. v2 expands evaluation scenarios to train–test description mismatches, including removed or placeholder descriptions, and explicitly examines several occlusion conditions. These extend input-condition coverage without introducing another dataset or pose-estimation task.

E2.justification: GraphCAPE-S and CapeX remain the benchmark comparators. v2 newly evaluates a LocLLM-style training control in Tables 3–4. Figure 5 also introduces a ground-truth-centered, fixed-variance Gaussian as a qualitative reference distribution.

E3.justification: New experiments compare training strategies under single versus cumulative inference, vary description substitution, test resolutions through 336×336, and evaluate seven decoding strategies. The original benchmark splits and default training settings remain. Separately, the stated Hiera token count changes from less than 20% of other encoders' tokens to 20% fewer; no changed implementation or rerun is established.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands diagnostic analyses: cumulative reasoning, training-strategy controls, vague and missing descriptions, resolution sensitivity, decoding alternatives, occlusion cases and predictive-density comparisons (Tables 3–9; Figures 4–5). Earlier instruction, backbone and pre-training ablations largely survive in the appendices rather than being removed.

E5.justification: Figure 5 newly visualizes predictive uncertainty using multiple decoded samples and kernel density estimation. Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests for benchmark scores. The new density visualization does not establish uncertainty in reported PCK averages.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results, including dynamic-training PCK@0.2 of 96.05 with single inference versus 97.28 with cumulative inference, and LocLLM-style mPCK of 84.00 versus fixed-round 91.98. Existing benchmark split scores remain unchanged; Table 2 corrects the query-only average from 91.60 to 92.60. Several retained appendix tables omit previously reported intermediate PCK thresholds.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figure 2 to depict coordinate-token decoding, adds occlusion and density figures, and removes v1's qualitative name-variation figure. improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of CapeLLM's adaptation: Tables 3–4 add the missing LocLLM-style training control and reveal when cumulative inference helps or hurts. arxiv_record.abstract: 3D semantic occupancy and flow prediction are fundamental to spatiotemporal scene understanding. This paper proposes a vision-based framework with three targeted improvements. First, we introduce an occlusion-aware adaptive lifting mechanism incorporating depth denoising. This enhances the robustness of 2D-to-3D feature transformation while mitigating reliance on depth priors. Second, we enforce 3D-2D semantic consistency via jointly optimized prototypes, using confidence- and category-aware sampling to address the long-tail classes problem. Third, to streamline joint prediction, we devise a BEV-centric cost volume to explicitly correlate semantic and flow features, supervised by a hybrid classification-regression scheme that handles diverse motion scales. Our purely convolutional architecture establishes new SOTA performance on multiple benchmarks for both semantic occupancy and joint occupancy semantic-flow prediction. We also present a family of models offering a spectrum of efficiency-performance trade-offs. Our real-time version exceeds all existing real-time methods in speed and accuracy, ensuring its practical viability.

native_poster_event.abstract: Vision-based semantic occupancy and flow prediction provide critical spatiotemporal cues for real-world tasks like autonomous driving and robotics. In this work, we strive to improve performance by introducing a series of targeted improvements for 3D semantic occupancy prediction and flow estimation. First, we propose an occlusion-aware adaptive lifting mechanism with depth denoising to improve the robustness of 2D-to-3D feature transformation and reduce reliance on depth priors. Second, we enhance semantic consistency between 3D and 2D features using shared semantic prototypes to jointly constrain both modalities. This is supported by confidence- and category-based sampling to tackle long-tail challenges in 3D space. Third, to ease the feature encoding burden in joint semantics and flow prediction, we introduce a BEV cost volume-based method. It connects flow and semantic features via the cost volume and applies a classification-regression supervision scheme to manage varying flow scales in dynamic scenes. Our purely convolutional framework achieves SOTA results across multiple benchmarks for 3D semantic occupancy prediction and joint semantic occupancy-flow prediction. It is also the 2nd solution for the Occupancy and Flow in Autonomous Driving Challenge. We provide multiple model variants that optimally balance efficiency and performance. Our real-time version exceeds all existing real-time methods in speed and accuracy, showcasing unmatched deployability. Code and models will be publicly released.

arxiv_record.abstract: In this work, we introduce JDCL - a new method for continual learning with generative rehearsal based on joint diffusion models. Neural networks suffer from catastrophic forgetting defined as abrupt loss in the model's performance when retrained with additional data coming from a different distribution. Generative-replay-based continual learning methods try to mitigate this issue by retraining a model with a combination of new and rehearsal data sampled from a generative model. In this work, we propose to extend this idea by combining a continually trained classifier with a diffusion-based generative model into a single - jointly optimized neural network. We show that such shared parametrization, combined with the knowledge distillation technique allows for stable adaptation to new tasks without catastrophic forgetting. We evaluate our approach on several benchmarks, where it outperforms recent state-of-the-art generative replay techniques. Additionally, we extend our method to the semi-supervised continual learning setup, where it outperforms competing buffer-based replay techniques, and evaluate, in a self-supervised manner, the quality of trained representations.

arxiv_record.abstract: Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation aims to assign semantic labels to each pixel without being constrained by a predefined set of categories. While Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) excels in zero-shot classification, it struggles to align image patches with category embeddings because of its incoherent patch correlations. This study reveals that inter-class correlations are the main reason for impairing CLIP's segmentation performance. Accordingly, we propose CorrCLIP, which reconstructs the scope and value of patch correlations. Specifically, CorrCLIP leverages the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to define the scope of patch interactions, reducing inter-class correlations. To mitigate the problem that SAM-generated masks may contain patches belonging to different classes, CorrCLIP incorporates self-supervised models to compute coherent similarity values, suppressing the weight of inter-class correlations. Additionally, we introduce two additional branches to strengthen patch features' spatial details and semantic representation. Finally, we update segmentation maps with SAM-generated masks to improve spatial consistency. Based on the improvement across patch correlations, feature representations, and segmentation maps, CorrCLIP achieves superior performance across eight benchmarks. Codes are available at: https://github.com/zdk258/CorrCLIP.
arxiv_record.authors: Dengke Zhang, Fagui Liu, Quan Tang

arxiv_record.abstract: Gaze estimation encounters generalization challenges when dealing with out-of-distribution data. To address this problem, recent methods use neural radiance fields (NeRF) to generate augmented data. However, existing methods based on NeRF are computationally expensive and lack facial details. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become the prevailing representation of neural fields. While 3DGS has been extensively examined in head avatars, it faces challenges with accurate gaze control and generalization across different subjects. In this work, we propose GazeGaussian, the first high-fidelity gaze redirection method that uses a two-stream 3DGS model to represent the face and eye regions separately. Leveraging the unstructured nature of 3DGS, we develop a novel representation of the eye for rigid eye rotation based on the target gaze direction. To enable synthesis generalization across various subjects, we integrate an expression-guided module to inject subject-specific information into the neural renderer. Comprehensive experiments show that GazeGaussian outperforms existing methods in rendering speed, gaze redirection accuracy, and facial synthesis across multiple datasets. The code is available at: https://ucwxb.github.io/GazeGaussian.
arxiv_record.authors: Xiaobao Wei, Peng Chen, Guangyu Li, Ming Lu, Hui Chen, Feng Tian
arxiv_record.title: GazeGaussian: High-Fidelity Gaze Redirection with 3D Gaussian Splatting

arxiv_record.abstract:
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities across
diverse visual tasks, including image recognition, video understanding, and
Visual Question Answering (VQA) when explicitly trained for these tasks.
Despite these advances, we find that present-day VLMs (including the
proprietary GPT-4o) lack a fundamental cognitive ability: learning to localize
specific objects in a scene by taking into account the context. In this work,
we focus on the task of few-shot personalized localization, where a model is
given a small set of annotated images (in-context examples) -- each with a
category label and bounding box -- and is tasked with localizing the same
object type in a query image. Personalized localization can be particularly
important in cases of ambiguity of several related objects that can respond to
a text or an object that is hard to describe with words. To provoke
personalized localization abilities in models, we present a data-centric
solution that fine-tunes them using carefully curated data from video object
tracking datasets. By leveraging sequences of frames tracking the same object
across multiple shots, we simulate instruction-tuning dialogues that promote
context awareness. To reinforce this, we introduce a novel regularization
technique that replaces object labels with pseudo-names, ensuring the model
relies on visual context rather than prior knowledge. Our method significantly
enhances the few-shot localization performance of recent VLMs ranging from 7B
to 72B in size, without sacrificing generalization, as demonstrated on several
benchmarks tailored towards evaluating personalized localization abilities.
This work is the first to explore and benchmark personalized few-shot
localization for VLMs -- exposing critical weaknesses in present-day VLMs, and
laying a foundation for future research in context-driven vision-language
applications.

arxiv_record.title: Teaching VLMs to Localize Specific Objects from In-context Examples

snapshot_arxiv_record.abstract:
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities across
diverse visual tasks, including image recognition, video understanding, and
Visual Question Answering (VQA) when explicitly trained for these tasks.
Despite these advances, we find that present-day VLMs (including the
proprietary GPT-4o) lack a fundamental cognitive ability: learning to localize
specific objects in a scene by taking into account the context. In this work,
we focus on the task of few-shot personalized localization, where a model is
given a small set of annotated images (in-context examples) -- each with a
category label and bounding box -- and is tasked with localizing the same
object type in a query image. Personalized localization can be particularly
important in cases of ambiguity of several related objects that can respond to
a text or an object that is hard to describe with words. To provoke
personalized localization abilities in models, we present a data-centric
solution that fine-tunes them using carefully curated data from video object
tracking datasets. By leveraging sequences of frames tracking the same object
across multiple shots, we simulate instruction-tuning dialogues that promote
context awareness. To reinforce this, we introduce a novel regularization
technique that replaces object labels with pseudo-names, ensuring the model
relies on visual context rather than prior knowledge. Our method significantly
enhances the few-shot localization performance of recent VLMs ranging from 7B
to 72B in size, without sacrificing generalization, as demonstrated on several
benchmarks tailored towards evaluating personalized localization abilities.
This work is the first to explore and benchmark personalized few-shot
localization for VLMs -- exposing critical weaknesses in present-day VLMs, and
laying a foundation for future research in context-driven vision-language
applications.

C1.justification: The central claim of improving personalized localization through curated instruction tuning while retaining generalization remains. v2 drops the headline contribution of a copying-related metric and explicitly emphasizes GPT-4o's weaknesses and effectiveness across 7B–72B models in the abstract and introduction.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands explanations of failure through prompt-format compliance, model-scale effects, and possible difficulty with longer contexts. Section 5 explicitly limits the studied setting to single-object output and hypothesizes a training-data explanation for poor multi-object localization. The earlier copying-based interpretation is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds test-set category, object-density, and conversation counts; exact baseline prompts; the GPT-4o model snapshot and high-detail image setting; and a planned release of the data mixes. Conversely, SEED split sample counts disappear. Training documentation still largely refers to LlamaFactory defaults.

E1.justification: The training datasets and principal localization and generalization benchmarks remain unchanged. Section 5 adds a briefly reported MS-COCO multi-object localization test; v1 mentioned COCO but did not report this evaluation.

E2.justification: Beyond the three original VLM baselines, v2 Table 2 adds Pixtral-12B, GPT-4o, Qwen2-VL-72B, and InternVL2-76B. Tables 7–8 additionally compare IPLoc with CD-ViTO, TFA, and OwlViT, substantially broadening the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 introduces 72B fine-tuning and larger-model evaluations, a denser 1–8-shot ICL-LASOT evaluation, and baseline prompt sweeps with selection by aggregate performance (Appendix D). It removes evaluation with IoUex. The principal mIoU metric and stated 50/50 LaSOT category split remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds extensive prompt-sensitivity experiments and response-level failure cases, a denser shot-count analysis, and 72B generalization-retention checks. Existing data-source, semantic-coherence, pseudo-name, and LLaVA analyses largely remain. The copying examples and IoUex diagnostic in v1 Figures 3–4 are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Both principally report point estimates; SEED refers to a benchmark, not random-seed reporting.

E6.justification: Between v1 Table 1 and v2 Table 2, Qwen2-VL-7B's ICL-LASOT 4-shot score changes from 21.89 to 46.29, and IPLoc-7B's Real + Pseudo 8-shot score changes from 33.95 to 55.21. The PDFs do not explain these revisions. Numerous larger-model, detector, prompt-ablation, and multi-object results are added, while the IoUex results and detailed SEED image/video scores are removed.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure remains video-based conversation construction, maximum-interval frame sampling, real/pseudo-name mixing, and LoRA fine-tuning with next-token prediction. Applying this recipe to larger models and testing baseline prompts does not change IPLoc itself.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and results discussion receive targeted rewrites. Model and metric descriptions are removed, ablations are reordered, and limitations and a prompt-ablation appendix are introduced. The main section sequence and most methodological prose remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 transposes and expands the main results table, replaces several ablation bar charts with tables, revises Figure 1's examples, and adds a shot-count curve, dataset statistics, and extensive prompt/response displays. The older appendix localization examples are retained but redistributed throughout the expanded supplement.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations supporting the new VLM and detector comparisons and discussion of scaling and context length, while removing the earlier Qwen technical-report reference. The related-work section's principal VLM/ICL framing and the claimed novelty of personalized localization remain substantially intact.

T1.justification: v1's Equation 1 defining IoUex, its mathematical explanation, and its multi-shot selection rule are deleted. The conversation and bounding-box notation remain, with no added theorems, proofs, or substantive derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical foundation through stronger VLM and detector comparisons and explicit prompt controls. Appendix D shows why these controls matter: Qwen2-VL-72B's mean score changes from 7.69 with the original prompt to 34.21 with the selected prompt. Scaling and retention checks better support applicability, and the single-object limitation clarifies scope. Removed copying diagnostics and SEED details, unexplained score revisions, and inconsistencies such as Table 4's 72B label versus Section 4.3's 7B description temper, but do not outweigh, these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IPLoc research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support matching retained, relocated, added, and removed content.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds larger-model evaluations, detector comparisons, and quantitative prompt ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original localization experiments, data-curation ablations, and generalization evaluations in the main text and appendices.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large text-to-image models demonstrate impressive generation capabilities; however, their substantial size necessitates expensive cloud servers for deployment. Conversely, light-weight models can be deployed on edge devices at lower cost but often with inferior generation quality for complex user prompts. To strike a balance between performance and cost, we propose a routing framework, called RouteT2I, which dynamically selects either the large cloud model or the light-weight edge model for each user prompt. Since generated image quality is challenging to measure and compare directly, RouteT2I establishes multi-dimensional quality metrics, particularly, by evaluating the similarity between the generated images and both positive and negative texts that describe each specific quality metric. RouteT2I then predicts the expected quality of the generated images by identifying key tokens in the prompt and comparing their impact on the quality. RouteT2I further introduces the Pareto relative superiority to compare the multi-metric quality of the generated images. Based on this comparison and predefined cost constraints, RouteT2I allocates prompts to either the edge or the cloud. Evaluation reveals that RouteT2I significantly reduces the number of requesting large cloud model while maintaining high-quality image generation.
arxiv_record.authors: Zewei Xin, Qinya Li, Chaoyue Niu, Fan Wu, Guihai Chen
arxiv_record.title: Adaptive Routing of Text-to-Image Generation Requests Between Large Cloud Model and Light-Weight Edge Model

C1.justification: V1's contribution list claims a proposed contrastive multi-metric quality measure. V2 emphasizes the routing architecture built around multi-metric measures, while Section 4 attributes contrastive scoring to prior work. This narrows the novelty positioning of one component while retaining the central text-to-image routing and dual-gate MoE contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning preference alignment, edge-device suitability, customizable metrics, and semantic robustness across encoders. It removes v1's discussion of diminishing routing benefits at high cloud-routing rates. Its new description of 83.97% as a fraction of the full cloud gain is also imprecise: under the unchanged ΔP formula, v1 Table 2 assigns the cloud itself 80%, rather than 100%.

D1.justification: V2 discloses all ten positive/negative quality-prompt pairs, previously illustrated with only two examples. It adds generator and encoder specifications, explains baseline adaptation, and reports router size, training time, memory use, deployment hardware, and LAION sample counts. These materially expand reproducibility information. V1's statement that generators use official default hyperparameters is dropped.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates COCO2014 captions only. V2 adds training and evaluation on LAION2B-en-aesthetic prompts (Appendix F), extending coverage from concise object descriptions to more colloquial and stylistic requests. The text-to-image routing task remains the same.

E2.justification: The baseline families remain RouteLLM-BERT, RouteLLM-MF, Hybrid LLM, ZOOTER, and random routing. However, v1 compares the learned baselines only for SD3/SD2.1, while its other generator-pair results report RouteT2I alone. V2 Appendix Tables 6–14 add all four learned baselines to those nine already-tested pairs, substantially expanding comparator participation.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce a 20,000-training/10,000-validation LAION split, HPSv2 and MPS scoring at 50% routing, ImageReward analysis by noun count, and Jetson deployment measurements. Generator configurations expand from ten to eighteen pairs, including PixArt-α and Infinity. The stated optimizer, learning rate, batch size, and approximately ten training epochs remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds an empirical test of prompt complexity versus generator quality gaps (Figures 2–3), validation against preference-scoring models (Appendix D), and visual routing case studies (Appendix G). Appendix H also analyzes behavior across encoder and generator architectures. The original three component ablations and their Table 6 values are retained.

E5.justification: V2 Figure 3 introduces shaded bands around the noun-count curves, but neither its caption nor the text identifies what the bands represent or how they were estimated. Neither version specifies seeds or repeated-run counts. The bands therefore cannot reliably be classified as a documented change in statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The headline SD3/SD2.1 results and ablation values remain, but Table 5 revises existing entries: SD3/SDXL at 40% routing changes from 27.10% to 29.78%. V2 adds LAION results, preference scores, additional pair comparisons, and runtime/memory measurements; v1's pairwise win-rate matrix is removed. These are revised and expanded reported results, without evidence establishing an underlying method improvement.

M1.justification: Sections 4–5 retain the contrastive quality scores, PRS normalization and aggregation, dual-gate token-selection MoE, projection and score matrices, multiple prediction heads, and threshold-based routing. Added explanations and generator configurations do not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most method exposition remain. V2 revises the title and authorship information, adds acknowledgments, edits related-work and results prose, clarifies metric terminology, and organizes additional material into Appendices A–H. These are targeted editorial and structural refinements rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 1, adds prompt examples and complexity plots, removes v1's pairwise win-rate heatmap, and narrows the displayed routing-rate range in the performance curves. It restructures and expands the generator-pair table and adds extensive appendix tables and a routing-example image grid. The architecture diagram is retained with renumbering.

R1.justification: V2 substantially strengthens grounding of the central components: contrastive scoring is attributed to Liang et al. and Wang et al.; metric selection is connected to HEIM, T2I-Scorer, and VisionPrefer; and MoE positioning adds token-mixture and expert-choice work. Related-work discussion further distinguishes T2I from LLM routing, alongside references supporting the new evaluations.

T1.justification: New Appendix B formalizes text and image space cardinalities, defines their logarithmic size ratio, and derives numerical comparisons for CLIP and T5 inputs. V1 only gives the qualitative space-size argument. This is a limited mathematical addition; the core routing equations are retained, and no routing optimality proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow validation through LAION evaluation, preference-scoring models outside the routing objective, broader baseline comparisons, and measured Jetson deployment costs. The complete quality-prompt specification also improves reproducibility. Unexplained score revisions, undefined uncertainty bands, and imprecise normalized-gain interpretations remain weaknesses, but the new evidence materially strengthens assessment of generalization, quality alignment, and practical feasibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RouteT2I, with matching core methods and experiments despite the changed title. The text, equations, figures, and tables support comparison. V1 ends after its references; v2 additionally supplies Appendices A–H, which were included in the assessment.

after.justification: V2 retains original routing experiments and adds LAION results, preference-model scoring, prompt-complexity analysis, additional generator-pair comparisons, and measured deployment costs.

before.justification: V1 reports original COCO routing experiments, comparisons with other routers, results across ten generator pairs, and component ablations in Section 6.

arxiv_record.abstract: Foundation models that bridge vision and language have made significant progress. While they have inspired many life-enriching applications, their potential for abuse in creating new threats remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we reveal that vision-language models (VLMs) can be weaponized to enhance gradient inversion attacks (GIAs) in federated learning (FL), where an FL server attempts to reconstruct private data samples from gradients shared by victim clients. Despite recent advances, existing GIAs struggle to reconstruct high-resolution images when the victim has a large local data batch. One promising direction is to focus reconstruction on valuable samples rather than the entire batch, but current methods lack the flexibility to target specific data of interest. To address this gap, we propose Geminio, the first approach to transform GIAs into semantically meaningful, targeted attacks. It enables a brand new privacy attack experience: attackers can describe, in natural language, the data they consider valuable, and Geminio will prioritize reconstruction to focus on those high-value samples. This is achieved by leveraging a pretrained VLM to guide the optimization of a malicious global model that, when shared with and optimized by a victim, retains only gradients of samples that match the attacker-specified query. Geminio can be launched at any FL round and has no impact on normal training (i.e., the FL server can steal clients' data while still producing a high-utility ML model as in benign scenarios). Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness in pinpointing and reconstructing targeted samples, with high success rates across complex datasets and large batch sizes with resilience against defenses.
arxiv_record.authors: Junjie Shan, Ziqi Zhao, Jialin Lu, Rui Zhang, Siu Ming Yiu and Ka-Ho Chow
arxiv_record.title: Geminio: Language-Guided Gradient Inversion Attacks in Federated Learning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion newly claim attacks at any FL round while preserving normal model utility. The central contributions—natural-language targeted inversion, compatibility with reconstruction algorithms, and resistance to existing defenses—retain their original scope.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands applicability explanations and limitations: auxiliary data must represent queried features, advanced VLMs better handle complex queries, and reconstruction deteriorates beyond roughly 16 matches with the tested backend. arxiv_record.abstract: Photorealistic reconstruction of street scenes is essential for developing real-world simulators in autonomous driving. While recent methods based on 3D/4D Gaussian Splatting (GS) have demonstrated promising results, they still encounter challenges in complex street scenes due to the unpredictable motion of dynamic objects. Current methods typically decompose street scenes into static and dynamic objects, learning the Gaussians in either a supervised manner (e.g., w/ 3D bounding-box) or a self-supervised manner (e.g., w/o 3D bounding-box). However, these approaches do not effectively model the motions of dynamic objects (e.g., the motion speed of pedestrians is clearly different from that of vehicles), resulting in suboptimal scene decomposition. To address this, we propose Explicit Motion Decomposition (EMD), which models the motions of dynamic objects by introducing learnable motion embeddings to the Gaussians, enhancing the decomposition in street scenes. The proposed plug-and-play EMD module compensates for the lack of motion modeling in self-supervised street Gaussian splatting methods. We also introduce tailored training strategies to extend EMD to supervised approaches. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, achieving state-of-the-art novel view synthesis performance in self-supervised settings. The code is available at: https://qingpowuwu.github.io/emd.
arxiv_record.authors: Xiaobao Wei, Qingpo Wuwu, Zhongyu Zhao, Zhuangzhe Wu, Nan Huang, Ming Lu, Ningning MA, Shanghang Zhang

arxiv_record.abstract:
We present VideoOrion, a Video Large Language Model (Video-LLM) that
explicitly captures the key semantic information in videos - the
spatial-temporal dynamics of objects throughout the videos. VideoOrion employs
expert vision models to extract object dynamics through a detect-segment-track
pipeline, encoding them into a set of object tokens by aggregating
spatial-temporal object features. Our method addresses the persistent challenge
in Video-LLMs of efficiently compressing high-dimensional video data into
semantic tokens that are comprehensible to LLMs. Compared to prior methods
which resort to downsampling the original video or aggregating visual tokens
using resamplers, leading to information loss and entangled semantics,
VideoOrion not only offers a more natural and efficient way to derive compact,
disentangled semantic representations but also enables explicit object modeling
of video content with minimal computational cost. Moreover, the introduced
object tokens naturally allow VideoOrion to accomplish video-based referring
tasks. Experimental results show that VideoOrion can learn to make good use of
the object tokens, and achieves competitive results on both general video
question answering and video-based referring benchmarks.

Yicheng Feng, Yijiang Li, Wanpeng Zhang, Hao Luo, Zihao Yue, Sipeng
  Zheng, and Zongqing Lu

arxiv_record.abstract:
Deformable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) is limited by missing intermediate
motion information due to the low temporal resolution of RGB cameras. To
address this, we introduce the first approach combining event cameras, which
capture high-temporal-resolution, continuous motion data, with deformable 3D-GS
for dynamic scene reconstruction. We observe that threshold modeling for events
plays a crucial role in achieving high-quality reconstruction. Therefore, we
propose a GS-Threshold Joint Modeling strategy, creating a mutually reinforcing
process that greatly improves both 3D reconstruction and threshold modeling.
Moreover, we introduce a Dynamic-Static Decomposition strategy that first
identifies dynamic areas by exploiting the inability of static Gaussians to
represent motions, then applies a buffer-based soft decomposition to separate
dynamic and static areas. This strategy accelerates rendering by avoiding
unnecessary deformation in static areas, and focuses on dynamic areas to
enhance fidelity. Additionally, we contribute the first event-inclusive 4D
benchmark with synthetic and real-world dynamic scenes, on which our method
achieves state-of-the-art performance.
arxiv_record.authors: Wenhao Xu, Wenming Weng, Yueyi Zhang, Ruikang Xu, Zhiwei Xiong
arxiv_record.title: Event-boosted Deformable 3D Gaussians for Dynamic Scene Reconstruction

native_poster_event.abstract: Deformable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) is limited by missing intermediate motion information due to the low temporal resolution of RGB cameras. To address this, we introduce the first approach combining event cameras, which capture high-temporal-resolution, continuous motion data, with deformable 3D-GS for dynamic scene reconstruction. We observe that threshold modeling for events plays a crucial role in achieving high-quality reconstruction. Therefore, we propose a GS-Threshold Joint Modeling strategy, creating a mutually reinforcing process that greatly improves both 3D reconstruction and threshold modeling. Moreover, we introduce a Dynamic-Static Decomposition strategy that first identifies dynamic areas by exploiting the inability of static Gaussians to represent motions, then applies a buffer-based soft decomposition to separate dynamic and static areas. This strategy accelerates rendering by avoiding unnecessary deformation in static areas, and focuses on dynamic areas to enhance fidelity. Additionally, we contribute the first event-inclusive 4D benchmark with synthetic and real-world dynamic scenes, on which our method achieves state-of-the-art performance.

C1.justification: The principal GTJM and DSD contribution claims persist. The dataset contribution is strengthened from a comprehensive dynamic-scene dataset to the claimed first event-inclusive 4D benchmark containing synthetic and real-world scenes, with state-of-the-art performance emphasized in the abstract and introduction.

C2.justification: V2 removes v1's explicit synthetic-only evaluation limitation and proposed future real-world collection, consistent with its added captured-data experiments. It also attributes the blurry-scene advantage to event-based deblurring. The central geometric-consistency and deformation-capacity explanations remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds substantial capture documentation: beam splitter, Prophesee Gen4, Basler ace, STM32 synchronization, rotating turntable, and frame-selection details. Conversely, it removes v1's implementation paragraph specifying PyTorch, random-point initialization, and the 7k threshold/47k joint-optimization budgets; the 3k static warm-up remains elsewhere. Both versions still promise future code and dataset release.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates eight synthetic scenes only. V2 retains these and adds four captured scenes—Excavator, Jeep, Flowers, and Eagle—plus dynamic blurry-scene evaluation. This substantially expands coverage to real sensor data and blurred inputs.

E2.justification: The original synthetic comparator set remains unchanged, and the real-world comparison reuses 4D-GS, Deformable-3DGS, and Event-4DGS. V2 additionally evaluates a blur-adapted Deformable-3DGS comparator in Figure 9; Section 4.2 describes extending comparison methods with blur loss and EDI. DE-NeRF remains unevaluated.

E3.justification: V2 introduces real-video evaluation using downsampled training frames and intermediate test frames, alongside the blurry-scene comparison procedure. The existing synthetic training count and PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/FPS metrics persist. Newly specifying uniform synthetic sampling and intermediate test-frame selection documents the protocol without establishing a changed split or rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds a motion-blur case study testing the adapted method (Figure 9). The GTJM, DSD, and buffer ablations and existing sensitivity analyses remain, although ablation reporting is condensed to averages. Real-world ablations are referenced but their results are absent from the supplied PDF.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V2's aggregate ablation scores summarize scenes rather than introducing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 2 retain their numerical results, including all 224 synthetic comparison values. V2 adds quantitative results for four real-world scenes and a blurry-scene result of 28.98 dB versus Deformable-3DGS's 24.19 dB (Figure 9). These are new evaluations, not same-setting gains over v1. Per-scene ablation entries are replaced by aggregate scores.

M1.justification: The core threshold optimization, event supervision, and dynamic-static decomposition procedures remain unchanged. V2 adds an adaptation using blur loss and EDI for dynamic blurry scenes (Section 4.2), although its detailed implementation is deferred to unavailable supplementary material.

P1.justification: V2 drops 'Fast' from the title, revises the abstract and experimental narrative, replaces 'intensity' with 'brightness,' and clarifies threshold notation. Comparisons gain quantitative, qualitative, and blurry-scene subheadings, but the overall section sequence and most method prose remain.

P2.justification: The experimental presentation is substantially reorganized through a new real-world results table and acquisition, real-world rendering, and blur figures. The synthetic comparison loses its Musicbox row, and the wide per-scene ablation table becomes a compact aggregate table. Existing diagnostic figures are largely retained but relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: V2 expands benchmark novelty positioning and revises its discussion of prior datasets. It removes the dedicated Robust e-NeRF discussion while retaining that citation, and removes Structure-from-Motion Revisited with the initialization paragraph. Most other reference differences are renumbering or metadata updates.

T1.justification: Equations 1–14 retain the same mathematical substance. Distinguishing estimated thresholds with a hat and expanding the event-count summation indices clarify notation rather than introduce new derivations or assumptions. Neither version contains formal theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V1 explicitly identifies synthetic-only validation as a limitation. V2 substantially addresses it with a documented capture setup and quantitative and qualitative comparisons on four real-world scenes (Table 3; Figures 6 and 8), strengthening evidence for practical applicability. The blur example provides additional support. Removed training details and reduced ablation granularity weaken reproducibility and diagnosis, but the real-sensor validation resolves an important deficiency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GTJM/DSD framework and are readable throughout, including equations, figures, and tables. Both end with references and contain no appendices. Separately referenced supplementary material is not included, so its contents cannot be compared.

after.justification: V2 retains original synthetic experiments and additionally reports real-world reconstruction results and a dynamic blurry-scene comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic-scene reconstruction results, baseline comparisons, ablations, and sensitivity analyses in Tables 1–3 and associated figures.

arxiv_record.abstract: Traditionally, algorithms that learn to segment object instances in 2D images have heavily relied on large amounts of human-annotated data. Only recently, novel approaches have emerged tackling this problem in an unsupervised fashion. Generally, these approaches first generate pseudo-masks and then train a class-agnostic detector. While such methods deliver the current state of the art, they often fail to correctly separate instances overlapping in 2D image space since only semantics are considered. To tackle this issue, we instead propose to cut the semantic masks in 3D to obtain the final 2D instances by utilizing a point cloud representation of the scene. Furthermore, we derive a Spatial Importance function, which we use to resharpen the semantics along the 3D borders of instances. Nevertheless, these pseudo-masks are still subject to mask ambiguity. To address this issue, we further propose to augment the training of a class-agnostic detector with three Spatial Confidence components aiming to isolate a clean learning signal. With these contributions, our approach outperforms competing methods across multiple standard benchmarks for unsupervised instance segmentation and object detection.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central claims: using 3D information for 2D unsupervised instance segmentation through LocalCut, Spatial Importance Sharpening, and Spatial Confidence, with improved benchmark performance. Updated margins and additional experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: Section 5 adds interpretations concerning robustness to imperfect depth and CutLER's plateau under matched training. The appendix explains the confidence-source comparison, identifies initial semantic-cut failures, and qualifies pseudo-mask evaluation through ImageNet's limited box annotations. The main limitations concerning indistinct boundaries, small objects, and unavailable depth remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Unlike v1's references to unavailable supplementary settings, v3 supplies extraction thresholds, batch sizes, learning rates, optimization, initialization, augmentation, and training budgets in Appendix E and Tables 15–17. It also adds a project-page link, a configuration-file availability statement, and computational-overhead figures. These are substantial disclosures, although the one-versus-three-round inconsistency limits reproducibility.

E1.justification: OpenImages object-detection evaluation is removed from Section 4 and Table 2. ImageNet training and the remaining COCO, COCO20K, LVIS, VOC, Objects365, and KITTI coverage remain. The added ImageNet validation experiment evaluates an existing domain rather than introducing another domain.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds UnSAM and removes LOST and MaskDistill, while retaining the principal competing methods. v3 also includes CutLER in the training-round comparison (Table 5) and MaskCut in the direct pseudo-mask comparison (Table 14), extending comparator participation beyond the corresponding v1 analyses.

E3.justification: The main evaluation changes from one to three self-training rounds, with explicit comparisons across matched backbones and rounds in Table 5. v3 adds ImageNet validation bounding-box evaluation and size-specific AP and recall reporting. However, Appendix E.3 and Table 17 still specify one self-training round, conflicting with the main protocol.

E4.justification: v3 adds SIS-only and CRF-versus-depth confidence controls, a lower-quality MiDaS depth test, extended Kick Back & Relax training, direct pseudo-mask evaluation, and qualitative failure analyses. Conversely, Table 4 drops the DINO component-ablation results. The confidence-floor and mask-alignment tests are moved from v1 Table 5 to v3 Table 10, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports independent repeated-run counts, random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Additional self-training rounds are sequential training stages; Spatial Confidence measures pseudo-mask confidence rather than uncertainty in experimental estimates.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the DiffNCuts model's COCO val2017/COCO20K mask AP of 10.2/10.3 with 10.7/10.9 under increased self-training, so these are not same-setting gains. In-domain LVIS mask AP changes from 5.6 to 4.5 in Table 3. Numerous roundwise, depth, confidence, pseudo-mask, and detailed AP/recall results are also added.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 revises the stated LocalCut procedure: v1 retains only points inside the semantic cut, whereas v3 assigns background z-coordinates to points outside it. This is a localized procedural revision; the three principal components, detector architecture, and loss remain.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the abstract, introduction, method, and conclusion remain intact. Changes include localized rewriting and condensation, reorganized ablation discussion, a structured supplement, updated affiliations, and acknowledgements; there is no wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v3 adds a first-page qualitative/bar-chart overview, redraws the Spatial Confidence diagram, restructures comparison tables with difference rows and revised columns, and adds extensive appendix tables and visualizations. Existing confidence ablations are relocated, and Equation 2's rendering is repaired. These substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds SAM and UnSAM references and distinguishes UnSAM's multi-granularity discovery objective from precise instance segmentation. It removes the dedicated LOST description and OpenImages reference. The broader positioning around CutLER, self-supervised features, and 3D information remains.

T1.justification: The NCut/min-cut formulation, confidence definitions, and loss mathematics remain substantively unchanged, with no new proofs or derivations. v3 repairs the malformed typesetting of Equation 2's already-described normalization to [beta, 1]; this does not introduce a different normalization principle.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens experimental support and technical documentation. Matched backbone/training-round comparisons, confidence-source controls, depth-quality tests, and direct pseudo-mask evaluation better test the proposed mechanisms, while the appendix supplies settings absent from the supplied v1. These gains outweigh the reduced OpenImages coverage and documentation inconsistencies, although the conflicting self-training schedules and occasional table discrepancies still require correction.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CutS3D, with matching authors, core components, and experiments. All pages are readable. v3 includes supplementary Sections A–E; the supplied v1 ends after its references despite mentioning supplementary material. Comparisons concern what is present in these PDFs.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark results and ablations, including additional training-round comparisons, depth experiments, and ImageNet pseudo-mask evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original instance-segmentation and object-detection results, in-domain self-training experiments, and component ablations in Tables 1–8.

arxiv_record.abstract: We propose Quadratic Gaussian Splatting (QGS), a novel representation that replaces static primitives with deformable quadric surfaces (e.g., ellipse, paraboloids) to capture intricate geometry. Unlike prior works that rely on Euclidean distance for primitive density modeling--a metric misaligned with surface geometry under deformation--QGS introduces geodesic distance-based density distributions. This innovation ensures that density weights adapt intrinsically to the primitive curvature, preserving consistency during shape changes (e.g., from planar disks to curved paraboloids). By solving geodesic distances in closed form on quadric surfaces, QGS enables surface-aware splatting, where a single primitive can represent complex curvature that previously required dozens of planar surfels, potentially reducing memory usage while maintaining efficient rendering via fast ray-quadric intersection. Experiments on DTU, Tanks and Temples, and MipNeRF360 datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art surface reconstruction, with QGS reducing geometric error (chamfer distance) by 33% over 2DGS and 27% over GOF on the DTU dataset. Crucially, QGS retains competitive appearance quality, bridging the gap between geometric precision and visual fidelity for applications like robotics and immersive reality.
arxiv_record.authors: Ziyu Zhang, Binbin Huang, Hanqing Jiang, Liyang Zhou, Xiaojun Xiang, Shunhan Shen
arxiv_record.title: Quadratic Gaussian Splatting: High Quality Surface Reconstruction with Second-order Geometric Primitives

C1.justification: The central claims about quadric primitives, geodesic Gaussian weights, and detailed reconstruction remain. v2 adds explicit claims about density consistency during deformation and fewer primitives/potential memory savings, quantifies DTU error reductions as 33% versus 2DGS and 27% versus GOF, and drops stricter sorting from the three highlighted contributions.

C2.justification: v2 develops a substantive explanation of geodesic weights preserving density under deformation and attributes low-texture artifacts to missing multi-view regularization. It presents tighter bounds as addressing the earlier speed problem. However, it removes the fog/transparency limitation and several reconstruction tradeoffs, and replaces v1's acknowledged Neuralangelo gap with overbroad superiority language despite the no-MV variant's 0.71 versus Neuralangelo's 0.61 in Table 1.

D1.justification: v2 documents the tighter bounding construction and mentions GPU memory-access optimization. It removes v1's explicit 60,000-iteration Courthouse/aerial training schedule, densification and opacity-reset settings, baseline gradient threshold, and depth-distortion stop-gradient detail. These are documentation losses; they do not establish that those underlying procedures changed.

E1.justification: v2 adds a weakly textured, geometry-rich Google Scanned Objects subset for geometry-versus-point-count evaluation and primitive visualization (Figures 1 and 11). DTU, Tanks and Temples, Mip-NeRF 360, and the supplementary aerial urban scene were already covered in v1.

E2.justification: DTU Table 1 adds 3DGS, Gaussian surfels, GSDF, GS-pull, and PGSR as evaluated comparators. PGSR also enters the TNT and Mip-NeRF 360 comparisons, while NeuS is removed from TNT Table 2. The qualitative DTU comparisons are expanded to include PGSR and, in the supplement, GOF.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes reported mesh extraction from equally weighted median/expected depth to median depth alone, and the TSDF truncation threshold from 0.002 to 0.02. v2 also introduces gradient-threshold sweeps, fixed-scale and Euclidean-distance controls, and FPS/storage evaluation. These alter evaluation conditions; the PDFs do not establish same-setting comparability for all revised scores.

E4.justification: v1's two-scene curvature study and four-scan sorting study are replaced by six-scene TNT component ablations, including multi-view regularization (v2 Table 4). New controls test fixed disk-like primitives and Euclidean distance (Table 5), while Figure 1 and supplementary Table 6 examine point-count efficiency and tighter bounds. The separate per-tile sorting comparison from v1 is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Gaussian distribution parameters in the method are not uncertainty estimates for experimental results.

E6.justification: DTU mean Chamfer distance changes from v1's 0.73 mm to v2's 0.71 without multi-view regularization and 0.54 with it; TNT mean F1 changes from 0.44 to 0.45 and 0.50, respectively. These are revised results under changed method/settings. Table 3 also revises rendering scores, including 3DGS indoor PSNR from 30.99 to 30.52. arxiv_record.abstract:
Token merging can effectively accelerate various vision systems by processing
groups of similar tokens only once and sharing the results across them.
However, existing token grouping methods are often ad hoc and random,
disregarding the actual content of the samples. We show that preserving
high-information tokens during merging - those essential for semantic fidelity
and structural details - significantly improves sample quality, producing finer
details and more coherent, realistic generations. Despite being simple and
intuitive, this approach remains underexplored.
  To do so, we propose an importance-based token merging method that
prioritizes the most critical tokens in computational resource allocation,
leveraging readily available importance scores, such as those from
classifier-free guidance in diffusion models. Experiments show that our
approach significantly outperforms baseline methods across multiple
applications, including text-to-image synthesis, multi-view image generation,
and video generation with various model architectures such as Stable Diffusion,
Zero123++, AnimateDiff, or PixArt-$\alpha$.
arxiv_record.authors: Haoyu Wu, Jingyi Xu, Hieu Le, Dimitris Samaras
arxiv_record.title: Importance-Based Token Merging for Efficient Image and Video Generation

C1.justification: The central claim that preserving important tokens improves generation quality at comparable computational cost remains. v2 broadens the contribution framing from CFG-based selection to a framework accepting different importance signals and explicitly extends its performance claims across U-Net and transformer architectures.

C2.justification: v2 adds a gradient-based saliency interpretation of CFG and revises the step-distilled-model limitation by explaining and demonstrating an attention-map workaround. It acknowledges the alternative’s possible memory cost and suggests weighted importance signals for multi-guidance scenarios. The existing warning about temporal merging reducing video dynamics remains.

D1.justification: v2 supplies implementation information for the extensions, including PixArt-α layer placement, sampling settings and spatial matching, final-block attention-map averaging, and the LCM Dreamshaper v7 configuration. It also supplies new qualitative prompts. Most original sampling, pruning, hardware, and metric-library details remain, with several moved into Appendix B.

E1.justification: Both versions cover text-to-image, image-conditioned multi-view, and text-to-video generation, retaining MS-COCO, GSO, and VBench evaluations. PixArt-α, consistency models, and acceleration combinations expand model configurations without establishing new datasets, task requirements, or input environments.

E2.justification: v2 adds ToFu to the Stable Diffusion quantitative and qualitative comparisons (Table 1 and Figures 5 and 9). It also adds unmerged Zero123++ outputs to the supplementary multi-view comparison (Figure 11). ToMeSD and the qualitative ATC comparison remain.

E3.justification: v2 substantially expands evaluation configurations: PixArt-α uses 20 sampling steps, CFG 4.5, and merging in self- and cross-attention layers 7–20; Appendix A adds a four-step consistency model, controlled top/bottom-30% pruning, and acceleration combinations. The design ablation also replaces r=0.6 with r=0.7. Original Stable Diffusion, Zero123++, and AnimateDiff settings are largely retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of cross-attention importance, whether high-CFG tokens matter more than low-CFG tokens, compatibility with DeepCache/Faster Diffusion/FRDiff, and sensitivity to pruning duration across three tasks (Tables 8, 10, 12, and 15). The original early-pruning and sampling-step analyses remain as Tables 14 and 13.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. The additional v2 tables retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive quantitative and qualitative results for ToFu, PixArt-α, cross-attention, consistency models, and supplementary analyses. For example, its new PixArt-α comparison reports FID 34.02 versus ToMeSD’s 65.46 at r=0.5. Within retained multi-view settings, the proposed method’s r=0.6 PSNR changes from 14.83 to 14.85 and LPIPS from 0.269 to 0.263 (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 3). The changed design-ablation rows use different merging ratios, rather than demonstrate same-setting gains.

M1.justification: The core important-token pool, destination sampling, and partitioning procedure remain. v2 adds an implemented cross-attention-based importance variant and uses pixel-location distance instead of feature similarity for PixArt-α matching (Section 4.3 and Appendix B). The original early-pruning procedure is retained in Appendix B.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution statements, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around general importance-based merging. The standalone preliminaries section is removed and its relevant explanations integrated elsewhere. Early-pruning discussion and several implementation settings move to the appendix, substantially revising the narrative structure.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the examples in Figures 1 and 4, transposes and expands Figure 5 to include ToFu, and adds PixArt-α visual comparisons. Table 1 gains comparator columns, several new experimental tables appear, and supplementary image grids expand to include additional method variants and unmerged Zero123++ outputs.

R1.justification: v2 adds five cited works, including InstructPix2Pix, Faster Diffusion, ToMA, and LCM-LoRA, while retaining the earlier references. ToFu was already cited in v1 but receives an explicit methodological contrast in v2. Architectural background expands without substantially reorganizing the related-work positioning.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 2 adds the approximate relationship between CFG magnitude and the conditional log-likelihood gradient. It also corrects the ablation discussion’s pool-size expression from (1+r)(1+p) to (1−r)(1+p), matching the formula already used in v1’s method. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1’s broad applicability claim rested on related U-Net-based models and left step-distilled models as a limitation. v2 materially strengthens that evidence through PixArt-α and attention-based consistency-model experiments, a relevant ToFu comparison, and a direct test of CFG token importance (Tables 2, 11, 1, and 10). A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same importance-based token-merging work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, references, and Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable comparison despite the changed title and organization.

arxiv_record.abstract: With recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), grounding and referring capabilities have gained increasing attention for achieving detailed understanding and flexible user interaction. However, these capabilities still remain underdeveloped in visual document understanding due to the scarcity of fine-grained datasets and comprehensive benchmarks. To fill this gap, we propose the DOcument Grounding and Referring data engine (DOGR-Engine), which generates two types of high-quality fine-grained document data: (1) multi-granular parsing data to improve text localization and recognition, and (2) instruction-tuning data to activate MLLMs' grounding and referring capabilities in dialogue and reasoning. Using the DOGR-Engine, we construct DOGR-Bench, a benchmark covering seven grounding and referring tasks across three document types (chart, poster, and PDF document), offering a comprehensive evaluation of fine-grained document understanding. Leveraging the generated data, we further develop DOGR, a strong baseline model that excels in text localization and recognition, while precisely grounds and refers to key textual information during conversation and reasoning, thereby advancing document understanding to a finer granularity and enable flexible interaction paradigms.

arxiv_record.abstract: Decomposing physically-based materials from images into their constituent properties remains challenging, particularly when maintaining both computational efficiency and physical consistency. While recent diffusion-based approaches have shown promise, they face substantial computational overhead due to multiple denoising steps and separate models for different material properties. We present SuperMat, a single-step framework that achieves high-quality material decomposition with one-step inference. This enables end-to-end training with perceptual and re-render losses while decomposing albedo, metallic, and roughness maps at millisecond-scale speeds. We further extend our framework to 3D objects through a UV refinement network, enabling consistent material estimation across viewpoints while maintaining efficiency. Experiments demonstrate that SuperMat achieves state-of-the-art PBR material decomposition quality while reducing inference time from seconds to milliseconds per image, and completes PBR material estimation for 3D objects in approximately 3 seconds. The project page is at https://hyj542682306.github.io/SuperMat/.
arxiv_record.authors: Yijia Hong, Yuan-Chen Guo, Ran Yi, Yulong Chen, Yan-Pei Cao, Lizhuang Ma
arxiv_record.title: SuperMat: Physically Consistent PBR Material Estimation at Interactive Rates

native_poster_event.abstract: Decomposing physically-based materials from images into their constituent properties remains challenging, particularly when maintaining both computational efficiency and physical consistency. While recent diffusion-based approaches have shown promise, they face substantial computational overhead due to multiple denoising steps and separate models for different material properties. We present SuperMat, a single-step framework that achieves high-quality material decomposition with one-step inference. This enables end-to-end training with perceptual and re-render losses while decomposing albedo, metallic, and roughness maps at millisecond-scale speeds. We further extend our framework to 3D objects through a UV refinement network, enabling consistent material estimation across viewpoints while maintaining efficiency. Experiments demonstrate that SuperMat achieves state-of-the-art PBR material decomposition quality while reducing inference time from seconds to milliseconds per image, and completes PBR material estimation for 3D objects in approximately 3 seconds.

C1.justification: The headline claims of state-of-the-art single-step decomposition, millisecond inference, and approximately three-second 3D processing remain. The 3D contribution is refined to explicitly incorporate SuperMatMV and joint cross-view prediction, without changing the paper's overall objectives.

C2.justification: New Section 10 explains limitations involving detail sharpness, inability to obtain alternative predictions by rerunning the deterministic model, and difficulty with transparent, multilayered, or highly reflective materials. v4 also interprets training-data diversity as improving generalization and assigns cross-view consistency more directly to SuperMatMV, emphasizing missing-region completion for UV refinement.

D1.justification: v4 adds a project-page link, the expert branches' parameter overhead, RM-channel conventions, and SuperMatMV initialization and training details, including three epochs with batches of eight six-view inputs. It removes v1's exact VGG feature-layer selection. These are targeted additions and losses of reproducibility information alongside the protocol revisions.

E1.justification: v4 adds Digital Twin Catalog to training and image-space evaluation, retaining Objaverse and BlenderVault. It also introduces StanfordORB and a distinct evaluation of complete 3D objects under novel viewpoints and lighting. Conversely, v1's standalone captured-photograph demonstrations in Figure 14 are removed.

E2.justification: v4 adds StableMaterialMV to Table 1 and the corresponding per-dataset comparisons. All six original baselines remain, so comparator membership expands by one relevant multi-view variant.

E3.justification: Reported SuperMat training changes from 100k to 75k objects, three to sixteen rendered lighting conditions, 115 to 30 epochs, batch size 16 to 32, and learning rate 1e-5 to 2e-5. The re-render lighting pool changes from 716 to 50 maps. v4 also explicitly retrains IIR and RGB→X on its data and introduces a 3D evaluation using 28 objects, 60 novel viewpoints, and three environment maps.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained end-to-end, re-render-loss, and loss-function ablations, v4 adds synthetic-only, real-captured-only, and mixed-data training comparisons in Table 3. Table 4 adds numerical evaluation before and after UV refinement, substantially strengthening v1's qualitative analysis of that component.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and averages without independent-run variability, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The additional experiments retain this reporting practice.

E6.justification: Main and per-dataset results are extensively revised, with new SuperMatMV and DTC entries. New Table 5 reports pipeline relighting PSNRs of 27.00 on BlenderVault and 24.99 on StanfordORB. Table 2 also changes the loss ranking: perceptual loss leads every metric in v1, whereas L1 leads albedo and metallic SSIM in v4. Changed training and evaluation conditions prevent interpreting revised scores as direct same-setting improvements.

M1.justification: v1 processes views independently with SuperMat before UV blending and refinement. v4 introduces SuperMatMV, using 3D self-attention and camera-extrinsic conditioning to jointly decompose six views, and incorporates it into the 3D pipeline. This substantially changes cross-view processing; the original single-view architecture and losses remain.

P1.justification: The main narrative order and much of the prose remain. v4 rewrites portions of the introduction and related work, moves the PBR subsection into the supplement and training-data description into the main experiments, reorganizes supplementary discussions, and updates terminology and affiliations.

P2.justification: Qualitative comparison grids are extensively rebuilt with paired viewpoints and additional multi-view columns. v4 adds novel-view relighting and DTC figures, removes the captured-photograph gallery, adds three experimental tables, and expands the detailed tables with DTC columns. Figure 2 is relocated, while several existing pipeline and result illustrations are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning across material generation, inverse rendering, image decomposition, and UV-space generation. New citations include rendering-aware material estimation, MVDream for multi-view conditioning, and Clay for expert branches, alongside broader generation literature. This changes attribution and contextualization beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The rendering equation, perceptual and re-render losses, and UV-blending mathematics are retained. The PBR formulation moves from v1 Section 3.1 to v4 supplementary Section 6, with equation renumbering but no substantive mathematical revision or new proof.

improvement.justification: v1's central 3D-pipeline claim was supported mainly by qualitative examples. v4 adds quantitative ground-truth novel-view relighting comparisons and UV-refinement validation, addressing an important evidential gap. Training-data ablations, explicit baseline retraining, and substantive limitations further improve rigor. These gains outweigh the loss of the captured-photo gallery and exact VGG-layer specification. The improvement rests on stronger validation and clearer boundaries, not on directly comparing aggregate scores obtained under changed settings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SuperMat and contain readable main texts, equations, tables, figures, and supplementary material. Corresponding components and relocated material can be matched reliably despite substantial experimental and methodological additions.

after.justification: v4 reports original SuperMat and SuperMatMV results, training-data ablations, quantitative UV-refinement evaluation, and novel-view relighting experiments in the main text and supplement.

before.justification: v1 reports original material-decomposition and relighting results in Table 1, loss-function experiments in supplementary Table 2, and qualitative 3D reconstruction and ablation results.
