arxiv_record.abstract:
We present PersonaCraft, a framework for controllable and occlusion-robust
full-body personalized image synthesis of multiple individuals in complex
scenes. Current methods struggle with occlusion-heavy scenarios and complete
body personalization, as 2D pose conditioning lacks 3D geometry, often leading
to ambiguous occlusions and anatomical distortions, and many approaches focus
solely on facial identity. In contrast, our PersonaCraft integrates diffusion
models with 3D human modeling, employing SMPLx-ControlNet, to utilize 3D
geometry like depth and normal maps for robust 3D-aware pose conditioning and
enhanced anatomical coherence. To handle fine-grained occlusions, we propose
Occlusion Boundary Enhancer Network that exploits depth edge signals with
occlusion-focused training, and Occlusion-Aware Classifier-Free Guidance
strategy that selectively reinforces conditioning in occluded regions without
affecting unoccluded areas. PersonaCraft can seamlessly be combined with Face
Identity ControlNet, achieving full-body multi-human personalization and thus
marking a significant advancement beyond prior approaches that concentrate only
on facial identity. Our dual-pathway body shape representation with SMPLx-based
shape parameters and textual refinement, enables precise full-body
personalization and flexible user-defined body shape adjustments. Extensive
quantitative experiments and user studies demonstrate that PersonaCraft
significantly outperforms existing methods in generating high-quality,
multi-person images with accurate personalization and robust occlusion
handling.

native_poster_event.abstract: Personalized image generation has been significantly advanced, enabling the creation of highly realistic and customized images. However, existing methods often struggle with generating images of multiple people due to occlusions and fail to accurately personalize full-body shapes. In this paper, we propose PersonaCraft, a novel approach that combines diffusion models with 3D human modeling to address these limitations. Our method effectively manages occlusions by incorporating 3D-aware pose conditioning with SMPLx-ControlNet and accurately personalizes human full-body shapes through SMPLx fitting. Additionally, PersonaCraft enables user-defined body shape adjustments, adding flexibility for individual body customization. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of PersonaCraft in generating high-quality, realistic images of multiple individuals while resolving occlusion issues, thus establishing a new standard for multi-person personalized image synthesis.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion add central contributions concerning fine-grained occlusion handling through OccNet and OccCFG, complementary depth/normal conditioning, and dual-pathway body representation. V1's broader full-body personalization and user-defined shape-control claims remain, but the claimed technical contribution substantially expands.

C2.justification: V2 qualifies the effectiveness of depth conditioning for fine-grained occlusions and explains complementary depth/normal information, oversaturation from uniformly strong guidance, and SMPLx's difficulty representing muscle versus fat distribution. These substantive mechanism explanations and applicability qualifications extend v1's discussion, while dependence on face networks and fitting accuracy remains acknowledged.

D1.justification: V2 specifies Canny thresholds of 5/15, regional guidance scales of 3/5, conditioning weights of 0.8, and implementation details for CLIP-based body descriptions and regional prompting. Existing backbone, optimizer, hardware, and embedding details largely remain. V1's project-page access pointer is omitted.

E1.justification: Both versions use MPII-derived training data and COCO-WholeBody evaluation covering one to five people, alongside custom scenes, body-shape control, and stylization. Pose-guided generation was already tested in v1 Figure 9(a); v2 substantially expands its evaluation within the existing human-generation coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds pose-generation comparisons with T2IAdapter-SDXL, ControlNet-Flux, and HumanSD-SD2, and evaluates training-data-matched OMG variants and ControlNet-SDXL in Tables S8-S9. The personalization baseline families remain, but Textual Inversion and IPA-Face+OMG disappear from corresponding handshake and birthday qualitative panels (v1 Figure 4; v2 Figure 6).

E3.justification: Denoising steps change from 50 to 30, and the reported single-person:multi-person training ratio reverses from 1:2 to 2:1; the PDFs do not establish whether the latter reflects resampling or correction. V2 adds MPJPE, AP-0.5, IS/KID, and matched-training controls. The personalization study changes from 7 cases/123 participants to 15/103, and a pose study uses 15 cases/114 participants.

E4.justification: V2 adds depth/normal/RGB comparisons, OccNet and OccCFG ablations, spatial-guidance comparisons, conflicting body-composition examples, and a fitting-failure case (Table 5; Figures 9-11 and S22-S23). Body-parameter and conditioning-scale studies remain, while v1's explicit face-masking ablation in Figure 9(b) is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Both present point estimates and preference percentages. Changed user-study sample sizes concern evaluation design, without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces overall face/body/CLIP scores of 0.305/0.531/0.252 with 0.317/0.560/0.273 under the revised method and settings, so these are not established same-setting gains. V2 adds pose, image-quality, component-ablation, and fine-tuned-baseline results; updates personalization preferences; and removes v1's cumulative Top-3 preference table.

M1.justification: V1 combines depth-only SCNet with masked face-identity conditioning. V2 adds depth-and-normal SCNets, an occlusion-boundary network trained on masked depth edges, occlusion-dependent residual fusion, and spatially varying classifier-free guidance. It also introduces optional CLIP-derived body descriptions with regional prompting (Sections 3.1-3.3 and B.1).

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, method narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Experiments are reorganized into personalization and pose-controlled generation sections. Stylization, efficiency, and body-parameter analysis move into the supplement, and the bibliography now precedes a separately headed supplementary section.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the pipeline and training diagrams, restructures qualitative comparisons into horizontal grids with enlarged detail views, and adds component-analysis and failure-case figures. Table 1 changes from individual identity-count columns to Single/Multi/Total groups and adds pose/image-quality columns. Numerous figures and tables are added, resized, or relocated.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around controllable human generation and spatial guidance, discussing HumanSD, Stable-Pose, HumanLDM, MIMO, StoryMaker, and ID-Patch. It additionally connects its new mechanisms to guidance-related prior work and MultiDiffusion, extending v1's emphasis on personalization and depth-based pose control.

T1.justification: V2 adds mathematical definitions for ray-intersection-based occlusion masks and spatial guidance, and revises residual fusion (Equations 2-5). V1's explicit SMPLx vertex-shaping equation is omitted. These are limited changes to algorithmic formalization; neither version develops theorem/proof-based analysis, and the appendix identity and CLIP metric formulas remain equivalent.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of pose and occlusion claims that v1 supported mainly qualitatively: direct pose metrics, component ablations, and matched-training comparisons in Tables 5 and S8-S9 make the advantages more assessable. Failure analysis also improves transparency. Reporting defects temper these gains: the lowest-KID claim contradicts Table 3 (HumanSD 0.082 versus PersonaCraft 0.091), and Table S6's body-shape total conflicts with Table 1. These defects do not outweigh the substantial improvement in experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PersonaCraft by the same authors. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, references, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revision and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 reports original personalization and pose-generation experiments, component ablations, comparisons with fine-tuned baselines, and two user studies.

before.justification: V1 reports original image-generation experiments, quantitative comparisons, ablations, inference timings, and a user study in the main text and appendix.

arxiv_record.abstract: Bridging the gap between ego-centric and exo-centric views has been a long-standing question in computer vision. In this paper, we focus on the emerging Ego-Exo object correspondence task, which aims to understand object relations across ego-exo perspectives through segmentation. While numerous segmentation models have been proposed, most operate on a single image (view), making them impractical for cross-view scenarios. PSALM, a recently proposed segmentation method, stands out as a notable exception with its demonstrated zero-shot ability on this task. However, due to the drastic viewpoint change between ego and exo, PSALM fails to accurately locate and segment objects, especially in complex backgrounds or when object appearances change significantly. To address these issues, we propose ObjectRelator, a novel approach featuring two key modules: Multimodal Condition Fusion (MCFuse) and SSL-based Cross-View Object Alignment (XObjAlign). MCFuse introduces language as an additional cue, integrating both visual masks and textual descriptions to improve object localization and prevent incorrect associations. XObjAlign enforces cross-view consistency through self-supervised alignment, enhancing robustness to object appearance variations. Extensive experiments demonstrate ObjectRelator's effectiveness on the large-scale Ego-Exo4D benchmark and HANDAL-X (an adapted dataset for cross-view segmentation) with state-of-the-art performance. Code is made available at: http://yuqianfu.com/ObjectRelator.

It also explains why visibility accuracy is relatively easy. Existing mechanism explanations, failure categories and the limitation of frame-level modeling largely remain.

D1.justification: V2 documents HANDAL-X construction, its 44,202 training and 14,074 test samples, and associated training settings and time. It replaces a promised release with a code-availability statement and project link. Most existing implementation details are retained or relocated, although the expanded learning-rate choices lack an experiment-specific mapping.

E1.justification: V2 adds HANDAL-X, covering cross-view images of manipulable objects intended for robotics applications, alongside the retained Ego-Exo4D domains. It also evaluates first-frame-only queries and includes target-invisible cases when evaluating visibility accuracy, substantially expanding the tested conditions.

arxiv_record.abstract: Depth completion (DC) aims to predict a dense depth map from an RGB image and a sparse depth map. Existing DC methods generalize poorly to new datasets or unseen sparse depth patterns, limiting their real-world applications. We propose OMNI-DC, a highly robust DC model that generalizes well zero-shot to various datasets. The key design is a novel Multi-resolution Depth Integrator, allowing our model to deal with very sparse depth inputs. We also introduce a novel Laplacian loss to model the ambiguity in the training process. Moreover, we train OMNI-DC on a mixture of high-quality datasets with a scale normalization technique and synthetic depth patterns. Extensive experiments on 7 datasets show consistent improvements over baselines, reducing errors by as much as 43%. Codes and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/princeton-vl/OMNI-DC.

arxiv_record.abstract: Standard clothing asset generation involves restoring forward-facing flat-lay garment images displayed on a clear background by extracting clothing information from diverse real-world contexts, which presents significant challenges due to highly standardized structure sampling distributions and clothing semantic absence in complex scenarios. Existing models have limited spatial perception, often exhibiting structural hallucinations and texture distortion in this high-specification generative task. To address this issue, we propose a novel Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework, termed RAGDiffusion, to enhance structure determinacy and mitigate hallucinations by assimilating knowledge from language models and external databases. RAGDiffusion consists of two processes: (1) Retrieval-based structure aggregation, which employs contrastive learning and a Structure Locally Linear Embedding (SLLE) to derive global structure and spatial landmarks, providing both soft and hard guidance to counteract structural ambiguities; and (2) Omni-level faithful garment generation, which introduces a coarse-to-fine texture alignment that ensures fidelity in pattern and detail components within the diffusing. Extensive experiments on challenging real-world datasets demonstrate that RAGDiffusion synthesizes structurally and texture-faithful clothing assets with significant performance improvements, representing a pioneering effort in high-specification faithful generation with RAG to confront intrinsic hallucinations and enhance fidelity.
arxiv_record.authors: Xianfeng Tan, Yuhan Li, Wenxiang Shang, Yubo Wu, Jian Wang, Xuanhong Chen, Yi Zhang, Ran Lin, Bingbing Ni
arxiv_record.title: RAGDiffusion: Faithful Cloth Generation via External Knowledge Assimilation

arxiv_record.abstract: Scene text recognition (STR) suffers from challenges of either less realistic synthetic training data or the difficulty of collecting sufficient high-quality real-world data, limiting the effectiveness of trained models. Meanwhile, despite producing holistically appealing text images, diffusion-based visual text generation methods struggle to synthesize accurate and realistic instance-level text at scale. To tackle this, we introduce TextSSR: a novel pipeline for Synthesizing Scene Text Recognition training data. TextSSR targets three key synthesizing characteristics: accuracy, realism, and scalability. It achieves accuracy through a proposed region-centric text generation with position-glyph enhancement, ensuring proper character placement. It maintains realism by guiding style and appearance generation using contextual hints from surrounding text or background. This character-aware diffusion architecture enjoys precise character-level control and semantic coherence preservation, without relying on natural language prompts. Therefore, TextSSR supports large-scale generation through combinatorial text permutations. Based on these, we present TextSSR-F, a dataset of 3.55 million quality-screened text instances. Extensive experiments show that STR models trained on TextSSR-F outperform those trained on existing synthetic datasets by clear margins on common benchmarks, and further improvements are observed when mixed with real-world training data. Code is available at https://github.com/YesianRohn/TextSSR.
arxiv_record.authors: Xingsong Ye, Yongkun Du, Yunbo Tao, Zhineng Chen
arxiv_record.title: TextSSR: Diffusion-based Data Synthesis for Scene Text Recognition

native_poster_event.abstract: Scene text recognition (STR) suffers from challenges of either less realistic synthetic training data or the difficulty of collecting sufficient high-quality real-world data, limiting the effectiveness of trained models. Meanwhile, despite producing holistically appealing text images, diffusion-based visual text generation methods struggle to synthesize accurate and realistic instance-level text on a large scale. To tackle this, we introduce TextSSR: a novel pipeline for Synthesizing Scene Text Recognition training data. TextSSR targets three key synthesizing characteristics: accuracy, realism, and scalability. It achieves accuracy through a proposed region-centric text generation with position-glyph enhancement, ensuring proper character placement. It maintains realism by guiding style and appearance generation using contextual hints from surrounding text or background. This character-aware diffusion architecture enjoys precise character-level control and semantic coherence preservation, without relying on natural language prompts. Therefore, TextSSR supports large-scale generation through combinatorial text permutations. Based on these, we present TextSSR-F, a dataset of 3.55 million quality-screened text instances. Extensive experiments show that STR models trained on TextSSR-F outperform those trained on existing synthetic datasets by clear margins on common benchmarks, and further improvements are observed when mixed with real-world training data. Code is available in Supplementary Materials.

arxiv_record.abstract: Tracking Any Point (TAP) plays a crucial role in motion analysis. Video-based approaches rely on iterative local matching for tracking, but they assume linear motion during the blind time between frames, which leads to point loss under large displacements or nonlinear motion. The high temporal resolution and motion blur-free characteristics of event cameras provide continuous, fine-grained motion information, capturing subtle variations with microsecond precision. This paper presents an event-based framework for tracking any point, which tackles the challenges posed by spatial sparsity and motion sensitivity in events through two tailored modules. Specifically, to resolve ambiguities caused by event sparsity, a motion-guidance module incorporates kinematic vectors into the local matching process. Additionally, a variable motion aware module is integrated to ensure temporally consistent responses that are insensitive to varying velocities, thereby enhancing matching precision. To validate the effectiveness of the approach, two event dataset for tracking any point is constructed by simulation. The method improves the $Survival_{50}$ metric by 17.9% over event-only tracking of any point baseline. Moreover, on standard feature tracking benchmarks, it outperforms all existing methods, even those that combine events and video frames.

P1.justification: The method overview and module explanations are substantially rewritten. R1.justification: v1 states that event-based TAP has not yet been proposed. v2 discusses FE-TAP and ETAP and positions MATE against their appearance-based matching, materially revising its novelty framing. T1.justification: v2 adds an explicit mathematical definition of temporally weighted supervision in Equation 8, including the gamma-based weighting absent from v1's MAE description. The surface-gradient, plane-fitting and event-rate derivations otherwise remain, with renumbering and notation changes rather than new proofs.

improvement.justification: Ev-Davis and event-adapted TAP comparisons substantially strengthen the evidence for generalization and comparative performance. Targeted ablations and the implementation supplement also address important gaps in assessing and reproducing v1. These gains outweigh the loss of FPS results, simulation instructions and the project link. Claims still need qualification: v2 says it outperforms all feature trackers, but Table 2 reports EC EFA of 0.875 versus ETAP's 0.876.

arxiv_record.abstract: 3D scene understanding is a long-standing challenge in computer vision and a key component in enabling mixed reality, wearable computing, and embodied AI. Providing a solution to these applications requires a multifaceted approach that covers scene-centric, object-centric, as well as interaction-centric capabilities. While there exist numerous datasets and algorithms approaching the former two problems, the task of understanding interactable and articulated objects is underrepresented and only partly covered in the research field. In this work, we address this shortcoming by introducing: (1) Articulate3D, an expertly curated 3D dataset featuring high-quality manual annotations on 280 indoor scenes. Articulate3D provides 8 types of annotations for articulated objects, covering parts and detailed motion information, all stored in a standardized scene representation format designed for scalable 3D content creation, exchange and seamless integration into simulation environments. (2) USDNet, a novel unified framework capable of simultaneously predicting part segmentation along with a full specification of motion attributes for articulated objects. We evaluate USDNet on Articulate3D as well as two existing datasets, demonstrating the advantage of our unified dense prediction approach. Furthermore, we highlight the value of Articulate3D through cross-dataset and cross-domain evaluations and showcase its applicability in downstream tasks such as scene editing through LLM prompting and robotic policy training for articulated object manipulation. We provide open access to our dataset, benchmark, and method's source code.

arxiv_record.abstract: Diffusion models have attracted significant attention due to its exceptional data generation capabilities in fields such as image synthesis. However, recent studies have shown that diffusion models are vulnerable to copyright infringement attacks, where attackers inject strategically modified non-infringing images into the training set, inducing the model to generate infringing content under the prompt of specific poisoned captions. To address this issue, we first propose a defense framework, CopyrightShield, to defend against the above attack. Specifically, we analyze the memorization mechanism of diffusion models and find that attacks exploit the model's overfitting to specific spatial positions and prompts, causing it to reproduce poisoned samples under backdoor triggers. Based on this, we propose a poisoned sample detection method using spatial masking and data attribution to quantify poisoning risk and accurately identify hidden backdoor samples. To further mitigate memorization of poisoned features, we introduce an adaptive optimization strategy that integrates a dynamic penalty term into the training loss, reducing reliance on infringing features while preserving generative performance. Experimental results demonstrate that CopyrightShield significantly improves poisoned sample detection performance across two attack scenarios, achieving average F1-scores of 0.665, retarding the First-Attack Epoch (FAE) of 115.2% and decreasing the Copyright Infringement Rate (CIR) by 56.7%. Compared to the SoTA backdoor defense in diffusion models, the defense effect is improved by about 25%, showcasing its superiority and practicality in enhancing the security of diffusion models.
arxiv_record.authors: Zhixiang Guo, Siyuan Liang, Aishan Liu, Dacheng Tao

It removes v1's substantive liability-attribution discussion. The limitations concerning real-world copyrighted images and future attack methods are retained.

D1.justification: V2 adds attribution pseudocode, trigger-prompt templates, baseline implementation descriptions, and disclosures of the default SD v1.4 model, SSCD/Disc-MixUp, guidance scale 7.5, and 1000 diffusion steps. E1.justification: V1 evaluates Pokemon character generation. V2 retains this coverage and adds a continual-pretraining scenario using COYO-700M clean images and Midjourney v5 copyright targets, extending evaluation to general imagery. SilentBadDiffusion remains the evaluated attack.

E2.justification: V1 compares defended models with undefended SilentBadDiffusion models. V2 additionally evaluates T2IShield and TERD as defense comparators in Table 2, and TRAK, Journey TRAK, and D-TRAK as detection comparators in Table 3. E3.justification: The detection threshold sweep changes from 0.2/0.25/0.3 to 0.3/0.35/0.4, with the experimental selection changing from 0.25 to 0.35. V2 adds FID/CLIP evaluation over 500 random prompts and specifies an LDS-based threshold procedure for attribution baselines. The 100-epoch budget and 100 generated images per poisoned caption for CIR are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds detection-only and training-only component ablations in Table 5, fixed-versus-adaptive penalty results in supplementary Table 6, and attribution-score analysis in Figure 2. V1 mentions a fixed-coefficient sweep but does not supply these comparative results. The earlier rotation and model-version analyses remain, with revised presentation.

E5.justification: Both versions report 20 independent experiments per evaluated scenario without reporting seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Applying the same practice to the additional scenario does not change uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: At Pokemon poisoning rate 0.1, reported defense CIR/FAE changes from 0.318/84.13 to 0.305/85.93; the undefended values remain 0.650/50.15. P2.justification: V2 redraws the framework diagram, expands the rotation illustration with attribution plots, restructures tables around datasets and comparators, and replaces v1's model-version table with bar charts. R1.justification: V2 introduces dedicated data-attribution related work covering TRAK, Journey TRAK, and D-TRAK, and positions CopyrightShield within a detection–cleaning–retraining framework. arxiv_record.abstract: Driving view synthesis along free-form trajectories is essential for realistic driving simulations, enabling closed-loop evaluation of end-to-end driving policies. Existing methods excel at view interpolation along recorded paths but struggle to generalize to novel trajectories due to limited viewpoints in driving videos. To tackle this challenge, we propose DriveX, a novel free-form driving view synthesis framework, that progressively distills generative prior into the 3D Gaussian model during its optimization. Within this framework, we utilize a video diffusion model to refine the degraded novel trajectory renderings from the in-training Gaussian model, while the restored videos in turn serve as additional supervision for optimizing the 3D Gaussian. Concretely, we craft an inpainting-based video restoration task, which can disentangle the identification of degraded regions from the generative capability of the diffusion model and remove the need of simulating specific degraded pattern in the training of the diffusion model. To further enhance the consistency and fidelity of generated contents, the pseudo ground truth is progressively updated with gradually improved novel trajectory rendering, allowing both components to co-adapt and reinforce each other while minimizing the disruption on the optimization. By tightly integrating 3D scene representation with generative prior, DriveX achieves high-quality view synthesis beyond recorded trajectories in real time--unlocking new possibilities for flexible and realistic driving simulations on free-form trajectories.
arxiv_record.authors: Zeyu Yang, Zijie Pan, Yuankun Yang, Xiatian Zhu, Li Zhang
arxiv_record.title: Driving View Synthesis on Free-form Trajectories with Generative Prior

E2.justification: V2 Table 2 adds evaluated comparisons with ReconDreamer and FreeVS alongside DriveDreamer4D. P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and methodological narrative are extensively rewritten. The title also adds DriveX and changes scene synthesis to view synthesis.

P2.justification: V2 expands Table 1 with recorded-view metrics, restructures Table 2 into different comparison panels, and adds a component-ablation table. Qualitative comparison grids are reorganized, and new figures cover fine-tuning, PandaSet, aggressive viewpoints, failure cases, and mask evolution. arxiv_record.abstract:
Diffusion-based models have recently revolutionized image generation,
achieving unprecedented levels of fidelity. However, consistent generation of
high-quality images remains challenging partly due to the lack of conditioning
mechanisms for perceptual quality. In this work, we propose methods to
integrate image quality assessment (IQA) models into diffusion-based
generators, enabling quality-aware image generation. We show that diffusion
models can learn complex qualitative relationships from both IQA models'
outputs and internal activations. First, we experiment with gradient-based
guidance to optimize image quality directly and show this method has limited
generalizability. To address this, we introduce IQA-Adapter, a novel framework
that conditions generation on target quality levels by learning the implicit
relationship between images and quality scores. When conditioned on high target
quality, IQA-Adapter can shift the distribution of generated images towards a
higher-quality subdomain, and, inversely, it can be used as a degradation
model, generating progressively more distorted images when provided with a
lower-quality signal. Under high-quality condition, IQA-Adapter achieves up to
a 10% improvement across multiple objective metrics, as confirmed by a user
preference study, while preserving generative diversity and content.
Furthermore, we extend IQA-Adapter to a reference-based conditioning scenario,
utilizing the rich activation space of IQA models to transfer highly specific,
content-agnostic qualitative features between images.

In this work, we propose methods to integrate image quality assessment (IQA) models into diffusion-based generators, enabling quality-aware image generation. We show that diffusion models can learn complex qualitative relationships from both IQA models’ outputs and internal activations. First, we experiment with gradient-based guidance to optimize image quality directly and show this method has limited generalizability. To address this, we introduce IQA-Adapter, a novel framework that conditions generation on target quality levels by learning the implicit relationship between images and quality scores. When conditioned on high target quality, IQA-Adapter can shift the distribution of generated images towards a higher-quality subdomain, and, inversely, it can be used as a degradation model, generating progressively more distorted images when provided with a lower-quality signal. Under high-quality condition, IQA-Adapter achieves up to a 10\% improvement across multiple objective metrics, as confirmed by a user preference study, while preserving generative diversity and content. Furthermore, we extend IQA-Adapter to a reference-based conditioning scenario, utilizing the rich activation space of IQA models to transfer highly specific, content-agnostic qualitative features between images.

C1.justification: V2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion elevate learning from internal IQA activations and content-agnostic reference-image quality transfer to central contributions. V1 centers on score-conditioned generation and its degradation and adversarial applications. The claims of up to 10% quality improvement and preservation of generative capabilities are retained.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations concerning semantic leakage from reference images, the suitability of IQA embeddings for distortion transfer, attention separation, and compatibility with other improvement methods. Its limitations discussion adds artifact-classifier and latent-space assessment directions, while Section 18 extends the adversarial-risk discussion to critic-based optimization. Most earlier IQA-bias and VAE limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 Section 9 newly discloses per-GPU batch sizes of 16 and 4, training on five nodes with 40 GPUs, and reference-adapter and negative-guidance settings. The timing experiment specifies hardware, precision, resolution, and sampling steps. These improve documentation; the newly disclosed batch sizes do not establish changed training. The promised code and weights release remains unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds direct KADID-10k evaluation of reference-conditioned distortion transfer in both SDEdit image editing and text-to-image generation (Section 4.5). These introduce reference images and distortion-reproduction requirements beyond v1's score-controlled generation. KADID previously appeared as training data for pretrained IQA models. Lexica.art, PartiPrompts, GenEval, and COCO coverage is retained.

E2.justification: V2 evaluates DiffusionDPO, Q-Refine, BeautifulPrompt, and Prompt Weighting against IQA-Adapter in quality, GenEval, and COCO comparisons, including several combinations with the adapter. The new distortion-transfer comparison adds IP-Adapter and, for text-to-image generation, StyleCrafter (Table 2). V1's comparisons primarily involved the base model, gradient guidance, and IQA-Adapter variants.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a distortion-transfer protocol using one reference source, 80 target images, and 125 distortion variants, evaluated through quality correlations, CLIP comparisons, and ARNIQA embedding similarity. It also adds HPSv2 scoring, architectural control configurations, and a controlled runtime evaluation. The original training schedule and basic SDXL sampling settings are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds a direct ablation of separate qualitative attention against concatenating quality and text tokens, with quantitative and visual evidence (Table 5, Figure 16). It also adds computational-overhead analysis and reference-transfer failure comparisons. V1's positional-encoding, adapter-scale, seed-consistency, and GradCAM analyses are largely retained and reorganized, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V2 Section 17.1 and Table 8 newly report timing averages over 1,000 generations with ± values, although the meaning of those spreads is unspecified. The original 25-prompt, 100-seed analysis, subjective-study counts, and Inception Score uncertainty-reporting practice remain unchanged.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial distortion-transfer, baseline, combination, ablation, and runtime results. Retained COCO values are also revised: base-model FID changes from 21.84 to 19.92, and TOPIQ+LAION-AES FID from 23.51 to 21.36 (v1 Table 5; v2 Table 7). These are reported-value revisions without an explanation establishing an algorithmic gain. The original main GenEval table and subjective-study results are retained.

M1.justification: V2 Sections 3.3–3.4 introduce Reference-based IQA-Adapter, which conditions generation on intermediate ARNIQA embeddings extracted from reference images and uses degradation augmentation during training. This substantially extends the score-based conditioning procedure in v1. The original attention mechanism and denoising objective remain; renaming the attention mechanism does not itself change the method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and related work are substantially rewritten. Discussion moves from the main paper into the supplement, while negative guidance moves into the main method description. The supplement gains a contents section and reorganizes limitations, ablations, and additional experiments. These are extensive narrative and structural changes beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 2 to include embedding-based conditioning and reorganizes comparison heatmaps with colored method categories. It adds distortion-transfer, ablation, and runtime tables, expands existing comparison tables, and introduces several qualitative comparison grids. Existing figures are relocated, while the earlier negative-guidance displays are reduced or replaced.

R1.justification: V2 adds a substantive Generation Quality Improvement discussion positioning IQA-Adapter against DiffusionDPO, Q-Refine, prompt enhancement, and other quality-improvement approaches. It also situates reference conditioning relative to IP-Adapter and StyleCrafter, with additional citations supporting the new experiments. The distinction between broad quality control and quality maximization becomes more explicit.

T1.justification: The negative-condition definition is generalized from qneg = -q in v1 Section 8 to qneg = -δq in v2 Section 3.2.1, introducing a tunable quality gap. The attention equations, denoising objective, relative-gain definition, and positional-encoding formula otherwise retain their mathematical content. No new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important evidential gaps in v1 through external quality-improvement baselines and a direct architectural ablation, substantially strengthening assessment of the method's usefulness and design choices. The reference-based extension receives quantitative and visual evaluation, and training disclosure improves. Unexplained revisions to retained scores and the Table 5 versus Section 11.1 SROCC mismatch remain reporting weaknesses; the improvement rests on stronger comparisons and controls, rather than higher reported numbers.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the IQA-Adapter research and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and supplementary material. Retained content can be matched across the substantial additions and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds reference-based distortion-transfer experiments, architectural ablations, external baseline comparisons, and timing measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original SDXL experiments, benchmark evaluations, sensitivity analyses, and a subjective study involving 1,017 participants.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled the creation of multi-modal LLMs that exhibit strong comprehension of visual data such as images and videos. However, these models usually rely on extensive visual tokens from visual encoders, leading to high computational demands, which limits their applicability in resource-constrained environments and for long-context tasks. In this work, we propose a training-free adaptive inference method for multi-modal LLMs that can accommodate a broad range of efficiency requirements with a minimum performance drop. Our method consists of a) iterative token merging based on embedding similarity before LLMs, and b) progressive token pruning within LLM layers based on multi-modal importance. With a minimalist design, our method can be applied to both video and image LLMs. Extensive experiments on diverse video and image benchmarks demonstrate that our method substantially reduces computation load (e.g., a $\textbf{7-fold}$ reduction in FLOPs) while preserving the performance of video and image LLMs. Further, at a similar computational cost, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in long video understanding (e.g., $\textbf{+4.6}$ on MLVU). Additionally, our in-depth analysis provides insights into token redundancy and LLM layer behaviors, offering guidance for future research in designing efficient multi-modal LLMs. Our code is available at https://github.com/LaVi-Lab/AIM.
arxiv_record.authors: Yiwu Zhong, Zhuoming Liu, Yin Li, Liwei Wang
arxiv_record.title: AIM: Adaptive Inference of Multi-Modal LLMs via Token Merging and Pruning

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same claims about training-free adaptive inference, image/video applicability, computational savings, and improved long-video performance. The stated approximately sevenfold video FLOP reduction and +4.6 MLVU result remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix B explicitly identifies incompatibility with FlashAttention because pruning requires attention values, discusses other efficiency techniques, and proposes future integration. Appendix A attributes larger Qwen2-VL performance losses to joint frame encoding and discusses LLaVA-Prumerge's incompatibility with that model. V2 also interprets the newly quantified overhead as negligible; the earlier TextVQA limitation remains.

D1.justification: The abstract changes code availability from a future promise to a statement that code is available at the same repository. Appendix A discloses a memory-driven MAX_PIXELS reduction, although its value is unspecified. Existing main-experiment hyperparameters and FLOP/prefill estimation details are retained; v2 removes the explicit statement that baseline official implementations were used.

E1.justification: The same six video benchmarks and seven image benchmarks remain in use. Appendix experiments reuse this coverage; the additional base model, frame counts, and merging configurations change experimental settings rather than datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and 3 add VTW and PDrop to the evaluated pruning baselines, with PDrop omitted from the lowest-budget image comparison. They remove VILA, PLLaVA, LLaVA-N-Video, IXC-2.5, BLIP-2, and InstructBLIP comparison rows. Appendix B additionally compares pruning against FlashAttention.

E3.justification: V2 adds Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct evaluation with reduced MAX_PIXELS, controlled 128-frame comparisons, temporal-versus-spatial merging experiments, and a merging-only/FlashAttention/pruning comparison. Appendix C adds another computation-budget configuration. The original main-experiment splits, metrics, and stated defaults remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained ablations, v2 tests whether dense frames alone explain improvements, directly compares temporal and spatial merging, and examines dependence on the base model (Tables A–C). Table 7 quantifies merging/pruning overhead, while Table D compares pruning with FlashAttention. These substantially expand the evidence examining design choices and efficiency.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests for its experiments. The additional results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial baseline, overhead, and appendix results, including Qwen2-VL+AIM scoring 52.8 on VideoMME in Table C, while removing several reference-model result rows. Main AIM scores are retained. FastV's higher-budget MMB score changes from 72.7 to 72.1 in Table 3; Table 1's relative FLOP/prefill percentages change from 62.4%/63.3% to 69.5%/69.2%, consistent with comparison against FastV.

M1.justification: Both versions use within-frame similarity-based merging before the LLM, PageRank-based visual-token pruning, preserved text tokens, and the same piecewise scheduler. V2 clarifies encoder placement and corrects a token-count expression, without establishing a different implemented procedure.

P1.justification: V2 condenses portions of related work, clarifies the merging explanation, revises baseline descriptions, and corrects the erroneous reference to Experiment 16 to Experiment 6. It adds acknowledgements and appendix sections while retaining the main section order and most existing prose.

P2.justification: V2 adds an overhead table and Appendix Tables A–E, substantially extending the displayed evidence. Tables 1 and 3 have revised comparison rows, while existing figures and tables are resized and repositioned with revised captions and highlighting. Figures 1–2 retain their substantive content, and the original adaptive-inference Table 7 becomes Table 8.

R1.justification: V2 updates related work with VTW, DyCoke, multimodal chain-of-thought work, and adaptive inference for MLLMs, and adds references supporting the FlashAttention, sparse-attention, and quantization discussion. PDrop receives explicit positioning beyond the earlier concurrent-work citation. Some background references disappear, but AIM's central positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 corrects the next-layer token-count expression from N_0 r^l to N^1 r^l, using the post-merging count instead of the original count. This is a limited mathematical correction. The PageRank equation, piecewise scheduler, and absence of formal proofs are otherwise unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for AIM's efficiency and design choices through overhead accounting, controlled dense-frame and temporal-merging tests, another base model, and additional relevant pruning baselines. Its explicit FlashAttention limitation also improves the assessment of practical applicability. These address important evidential gaps in v1 and outweigh the loss of several broad reference-model comparisons, although the new Qwen2-VL pixel setting remains underspecified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AIM with the same authors, central method, and main experiments. Text, equations, figures, and tables support reliable comparison. V1 ends with references; v2 additionally contains Appendices A–C.

after.justification: V2 retains these original evaluations and adds baseline results, computational-overhead measurements, and experiments in Appendix Tables A–E.

before.justification: V1 reports original image and video benchmark evaluations, token-merging and pruning ablations, and accuracy-efficiency results in Tables 1–7.

arxiv_record.abstract: We derive methods to compute higher order differentials (Hessians and Hessian-vector products) of the rendering operator. Our approach is based on importance sampling of a convolution that represents the differentials of rendering parameters and shows to be applicable to both rasterization and path tracing. We further suggest an aggregate sampling strategy to importance-sample multiple dimensions of one convolution kernel simultaneously. We demonstrate that this information improves convergence when used in higher-order optimizers such as Newton or Conjugate Gradient relative to a gradient descent baseline in several inverse rendering tasks.
arxiv_record.authors: Zican Wang, Michael Fischer, Tobias Ritschel
arxiv_record.title: Stochastic Gradient Estimation for Higher-order Differentiable Rendering

C1.justification: The central claims about importance-sampled Hessians/HVPs, aggregate sampling, applicability to rasterization and path tracing, and improved convergence remain. Both versions retain the headline 2.71-fold speedup; the added experiments do not introduce a new central contribution.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly discusses diminishing advantages with dimensionality and hypothesizes sparse sampling and increased Monte Carlo noise as causes. New analyses explain accuracy costs relative to analytic derivatives, sample-count versus runtime tradeoffs, and qualified robustness to rendering and compression noise, substantially expanding applicability boundaries and interpretation.

D1.justification: Appendix L/Table 3 supplies previously absent per-task sampling counts, bandwidth schedules, learning rates, trust regions, and line-search settings. v3 also documents antithetic sampling, the pycma implementation, and states that all methods use Adam, although its relationship to the stated GD/CG procedures remains unclear.

E1.justification: v3 adds SUZANNE and BANANA mesh reconstruction, seven-parameter Phong BRDF fitting, a non-PSD-Hessian test scenario, caustic heightfield optimization, and bunny optimization through two mirrors. These substantially broaden the represented geometry, reflectance, and light-transport tasks.

E2.justification: CMA-ES is added throughout Table 2 and evaluated in the mesh and caustic experiments. Appendix G also introduces comparisons against analytic first- and second-order derivatives. The original Mitsuba, FR22, proposed variants, and Appendix F BFGS comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce analytic-derivative controls and controlled MUG sweeps over Hessian sample counts, rendering sample counts, and JPEG compression levels. The original Table 2 metrics remain unchanged; newly supplied hyperparameters alone do not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices G-I add tests of sampled-versus-analytic derivative accuracy, optimization with non-PSD Hessians, Hessian sample efficiency, rendering noise, and compression noise. The original variance analysis is retained as Appendix J/Figure 11, moved from Section 4.3/Figure 5.

E5.justification: Both versions report 20-run ensembles and the same temporal averaging and median summaries. Appendix I newly specifies that runs use random starting points, clarifying the source of run-to-run variation. No increased run count, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedure is established.

E6.justification: Existing Table 2 numerical entries are retained, but CMA-ES results change rankings: on QUAD, its normalized time for 99% image-error reduction is 0.13, versus 0.62 for OurHVP, previously fastest. v3 also adds mesh, analytic-reference, robustness, caustic, and mirror results, including successful caustic optimization where CMA-ES does not converge.

M1.justification: The Gaussian-convolution estimators, Hessian/HVP sampling, aggregate importance sampling, and grey-box differentiation remain unchanged. The added optimizer safeguards and implementation disclosures do not establish a revision to the proposed estimator.

P1.justification: The title changes to 'Stochastic Gradient Estimation for Higher-order Differentiable Rendering,' with author/affiliation edits and localized prose condensation. The variance section moves to Appendix J and the conclusion gains limitations, but the main narrative and derivation structure remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: Table 2 gains CMA-ES rows, bars, curves, and a revised legend; Table 3 adds a substantial hyperparameter display. New figures show mesh reconstruction, analytic comparisons, robustness, task outcomes, caustics, and mirrors. Figures 3 and 6 are redrawn, while the original variance figure is relocated.

R1.justification: v3 adds the Hansen-Ostermeier CMA-ES and Jensen et al. multiview-stereopsis references, discusses CMA-ES as an alternative, and explicitly relates aggregate sampling to multiple importance sampling with the balance heuristic. The broader positioning and existing cited works are retained.

T1.justification: Section 2 adds trust-region truncation and Hessian-definiteness discussion, and Appendix H adds Gaussian-convolution reasoning for a non-PSD example. The core derivations remain unchanged. The new example contains a sign inconsistency: convolution of two negated Gaussians is incorrectly described as another negated Gaussian.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's limited validation and implementation disclosure through analytic-reference checks, robustness experiments, harder rendering tasks, and detailed hyperparameters. Adding CMA-ES also exposes cases where another method wins, making the comparison more informative. Explicit limitations improve qualification of the findings. The new Appendix H sign inconsistency and unclear Adam/GD/CG relationship limit particular explanations, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in experimental support and reproducibility.

A1.justification: The PDFs describe the same research despite the changed title. All 11 pages of v1 and 14 pages of v3, including Appendices A-F and A-L respectively, support textual and visual comparison.

after.justification: The original experiments remain, with additional mesh optimization, analytic-derivative comparisons, robustness tests, and light-transport experiments in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: Section 4 and Table 2 report original optimization experiments, and Figure 5 reports estimator-variance measurements.

arxiv_record.abstract: Despite significant advancements in vision-language models (VLMs), there lacks effective approaches to enhance response quality by scaling inference-time computation. This capability is known to be a core step towards the self-improving models in recent large language model studies. In this paper, we present Vision Value Model (VisVM) that can guide VLM inference-time search to generate responses with better visual comprehension. Specifically, VisVM not only evaluates the generated sentence quality in the current search step, but also anticipates the quality of subsequent sentences that may result from the current step, thus providing a long-term value. In this way, VisVM steers VLMs away from generating sentences prone to hallucinations or insufficient detail, thereby producing higher quality responses. Experimental results demonstrate that VisVM-guided search significantly enhances VLMs' ability to generate descriptive captions with richer visual details and fewer hallucinations, compared with greedy decoding and search methods with other visual reward signals. Furthermore, we find that self-training the model with the VisVM-guided captions improve VLM's performance across a wide range of multimodal benchmarks, indicating the potential for developing self-improving VLMs. Our value model and code are available at https://github.com/si0wang/VisVM.

arxiv_record.abstract: Foreground-conditioned inpainting aims to seamlessly fill the background region of an image by utilizing the provided foreground subject and a text description. While existing T2I-based image inpainting methods can be applied to this task, they suffer from issues of subject shape expansion, distortion, or impaired ability to align with the text description, resulting in inconsistencies between the visual elements and the text description. To address these challenges, we propose Pinco, a plug-and-play foreground-conditioned inpainting adapter that generates high-quality backgrounds with good text alignment while effectively preserving the shape of the foreground subject. Firstly, we design a Self-Consistent Adapter that integrates the foreground subject features into the layout-related self-attention layer, which helps to alleviate conflicts between the text and subject features by ensuring that the model can effectively consider the foreground subject's characteristics while processing the overall image layout. Secondly, we design a Decoupled Image Feature Extraction method that employs distinct architectures to extract semantic and spatial features separately, significantly improving subject feature extraction and ensuring high-quality preservation of the subject's shape. Thirdly, to ensure precise utilization of the extracted features and to focus attention on the subject region, we introduce a Shared Positional Embedding Anchor, greatly improving the model's understanding of subject features and boosting training efficiency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance and efficiency in foreground-conditioned inpainting.
arxiv_record.authors: Guangben Lu, Yuzhen Du, Zhimin Sun, Ran Yi, Yifan Qi, Yizhe Tang, Tianyi Wang, Lizhuang Ma, Fangyuan Zou
arxiv_record.title: Pinco: Position-induced Consistent Adapter for Diffusion Transformer in Foreground-conditioned Inpainting

arxiv_record.abstract: Despite the remarkable performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) across diverse tasks, the substantial training and inference costs impede their advancement. In this paper, we propose p-MoD, an efficient MLLM architecture that significantly reduces training and inference costs while maintaining model performance. The majority of computation in MLLMs stems from the overwhelming volume of vision tokens processed by the transformer-based LLM. Accordingly, we leverage the Mixture-of-Depths (MoD) mechanism, where each LLM layer selects essential vision tokens to process while skipping redundant ones. However, integrating MoD into MLLMs is non-trivial. To address the challenges of training and inference stability as well as limited training data, we adapt the MoD module with two novel designs: tanh-gated weight normalization (TanhNorm) and symmetric token reweighting (STRing). Moreover, we observe that vision tokens exhibit higher redundancy in deeper layers and thus design a progressive ratio decay (PRD) strategy, which gradually reduces the token retention ratio layer by layer, employing a shifted cosine schedule. This crucial design fully unleashes the potential of MoD, significantly boosting the efficiency and performance of our models. Extensive experiments on two baseline models across 15 benchmarks show that our model matches or even surpasses the performance of corresponding baselines, while requiring only 55.6% TFLOPs and 53.7% KV cache storage during inference, and 77.7% GPU hours during training.
arxiv_record.authors: Jun Zhang, Desen Meng, Zhengming Zhang, Zhenpeng Huang, Tao Wu, Limin Wang

C2.justification: V2 adds discussion of OCR sensitivity, repeated scaling as an overflow mechanism, grounding performance losses, and the requirement for training or continued fine-tuning rather than training-free deployment. It removes v1's extensive argument that attention-score pruning is incompatible with FlashAttention. The earlier single-image applicability limitation is retained in Appendix C.3.

D1.justification: Training hyperparameters, hardware, encoder-freezing policies and code/data links are largely retained after relocation. However, v2 drops the detailed FastV pruning and attention-implementation settings, the explanation of retraining on released 779K rather than original 760K data, and the explicit MME normalization instruction. These are documentation losses, not established changes to the underlying settings.

E1.justification: V2 retains the original 14 benchmarks, adds VQAv2 to the main evaluation, and introduces visual grounding on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg in Appendix A.2. Grounding substantially extends task requirements beyond the earlier question-answering and multimodal-understanding evaluations. The training datasets remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's dense baselines and FastV comparison, v2 evaluates MQT and LLaVolta in Table 5; SparseVLM, VisionZip, PyramidDrop, FasterVLM, FreeVideoLLM, iLLaVA and LLaVA-PruMerge in Table 10; and concurrent γ-MoD in Table 11. These are substantial additions to the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: V2 adds a 13B-model evaluation and visual-grounding validation protocols using ACC@0.5. Figure 3 replaces the fixed 15% retention perturbation with retention-ratio sweeps across shallow, middle and deep layers. Ablation and efficiency tables also report different benchmark subsets, making their averages noncomparable across versions. The original 7B training recipe is retained.

E4.justification: V2's Table 3 adds a cumulative, equal-computation ablation of TanhNorm, STRing and PRD. Figure 3 expands the depth-redundancy investigation from one lowered retention setting to sensitivity curves. Conversely, v1's isolated STRing-removal row is no longer reported. The token-selection visualizations in Figures 5 and 6 retain the same evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. V2 adds results without introducing uncertainty estimation; its use of 'significantly' does not establish statistical testing.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive comparator, VQAv2, 13B, grounding and ablation results while preserving the shared main benchmark scores. Reported default KV-cache usage changes from 53.8% to 53.7%. M1.justification: The architecture and three components remain, but Eqs. (2)-(4) replace the selected-token additive term X_i with T(X_i). P1.justification: V2 revises the abstract, introduction and conclusion, reorders the experimental subsections, and promotes method comparisons into the main text. P2.justification: Figure 3 is redrawn from a four-bar experiment into retention-ratio curves, and Figure 1's radar display is updated. Main benchmark tables are regrouped from seven-plus-seven to ten-plus-five benchmarks, ablation tables are reorganized, and several comparison tables are added. The appendix layout changes substantially, while Figures 5 and 6 preserve their original image content.

R1.justification: V2 substantially broadens positioning around query-based compression, token merging and newer pruning methods. Appendix A.4 newly acknowledges concurrent γ-MoD and distinguishes its layer-selection approach from p-MoD. The earlier FlashAttention-based criticism and associated citations are removed, changing an important part of the comparison with prior work.

T1.justification: The selected-token definitions in Eqs. (2)-(4) change algebraically from adding X_i to adding T(X_i), rather than merely changing notation. The routing and cosine-decay definitions remain, and the unchanged clipping equation moves to Appendix D.3. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow comparison against alternative compression methods through broader comparisons, including γ-MoD, and strengthens component validation with cumulative ablations and retention sweeps. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe p-MoD and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Their shared methods and experiments can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

arxiv_record.abstract: This paper introduces UnZipLoRA, a method for decomposing an image into its constituent subject and style, represented as two distinct LoRAs (Low-Rank Adaptations). Unlike existing personalization techniques that focus on either subject or style in isolation, or require separate training sets for each, UnZipLoRA disentangles these elements from a single image by training both the LoRAs simultaneously. UnZipLoRA ensures that the resulting LoRAs are compatible, i.e., they can be seamlessly combined using direct addition. UnZipLoRA enables independent manipulation and recontextualization of subject and style, including generating variations of each, applying the extracted style to new subjects, and recombining them to reconstruct the original image or create novel variations. To address the challenge of subject and style entanglement, UnZipLoRA employs a novel prompt separation technique, as well as column and block separation strategies to accurately preserve the characteristics of subject and style, and ensure compatibility between the learned LoRAs. Evaluation with human studies and quantitative metrics demonstrates UnZipLoRA's effectiveness compared to other state-of-the-art methods, including DreamBooth-LoRA, Inspiration Tree, and B-LoRA.
arxiv_record.authors: Chang Liu, Viraj Shah, Aiyu Cui, Svetlana Lazebnik
arxiv_record.title: UnZipLoRA: Separating Content and Style from a Single Image

The earlier limitation concerning highly abstract styles is retained and moved into the conclusion.

D1.justification: V2 supplies more explicit trigger-phrase annotations and guidance, discloses unlabeled user comparisons with arbitrary ordering, and adds the ablation-study interface. SDXL hyperparameters, block assignments, hardware timings, and project/data access information are retained.

E1.justification: V2 adds cross-image composition, combining subject and style LoRAs learned from different images (Figures 6 and 19), extending v1's evaluation of decomposition and recombination from one image. Appendix B.4 also adds human-subject evaluations. Both versions still describe a 40-image collection.

E2.justification: The decomposition comparators remain DreamBooth-LoRA, Inspiration Tree, and B-LoRA. V2 expands recontextualization comparisons beyond v1's B-LoRA comparison by reporting preferences against all three methods. Figure 8 also adds B-LoRA outputs to the existing failure cases.

E3.justification: V2 adds component-wise user comparisons, controlled trigger-phrase tests, 20/30/40% column-selection experiments, and KOALA evaluations. The original SDXL budgets and eight-input, sixteen-sample alignment protocol remain. DreamBooth's stated style-training prompt changes from 'A subject in <s> style' to 'A <c> in <s> style'; this reporting revision does not establish rerunning existing comparisons.

E4.justification: V1 primarily supports component contributions through qualitative ablations. V2 adds component preference and alignment tables (Tables 3–4), subject/style trigger-phrase sensitivity tests (Figures 10–11), and column-fraction sensitivity tests (Figure 18). Existing failure analysis also gains a B-LoRA comparison.

E5.justification: Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run uncertainty estimates. The existing generation-sample protocol and seed-selection discussion are retained; the added user-study sample counts describe new evaluations rather than a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 2's alignment scores and Table 1's decomposition preferences remain identical. V2 adds recontextualization preferences of 98.10%, 79.17%, and 77.14% over DreamBooth-LoRA, Inspiration Tree, and B-LoRA, respectively, plus component results in Tables 3–4. Cross-image, KOALA, and sensitivity experiments substantially expand the reported findings.

M1.justification: The three separation mechanisms, losses, SDXL block assignments, and direct-addition inference are retained. V2 expresses the existing column fraction as N, retaining 30% for the main experiments. The additional applications do not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: prompt construction moves into the problem setup, preliminaries and comparisons are condensed, experimental subsections are restructured, and limitations enter the conclusion. P2.justification: Figure 2 is reformatted, qualitative panels are redistributed, and v1 Figures 6 and 12 are consolidated into v2 Figure 13. V2 expands Table 1, adds Tables 3–4, introduces application and sensitivity figures, and expands the user-study interface display.

R1.justification: V2 adds KOALA and DiT references and removes the LEGO discussion and citation. It also revises the characterization of B-LoRA's training and its contrast with UnZipLoRA. The broader literature positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: The low-rank formulation and Equations 1–5 are mathematically unchanged. V2 adds no theorem, proof, or substantive derivation; introducing N names an experimental hyperparameter.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the retained method: quantitative component ablations replace reliance on selected qualitative examples, while prompt and column-fraction tests address previously untested sensitivities. arxiv_record.abstract: Visual Place Recognition (VPR) enables coarse localization by comparing query images to a reference database of geo-tagged images. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning architectures and training regimes have led to methods with improved robustness to factors like environment appearance change, but with the downside that the required training and/or matching compute scales with the number of distinct environmental conditions encountered. Here, we propose Hyperdimensional One Place Signatures (HOPS) to simultaneously improve the performance, compute and scalability of these state-of-the-art approaches by fusing the descriptors from multiple reference sets captured under different conditions. HOPS scales to any number of environmental conditions by leveraging the Hyperdimensional Computing framework. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our approach is highly generalizable and consistently improves recall performance across all evaluated VPR methods and datasets by large margins. Arbitrarily fusing reference images without compute penalty enables numerous other useful possibilities, three of which we demonstrate here: descriptor dimensionality reduction with no performance penalty, stacking synthetic images, and coarse localization to an entire traverse or environmental section.
arxiv_record.authors: Connor Malone, Somayeh Hussaini, Tobias Fischer, Michael Milford
arxiv_record.title: A Hyperdimensional One Place Signature to Represent Them All: Stackable Descriptors For Visual Place Recognition

C1.justification: The abstract, principal contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about descriptor fusion, generalization, efficiency, synthetic references and dataset identification. The introduction clarifies that the quoted dimensionality reductions concern feature dimensions without materially redefining the contribution.

C2.justification: Section 9 interprets unstructured-reference compression as a storage and computation tradeoff with some recall loss. Section 12 attributes remaining failures mainly to visual similarity between geographically distant places. These add applicability qualifications while retaining the original explanations concerning feature reinforcement, nearby-match disambiguation and low-dimensional descriptors.

D1.justification: A HOPS repository address replaces v1's promise of code upon acceptance. The supplement specifies AnyLoc's author-released weights, 49,152-dimensional representation and omission of PCA, and identifies SALAD and cosine matching for dataset identification. Section 3.3 clarifies that core results use no random projection. These are additional disclosures, not evidence of changed implementations.

E1.justification: Section 9 adds evaluation on Google Landmarks v2 micro, extending coverage from repeated route traversals to an unstructured collection with varying numbers of reference images per place. This substantially broadens the input environment tested. Dataset identification and the three original datasets were already covered in v1.

E2.justification: Figure 4 adds pooling and distance-matrix averaging to the dimensionality comparison. Tables 9–10 add one-image and ten-image dataset-identification baselines and maximum/median distance aggregation; minimum aggregation is also displayed and matches pooling. Table 8 adds a dimensionality-reduction compression comparator. Tables 5–7 supply the AnyLoc comparisons previously mentioned without results in v1.

E3.justification: The new Landmarks evaluation fuses 7–9 images per place, reducing 23,294 references to 3,103, and compares this with retaining all references at 1024 dimensions under a similar storage budget. Dataset-identification comparisons introduce one-reference and ten-reference sampling controls. These substantially extend the evaluation design; the original datasets' sampling counts and matching tolerances remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Figures 5–10 expand dimensionality sensitivity analysis beyond v1's four-descriptor RobotCar Dusk example to all six main descriptors on six additional query sets. Figures 12–14 add successful and failed retrieval cases across the three original datasets, including failures where another method succeeds. These substantially expand sensitivity and error-analysis evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty estimates. v2's randomly selected dataset-identification baselines are reported without variability or repetition information.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain their values, but v2 adds extensive numerical and qualitative results. For example, AnyLoc on RobotCar Dusk achieves 84.0 R@1 with HOPS versus 69.7 for the best single reference. The new Landmarks comparison reports 69.7 for original references, 65.8 after HOPS compression and 59.7 with 1024-dimensional references. Section 4.3 also corrects the exception count from two to three, acknowledging CosPlace Night's already-tabulated 19.4 versus 21.2.

M1.justification: The descriptor summation, cosine-distance matching and optional Gaussian random projection remain unchanged. Section 3.3 clarifies that projection is used for the dimensionality experiment, while the supplement explains existing bundling applications. No new HOPS component or altered procedure is established.

P1.justification: The main section order and most wording remain intact. Changes include localized clarification of random projection, additional cross-references, the corrected outlier paragraph, publication headers and an organized supplementary narrative. The added scientific material is not accompanied by an extensive rewrite of the original paper.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5–10 and Figures 5–14, including multi-panel sensitivity plots, a dataset-identification diagram and three qualitative image galleries. Figure 4 gains comparator curves and a revised legend, while Figure 3's caption specifies error units. These substantially expand and refine the visual presentation.

R1.justification: The related-work sections and 86-work bibliography are retained. Section 11 adds a focused comparison with the already-cited approaches in references 22 and 51, emphasizing differences in reference storage and query-descriptor computation. This modestly expands research positioning.

T1.justification: Equations 1–6, the quasi-orthogonality reasoning, complexity statements and Johnson–Lindenstrauss motivation are retained. The supplement adds no formal theorem, proof, assumption or mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1's empirical support through multi-reference controls in the dimensionality plots, an unstructured compression benchmark, detailed dataset-identification comparisons and explicit failure examples. Previously referenced supplementary evidence becomes inspectable, making the benefits and limitations substantially easier to assess. Code access information and implementation clarifications further help reproducibility. Minor inconsistencies, such as Table 8's 8488/8448 descriptor dimensions, do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HOPS research, and their text, equations, tables and figures are readable. v1 ends after the references; v2 includes Supplementary Material, Sections 6–12. Supplementary additions below mean newly available content in the supplied PDFs, not necessarily newly conducted experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and supplies additional original results, including AnyLoc comparisons, Google Landmarks compression, dataset-identification baselines and qualitative retrieval examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original VPR experiments on RobotCar, Nordland and SFU-Mountain, dimensionality-reduction and synthetic-reference experiments, and dataset-identification outcomes.

arxiv_record.abstract: Instruction tuning fine-tunes pre-trained Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to handle real-world tasks. However, the rapid expansion of visual instruction datasets introduces data redundancy, leading to excessive computational costs. We propose a collaborative framework, DataTailor, which leverages three key principles--informativeness, uniqueness, and representativeness--for effective data selection. We argue that a valuable sample should be informative of the task, non-redundant, and represent the sample distribution (i.e., not an outlier). We further propose practical ways to score against each principle, which automatically adapts to a given dataset without tedious hyperparameter tuning. Comprehensive experiments on various benchmarks demonstrate that DataTailor achieves 101.3% of the performance of full-data fine-tuning with only 15% of the data, significantly reducing computational costs while maintaining superior results. This exemplifies the "Less is More" philosophy in MLLM development. The code and data is available in this \href{https://github.com/Yuqifan1117/DataTailor}{URL}.

arxiv_record.title: Mastering Collaborative Multi-modal Data Selection: A Focus on Informativeness, Uniqueness, and Representativeness

native_poster_event.abstract: Instruction tuning fine-tunes pre-trained Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to handle real-world tasks. However, the rapid expansion of visual instruction datasets introduces data redundancy, leading to excessive computational costs. We propose a collaborative framework, DataTailor, which leverages three key principles—informativeness, uniqueness, and representativeness—for effective data selection. We argue that a valuable sample should be informative of the task, non-redundant, and represent the sample distribution (i.e., not an outlier). We further propose practical ways to score against each principle, which automatically adapts to a given dataset without tedious hyperparameter tuning. Comprehensive experiments on various benchmarks demonstrate that DataTailor achieves 101.3\% of the performance of full-data fine-tuning with only 15\% of the data, significantly reducing computational costs while maintaining superior results. This exemplifies the "Less is More" philosophy in MLLM development. The code is in https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DataTailor-5BC3.

arxiv_record.abstract: Mitigating biases in computer vision models is an essential step towards the trustworthiness of artificial intelligence models. Existing bias mitigation methods focus on a small set of predefined biases, limiting their applicability in visual datasets where multiple, possibly unknown biases exist. To address this limitation, we introduce MAVias, an open-set bias mitigation approach leveraging foundation models to discover spurious associations between visual attributes and target classes. MAVias first captures a wide variety of visual features in natural language via a foundation image tagging model, and then leverages a large language model to select those visual features defining the target class, resulting in a set of language-coded potential visual biases. We then translate this set of potential biases into vision-language embeddings and introduce an in-processing bias mitigation approach to prevent the model from encoding information related to them. Our experiments on diverse datasets, including CelebA, Waterbirds, ImageNet, and UrbanCars, show that MAVias effectively detects and mitigates a wide range of biases in visual recognition tasks outperforming current state-of-the-art.
arxiv_record.authors: Ioannis Sarridis, Christos Koutlis, Symeon Papadopoulos, and Christos Diou
arxiv_record.title: MAVias: Mitigate any Visual Bias
