arxiv_record.abstract: In robotic visuomotor policy learning, diffusion-based models have achieved significant success in improving the accuracy of action trajectory generation compared to traditional autoregressive models. However, they suffer from inefficiency due to multiple denoising steps and limited flexibility from complex constraints. In this paper, we introduce Coarse-to-Fine AutoRegressive Policy (CARP), a novel paradigm for visuomotor policy learning that redefines the autoregressive action generation process as a coarse-to-fine, next-scale approach. CARP decouples action generation into two stages: first, an action autoencoder learns multi-scale representations of the entire action sequence; then, a GPT-style transformer refines the sequence prediction through a coarse-to-fine autoregressive process. This straightforward and intuitive approach produces highly accurate and smooth actions, matching or even surpassing the performance of diffusion-based policies while maintaining efficiency on par with autoregressive policies. We conduct extensive evaluations across diverse settings, including single-task and multi-task scenarios on state-based and image-based simulation benchmarks, as well as real-world tasks. CARP achieves competitive success rates, with up to a 10% improvement, and delivers 10x faster inference compared to state-of-the-art policies, establishing a high-performance, efficient, and flexible paradigm for action generation in robotic tasks.

arxiv_record.abstract: Recently, robotics has advanced significantly through the integration of larger models and large-scale datasets. However, challenges remain in applying these models to 3D spatial interactions and managing data collection costs. To address these issues, we propose the multimodal robotic manipulation model RoboTron-Mani and the comprehensive dataset RoboData. RoboTron-Mani, on one hand, enhances 3D perception through camera parameters and occupancy supervision. On the other hand, it further incorporates Modality-Isolation-Mask and multimodal decoder blocks based on OpenFlamingo, improving modality fusion and fine-grained perception. RoboData integrats several publicly-available datasets, achieving the first fusion of multi-view images, camera parameters, depth maps, actions, and space alignment, which facilitates comprehensive learning from diverse robotic datasets and offers one complete evaluation system. Trained on RoboData, RoboTron-Mani is the first generalist policy that surpasses expert models, enabling simultaneous evaluation of all tasks across multiple datasets, rather than being limited to specific data or task selections. Specifically, RoboTron-Mani boosts manipulation performance by increasing the average sequence length on CALVIN from 1.7 to 3.5, enabling cross-embodiment generalization, and achieving state-of-the-art results on both simulated and real-world datasets.

arxiv_record.abstract: Image tokenizers map images to sequences of discrete tokens, and are a crucial component of autoregressive transformer-based image generation. The tokens are typically associated with spatial locations in the input image, arranged in raster scan order, which is not ideal for autoregressive modeling. In this paper, we propose to tokenize the image spectrum instead, obtained from a discrete wavelet transform (DWT), such that the sequence of tokens represents the image in a coarse-to-fine fashion. Our tokenizer brings several advantages: 1) it leverages that natural images are more compressible at high frequencies, 2) it can take and reconstruct images of different resolutions without retraining, 3) it improves the conditioning for next-token prediction -- instead of conditioning on a partial line-by-line reconstruction of the image, it takes a coarse reconstruction of the full image, 4) it enables partial decoding where the first few generated tokens can reconstruct a coarse version of the image, 5) it enables autoregressive models to be used for image upsampling. We evaluate the tokenizer reconstruction metrics as well as multiscale image generation, text-guided image upsampling and editing.
arxiv_record.authors: Carlos Esteves, Mohammed Suhail, Ameesh Makadia
arxiv_record.title: Spectral Image Tokenizer

arxiv_record.abstract: End-to-end optimization, which simultaneously optimizes optics and algorithms, has emerged as a powerful data-driven method for computational imaging system design. This method achieves joint optimization through backpropagation by incorporating differentiable optics simulators to generate measurements and algorithms to extract information from measurements. However, due to high computational costs, it is challenging to model both aberration and diffraction in light transport for end-to-end optimization of compound optics. Therefore, most existing methods compromise physical accuracy by neglecting wave optics effects or off-axis aberrations, which raises concerns about the robustness of the resulting designs. In this paper, we propose a differentiable optics simulator that efficiently models both aberration and diffraction for compound optics. Using the simulator, we conduct end-to-end optimization on scene reconstruction and classification. Experimental results demonstrate that both lenses and algorithms adopt different configurations depending on whether wave optics is modeled. We also show that systems optimized without wave optics suffer from performance degradation when wave optics effects are introduced during testing. These findings underscore the importance of accurate wave optics modeling in optimizing imaging systems for robust, high-performance applications.

native_poster_event.abstract: End-to-end optimization, which integrates differentiable optics simulators with computational algorithms, enables the joint design of hardware and software in data-driven imaging systems. However, existing methods usually compromise physical accuracy by neglecting wave optics or off-axis effects due to the high computational cost of modeling both aberration and diffraction. This limitation raises concerns about the robustness of optimized designs. In this paper, we propose a differentiable optics simulator that accurately and efficiently models aberration and diffraction in compound optics and allows us to analyze the role and impact of diffraction in end-to-end optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that compared with ray-optics-based optimization, diffraction-aware optimization improves system robustness to diffraction blur. Through accurate wave optics modeling, we also apply the simulator to optimize the Fizeau interferometer and free form optics elements. These findings underscore the importance of accurate wave optics modeling in robust end-to-end optimization.

arxiv_record.abstract: Recently, Vision Large Language Models (VLLMs) integrated with vision encoders have shown promising performance in vision understanding. The key of VLLMs is to encode visual content into sequences of visual tokens, enabling VLLMs to simultaneously process both visual and textual content. However, understanding videos, especially long videos, remain a challenge to VLLMs as the number of visual tokens grows rapidly when encoding videos, resulting in the risk of exceeding the context window of VLLMs and introducing heavy computation burden. To restrict the number of visual tokens, existing VLLMs either: (1) uniformly downsample videos into a fixed number of frames or (2) reducing the number of visual tokens encoded from each frame. We argue the former solution neglects the rich temporal cue in videos and the later overlooks the spatial details in each frame. In this work, we present Balanced-VLLM (B-VLLM): a novel VLLM framework that aims to effectively leverage task relevant spatio-temporal cues while restricting the number of visual tokens under the VLLM context window length. At the core of our method, we devise a text-conditioned adaptive frame selection module to identify frames relevant to the visual understanding task. The selected frames are then de-duplicated using a temporal frame token merging technique. The visual tokens of the selected frames are processed through a spatial token sampling module and an optional spatial token merging strategy to achieve precise control over the token count. Experimental results show that B-VLLM is effective in balancing the number of frames and visual tokens in video understanding, yielding superior performance on various video understanding benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhuqiangLu/B-VLLM.
arxiv_record.authors: Zhuqiang Lu, Zhenfei Yin, Mengwei He, Zhihui Wang, Zicheng Liu, Zhiyong Wang and Kun Hu

native_poster_event.abstract: Recently, Vision Large Language Models (VLLMs)  with integrated vision encoders have shown promising performance in vision understanding. They encode visual content into sequences of visual tokens, enabling joint processing of visual and textual data. However, understanding videos, especially long videos, remains a challenge as the rapid growth of visual tokens during video encoding risks exceeding VLLMs' context window length and significantly escalates computational cost. To restrict the number of visual tokens, existing VLLMs either: (1) uniformly downsample videos into a fixed number of frames or (2) reducing the number of visual tokens encoded from each frame. We argue that the former neglects temporal dynamics in videos, while the latter fails to preserve spatial details within individual frame. In this work, we propose Balanced-VLLM (B-VLLM), a novel VLLM framework designed to model task relevant spatio-temporal cues, while restricting the number of visual tokens within the VLLM's context window length. Central to our framework is a text-conditioned adaptive frame selection module that dynamically identifies task-relevant frames, which are further de-duplicated with a temporal frame token merging strategy.The visual tokens of these frames then undergo spatial token sampling and an optional spatial token merging strategy for granular control against the token budget.  Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of B-VLLM in balancing the number of frames and visual tokens, moreover, our proposed method introduce 10\% performance gain on MVBench. Our code will be publicly available.

P1.justification: The abstract and selected introductory and discussion passages are edited. Implementation is condensed, training details move to the supplement, and limitations are redistributed between Section 5.4 and supplementary Section 8.6. Despite these organizational refinements, the main section sequence, method exposition and much of the benchmark narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is substantially redesigned with additional heatmaps and a token-budget curve. Figure 4 gains explicit frame-selection timelines, while supplementary Figure 5 and Figures 6–10 add sensitivity and conversation displays. Tables 4–10 are new; existing tables also change caption placement, styling and placement within the document.

R1.justification: v2 adds CLS-token literature, training-source references and citations concerning other vision applications, while removing the RegNet reference. T1.justification: Equations 1–5, the Gumbel-Softmax reasoning, cosine-threshold duplicate definition and averaging rules are retained. Neither version supplies additional theorems, proofs or substantive mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: v1 offered limited evidence for its specific selection mechanisms and accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs. v2 substantially strengthens their assessment through controlled alternatives in Tables 4 and 7, expanded sensitivity experiments, computational comparisons and previously unavailable dataset/setup details. Latency protocols remain underspecified and some text–table and temporal-order inconsistencies persist, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in methodological scrutiny and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same B-VLLM framework and contain readable text, equations, figures and tables. The supplied v1 ends with references; v2 additionally includes supplementary Sections 7–9. All supplied pages support comparison.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Preconditioned stochastic optimization algorithms, exemplified by Shampoo,
outperform first-order optimizers by offering theoretical convergence benefits
and practical gains in large-scale neural network training. However, they incur
substantial memory overhead due to the storage demands of non-diagonal
preconditioning matrices. To address this, we introduce 4-bit quantization for
Shampoo's preconditioners. We introduce two key methods: First, we apply
Cholesky decomposition followed by quantization of the Cholesky factors,
reducing memory usage by leveraging their lower triangular structure while
better preserving spectral properties to minimize information loss. To our
knowledge, this is the first quantization approach applied to Cholesky factors
of preconditioners. Second, we incorporate error feedback in the quantization
process, efficiently storing Cholesky factor and error state in the lower and
upper triangular parts of the same matrix. Through extensive experiments, we
demonstrate that combining Cholesky quantization with error feedback enhances
memory efficiency and algorithm performance in large-scale deep-learning tasks.
Theoretically, we also provide convergence proofs for quantized Shampoo under
both smooth and non-smooth stochastic optimization settings.
arxiv_record.authors: Jingyang Li, Kuangyu Ding, Kim-Chuan Toh, Pan Zhou
arxiv_record.title: Memory-Efficient 4-bit Preconditioned Stochastic Optimization

native_poster_event.abstract: Preconditioned stochastic optimization algorithms, exemplified by Shampoo, outperform first-order optimizers by offering theoretical convergence benefits and practical gains in large-scale neural network training. However, they incur substantial memory overhead due to the storage demands of non-diagonal preconditioning matrices. To address this, we introduce 4-bit quantization for Shampoo's preconditioners. We introduce two key methods: First, we apply Cholesky decomposition followed by quantization of the Cholesky factors, reducing memory usage by leveraging their lower triangular structure while better preserving spectral properties to minimize information loss. To our knowledge, this is the first quantization approach applied to Cholesky factors of preconditioners. Second, we incorporate error feedback in the quantization process, efficiently storing Cholesky factor and error state in the lower and upper triangular parts of the same matrix. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that combining Cholesky quantization with error feedback enhances memory efficiency and algorithm performance in large-scale deep-learning tasks. Theoretically, we also provide convergence proofs for quantized Shampoo under both smooth and non-smooth stochastic optimization settings. The source code is included in the supplementary and will be publicly released.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion emphasize preservation of spectral properties rather than only symmetry and positive definiteness. The conclusion extends demonstrated applicability to LLM pretraining. The central Cholesky-quantization, error-feedback, memory-efficiency, novelty, and convergence claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds spectral-fidelity and computational-cost explanations. Section 5.1 changes partial support for the eigenvalue assumption into an implementation-guarantee claim, although the added positivity criterion is conditional. The untested ImageNet-ViT limitation is replaced with boundaries involving other tasks, and Appendix C.3 acknowledges shortened LLM training.

D1.justification: V2 Appendix C.3 and Table 11 document LLaMA architecture dimensions, precision, training budgets, and gradient accumulation, alongside ViT-Base training details. Appendix C.2 specifies synthetic-matrix generation and eigenvalue ranges, and the hardware description adds the A100's 80GB capacity. Existing augmentation and memory explanations are largely relocated rather than newly disclosed.

E1.justification: V2 extends evaluation from image classification to LLaMA pretraining on C4 and adds synthetic ill-conditioned matrix tests. CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet classification remain. ViT-Base on ImageNet expands model configurations within retained task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Table 8 adds evaluated RMSprop, RMSprop plus 32-bit Shampoo, and RMSprop plus vanilla 4-bit Shampoo comparisons. SGDM/AdamW comparison families otherwise remain. Newly cited ReLoRA, GaLore, and Wang et al.'s 4-bit Shampoo are not separately evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: New protocols include LLaMA-130M/350M/1B evaluation using perplexity, bfloat16, 10K/10K/2K training steps, and effective batch size 512; ViT-Base/ImageNet training; and NRE/AE tests on synthetic and recorded preconditioners. V1 Appendix C.1 specifies error-feedback momentum 0.9 for CNNs and 0.95 for ViTs, whereas v2 C.3 specifies 0.95 throughout. This is a reported setting change, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds direct quantization-fidelity analyses on synthetic and real preconditioners (Tables 1 and 10), a toy matrix illustrating loss of positive definiteness (Table 9), a joint momentum-coefficient sensitivity sweep (Table 7), and RMSprop applicability testing (Table 8). Existing CQ/error-feedback and off-diagonal quantization comparisons remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The 100 synthetic matrices in v2 constitute a new evaluation sample, not repeated-training uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds C4, ViT-Base/ImageNet, fidelity, sensitivity, and RMSprop results. Matched ViT-Small/CIFAR-100 accuracies change from 78.21/76.50/76.76 to 77.95/77.34/77.74 for 32-bit/CQ/CQ+EF (v1 Table 1; v2 Table 3). Tiny-ImageNet CQ+EF scores change from 61.91 to 62.81 for Swin-Tiny and 57.45 to 57.51 for ViT-Small. ResNet-50 CQ+EF memory changes from 11455.2 to 11445.2 MB. CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet timing results are removed.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same Cholesky quantization, error-feedback updates, triangular storage, inverse-root computation, and preconditioned optimization procedure. arxiv_record.abstract:
Recently, generalizable feed-forward methods based on 3D Gaussian Splatting
have gained significant attention for their potential to reconstruct 3D scenes
using finite resources. These approaches create a 3D radiance field,
parameterized by per-pixel 3D Gaussian primitives, from just a few images in a
single forward pass. However, unlike multi-view methods that benefit from
cross-view correspondences, 3D scene reconstruction with a single-view image
remains an underexplored area. In this work, we introduce CATSplat, a novel
generalizable transformer-based framework designed to break through the
inherent constraints in monocular settings. First, we propose leveraging
textual guidance from a visual-language model to complement insufficient
information from a single image. By incorporating scene-specific contextual
details from text embeddings through cross-attention, we pave the way for
context-aware 3D scene reconstruction beyond relying solely on visual cues.
Moreover, we advocate utilizing spatial guidance from 3D point features toward
comprehensive geometric understanding under single-view settings. With 3D
priors, image features can capture rich structural insights for predicting 3D
Gaussians without multi-view techniques. Extensive experiments on large-scale
datasets demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of CATSplat in
single-view 3D scene reconstruction with high-quality novel view synthesis.

arxiv_record.abstract: Artificial intelligence generative models exhibit remarkable capabilities in content creation, particularly in face image generation, customization, and restoration. However, current AI-generated faces (AIGFs) often fall short of human preferences due to unique distortions, unrealistic details, and unexpected identity shifts, underscoring the need for a comprehensive quality evaluation framework for AIGFs. To address this need, we introduce FaceQ, a large-scale, comprehensive database of AI-generated Face images with fine-grained Quality annotations reflecting human preferences. The FaceQ database comprises 12,255 images generated by 29 models across three tasks: (1) face generation, (2) face customization, and (3) face restoration. It includes 32,742 mean opinion scores (MOSs) from 180 annotators, assessed across multiple dimensions: quality, authenticity, identity (ID) fidelity, and text-image correspondence. Using the FaceQ database, we establish F-Bench, a benchmark for comparing and evaluating face generation, customization, and restoration models, highlighting strengths and weaknesses across various prompts and evaluation dimensions. Additionally, we assess the performance of existing image quality assessment (IQA), face quality assessment (FQA), AI-generated content image quality assessment (AIGCIQA), and preference evaluation metrics, manifesting that these standard metrics are relatively ineffective in evaluating authenticity, ID fidelity, and text-image correspondence. The FaceQ database will be publicly available upon publication.
arxiv_record.authors: Lu Liu, Huiyu Duan, Qiang Hu, Liu Yang, Chunlei Cai, Tianxiao Ye, Huayu Liu, Xiaoyun Zhang, Guangtao Zhai

arxiv_record.abstract: Recent works on accelerating Vision-Language Models achieve strong performance across a variety of vision-language tasks despite highly compressing visual information. In this work, we examine the popular acceleration approach of early pruning of visual tokens inside the language model. Surprisingly, we find that while strong performance is maintained across many tasks, it exhibits drastically different behavior for a subset of vision-centric tasks such as localization. Upon further investigation, we uncover a core issue with the acceleration approach where most tokens towards the top of the image are pruned away. Yet, on many benchmarks aiming to evaluate vision-centric capabilities, strong performance persists with the flawed pruning strategy, highlighting these benchmarks' limited ability to assess fine-grained visual capabilities. Based on these findings, we propose FEATHER (Fast and Effective Acceleration wiTH Ensemble cRiteria), a straightforward approach that resolves the discovered early-layer pruning issue and further enhances the preservation of relevant tokens via multistage pruning with early uniform sampling to ensure broad image coverage. With comparable computational savings, we find that FEATHER achieves more than 5x performance improvement on the vision-centric localization benchmarks compared to the original acceleration approach.
arxiv_record.authors: Mark Endo, Xiaohan Wang, Serena Yeung-Levy
arxiv_record.title: Feather the Throttle: Revisiting Visual Token Pruning for Vision-Language Model Acceleration

In this work, we examine the popular acceleration approach of early pruning of visual tokens inside the language model. Surprisingly, we find that while strong performance is maintained across many tasks, it exhibits drastically different behavior for a subset of vision-centric tasks such as localization. Upon further investigation, we uncover a core issue with the acceleration approach where most tokens towards the top of the image are pruned away. Yet, on many benchmarks aiming to evaluate vision-centric capabilities, strong performance persists with the flawed pruning strategy, highlighting these benchmarks' limited ability to assess fine-grained visual capabilities. Based on these findings, we propose FEATHER (Fast and Effective Acceleration wiTH Ensemble cRiteria), a straightforward approach that resolves the discovered early-layer pruning issue and further enhances the preservation of relevant tokens via multistage pruning with early uniform sampling to ensure broad image coverage. With comparable computational savings, we find that FEATHER achieves more than 5x performance improvement on the vision-centric localization benchmarks compared to the original acceleration approach.

arxiv_record.abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models excel at generating photorealistic images but often fail to render accurate spatial relationships. We identify two core issues underlying this common failure: 1) the ambiguous nature of data concerning spatial relationships in existing datasets, and 2) the inability of current text encoders to accurately interpret the spatial semantics of input descriptions. We propose CoMPaSS, a versatile framework that enhances spatial understanding in T2I models. It first addresses data ambiguity with the Spatial Constraints-Oriented Pairing (SCOP) data engine, which curates spatially-accurate training data via principled constraints. To leverage these priors, CoMPaSS also introduces the Token ENcoding ORdering (TENOR) module, which preserves crucial token ordering information lost by text encoders, thereby reinforcing the prompt's linguistic structure. Extensive experiments on four popular T2I models (UNet and MMDiT-based) show CoMPaSS sets a new state of the art on key spatial benchmarks, with substantial relative gains on VISOR (+98%), T2I-CompBench Spatial (+67%), and GenEval Position (+131%). Code is available at https://github.com/blurgyy/CoMPaSS.

native_poster_event.abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models excel at generating photorealistic images, but commonly struggle to render accurate spatial relationships described in text prompts. We identify two core issues underlying this common failure: 1) the ambiguous nature of spatial-related data in existing datasets, and 2) the inability of current text encoders to accurately interpret the spatial semantics of input descriptions. We address these issues with CoMPaSS, a versatile training framework that enhances spatial understanding of any T2I diffusion model. CoMPaSS solves the ambiguity of spatial-related data with the Spatial Constraints-Oriented Pairing (SCOP) data engine, which curates spatially accurate training data through a set of principled spatial constraints. To better exploit the curated high-quality spatial priors, CoMPaSS further introduces a Token ENcoding ORdering (TENOR) module to allow better exploitation of high-quality spatial priors, effectively compensating for the shortcoming of text encoders. Extensive experiments on four popular open-weight T2I diffusion models covering both UNet- and MMDiT-based architectures demonstrate the effectiveness of CoMPaSS by setting new state-of-the-arts with substantial relative gains across well-known benchmarks on spatial relationships generation, including VISOR (+98%), T2I-CompBench Spatial (+67%), and GenEval Position (+131%).

E3.justification: V2 introduces a 500-image training control preserving category and relationship distributions, three-object evaluation with any/all correctness measures, and training/inference time and VRAM comparisons excluding bounding-box generation. E4.justification: V2 adds SCOP threshold sensitivity tests, reduced-data experiments, human validation of curated pairs, three-object generalization analysis, and a size-disparity failure case with targeted mitigation. E5.justification: Appendix B retains the same latency measurements and accompanying ± values. V2 introduces no new run-count, seed, confidence-interval, or significance-testing information. Its human-agreement percentage is an additional evaluation outcome without uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Matched original benchmark, fidelity, ablation, and latency values remain unchanged. Substantial new results include DPG-Bench overall scores of 80.63/84.42 and three-object all-correct rates of 13.1%/31.2% for base/CoMPaSS-enhanced FLUX.1, respectively. V2 also adds human agreement of 85.2%, efficiency and sensitivity results, and new qualitative examples.

M1.justification: The standard SCOP/TENOR procedure, attention supervision, and LoRA setup are retained. V2 adds a targeted adaptation: further fine-tuning FLUX.1+CoMPaSS on size-contrast data filtered through an adapted SCOP engine (Figure 7). This additional training stage is absent from v1.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, related work, method explanations, and experimental narrative. R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around reinforcement learning, preference optimization, training-based versus inference-only control, and qualitative spatial relations. improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for compositional generalization through long-prompt and three-object evaluations. These gains outweigh the loss of some VISOR protocol detail and incomplete specification of parts of the new studies; the original benchmark and ablation evidence is preserved.

arxiv_record.abstract: Monocular facial performance capture in-the-wild is challenging due to varied capture conditions, face shapes, and expressions. Most current methods rely on linear 3D Morphable Models, which represent facial expressions independently of identity at the vertex displacement level. We propose SEREP (Semantic Expression Representation), a model that disentangles expression from identity at the semantic level. We start by learning an expression representation from high-quality 3D data of unpaired facial expressions. Then, we train a model to predict expression from monocular images relying on a novel semi-supervised scheme using low quality synthetic data. In addition, we introduce MultiREX, a benchmark addressing the lack of evaluation resources for the expression capture task. Our experiments show that SEREP outperforms state-of-the-art methods, capturing challenging expressions and transferring them to new identities.

arxiv_record.abstract: Species distributions encode valuable ecological and environmental information, yet their potential for guiding representation learning in remote sensing remains underexplored. We introduce WildSAT, which pairs satellite images with millions of geo-tagged wildlife observations readily-available on citizen science platforms. WildSAT employs a contrastive learning approach that jointly leverages satellite images, species occurrence maps, and textual habitat descriptions to train or fine-tune models. This approach significantly improves performance on diverse satellite image recognition tasks, outperforming both ImageNet-pretrained models and satellite-specific baselines. Additionally, by aligning visual and textual information, WildSAT enables zero-shot retrieval, allowing users to search geographic locations based on textual descriptions. WildSAT surpasses recent cross-modal learning methods, including approaches that align satellite images with ground imagery or wildlife photos, demonstrating the advantages of our approach. Finally, we analyze the impact of key design choices and highlight the broad applicability of WildSAT to remote sensing and biodiversity monitoring.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly identifies poor zero-shot performance on anthropogenic classes and suggests combining wildlife and anthropogenic supervision. It also discusses African segmentation transfer and relates larger US bird-prediction gains to training geography. Conversely, it removes v1's polar-coverage and endangered-species caveats. The PEFT and location-encoder interpretations promoted into the main text already appeared in v1's appendix.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code/data repository pointer and discloses negative sampling, species/location text matching, use of supplied dataset splits, and average training time of eight hours on two NVIDIA L40S GPUs. It documents missing-band handling for the new multispectral experiments. The endangered-species exclusion/location-noise disclosure is removed, without establishing that the underlying processing changed.

E1.justification: v2 adds Cashew1k plantation segmentation in Benin and SAcrop3k crop segmentation in South Africa, substantially extending evaluation beyond image classification and bird encounter rates. It also evaluates zero-shot classification on selected EuroSAT and So2Sat20k classes, previously evaluated through trained linear probes.

E2.justification: RemoteCLIP joins the existing CLIP, TaxaBind and GRAFT classification comparison in v2 Tables 2 and A3, and participates in the new zero-shot comparison in Table A5. The previously evaluated comparators are retained.

E3.justification: New segmentation experiments train U-Net-style decoders with frozen encoders and report IoU and pixel accuracy. v2 also adds zero-shot classwise F1 evaluation and multispectral runs using available bands, zero-filling only unavailable bands instead of all non-RGB bands. These are additional protocols; the original RGB classification experiments and WildSAT training budget remain.

E4.justification: The component, location-encoder and PEFT ablations and So2Sat20k confusion matrices are retained unchanged. v2 adds focused multispectral checks, a diagnostic comparison of zero-shot performance on natural versus anthropogenic classes, and segmentation case studies highlighting corrected crop predictions (Tables A4–A5 and Figure A3).

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the paper's broad representation-learning claims. arxiv_record.abstract: Generating sewing patterns in garment design is receiving increasing attention due to its CG-friendly and flexible-editing nature. Previous sewing pattern generation methods have been able to produce exquisite clothing, but struggle to design complex garments with detailed control. To address these issues, we propose SewingLDM, a multi-modal generative model that generates sewing patterns controlled by text prompts, body shapes, and garment sketches. Initially, we extend the original vector of sewing patterns into a more comprehensive representation to cover more intricate details and then compress them into a compact latent space. To learn the sewing pattern distribution in the latent space, we design a two-step training strategy to inject the multi-modal conditions, \ie, body shapes, text prompts, and garment sketches, into a diffusion model, ensuring the generated garments are body-suited and detail-controlled. Comprehensive qualitative and quantitative experiments show the effectiveness of our proposed method, significantly surpassing previous approaches in terms of complex garment design and various body adaptability. Our project page: https://shengqiliu1.github.io/SewingLDM.

arxiv_record.abstract: Medical researchers and clinicians often need to perform novel segmentation tasks on a set of related images. Existing methods for segmenting a new dataset are either interactive, requiring substantial human effort for each image, or require an existing set of previously labeled images. We introduce a system, MultiverSeg, that enables practitioners to rapidly segment an entire new dataset without requiring access to any existing labeled data from that task or domain. Along with the image to segment, the model takes user interactions such as clicks, bounding boxes or scribbles as input, and predicts a segmentation. As the user segments more images, those images and segmentations become additional inputs to the model, providing context. As the context set of labeled images grows, the number of interactions required to segment each new image decreases. We demonstrate that MultiverSeg enables users to interactively segment new datasets efficiently, by amortizing the number of interactions per image to achieve an accurate segmentation. Compared to using a state-of-the-art interactive segmentation method, MultiverSeg reduced the total number of clicks by 36% and scribble steps by 25% to achieve 90% Dice on sets of images from unseen tasks. We release code and model weights at https://multiverseg.csail.mit.edu

native_poster_event.abstract: Recent probabilistic methods for 3D triangular meshes have shown promise in capturing diverse shapes by managing mesh connectivity in a differentiable manner. However, these methods are often limited by high computational costs that scale disproportionately with the level of detail, restricting their applicability for complex shapes requiring high face density. In this work, we introduce a novel differentiable mesh processing method that addresses these computational challenges in both 2D and 3D. Our method reduces time complexity from $O(N)$ to $O(\log N)$ and requires significantly less memory than previous approaches, enabling us to handle far more intricate structures. Building on this innovation, we present a reconstruction algorithm capable of generating complex 2D and 3D shapes from point clouds or multi-view images. We demonstrate its efficacy on various objects exhibiting diverse topologies and geometric details.

arxiv_record.abstract:
The field of self-supervised learning (SSL) for 3D medical images lacks
consistency and standardization. While many methods have been developed, it is
impossible to identify the current state-of-the-art, due to i) varying and
small pretraining datasets, ii) varying architectures, and iii) being evaluated
on differing downstream datasets. In this paper, we bring clarity to this field
and lay the foundation for further method advancements through three key
contributions: We a) publish the largest publicly available pre-training
dataset comprising 114k 3D brain MRI volumes, enabling all practitioners to
pre-train on a large-scale dataset. We b) benchmark existing 3D self-supervised
learning methods on this dataset for a state-of-the-art CNN and Transformer
architecture, clarifying the state of 3D SSL pre-training. Among many findings,
we show that pre-trained methods can exceed a strong from-scratch nnU-Net
ResEnc-L baseline. Lastly, we c) publish the code of our pre-training and
fine-tuning frameworks and provide the pre-trained models created during the
benchmarking process to facilitate rapid adoption and reproduction.

Resource availability is reported by the PDF, not independently verified.

Table 2 also includes default nnU-Net. v1 cites several methods but reports no such comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 introduces controlled benchmark protocols: development versus held-out datasets, 50/50 train/test splits with additional development validation splits, common architectures, 1000-epoch pre-training, and specified fine-tuning budgets and metrics. Appendix C.2 additionally specifies five-fold classification cross-validation, although its relationship to the blanket 50/50 split statement is unclear. These protocols were absent from v1.

E4.justification: v2 adds comparisons of five fine-tuning schedules, 150 versus 1000 fine-tuning epochs, image-quality and modality filtering, and anonymization-aware reconstruction losses (Tables 4–8). Tables 10–11 add VoCo and Volume Fusion hyperparameter studies. v1 discusses possible benefits of quality scores and masks without testing them.

E5.justification: Appendix C.2 newly reports five-fold cross-validation for classification, adding resampling-based performance estimation information absent from v1. Neither version supplies seed-based variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the two-rater image-quality assessment is retained.

Table 1 also changes OpenMind's reported volume count from 114,570 to 113,921 and modality count from 23 to 24, although some v2 prose retains 23 modalities.

M1.justification: Beyond v1's dataset construction pipeline and announced benchmark, v2 introduces operational adaptations of SSL methods to ResEnc-L and Primus-M. These include 3D SimCLR, architecture-specific dense and global output heads, and a two-layer decoder for Primus-M MAE pre-training (Figure 7 and Appendix D). These are substantial additions to the presented procedures, without establishing replacement of an earlier implemented benchmark.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands its positioning around rigorous benchmarking, CNN–transformer comparisons, and data selection, adding discussion and citations for Primus, nnU-Net revisited, Touchstone, DataComp, and SemDeDup. improvement.justification: v1 postpones the benchmark, leaving its intended comparative contribution unsupported. v2 supplies a controlled 15-dataset evaluation with strong baselines, targeted ablations, detailed implementation information, and explicit limitations, substantially resolving that evidentiary gap. These weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OpenMind dataset and SSL benchmarking project, and their text, tables, figures, and appendices are readable. The original DWI appendix is retained as Appendix B.2 in v2; the substantial expansion supports a reliable comparison.

arxiv_record.abstract: We present FaceLift, a novel feed-forward approach for generalizable high-quality 360-degree 3D head reconstruction from a single image. Our pipeline first employs a multi-view latent diffusion model to generate consistent side and back views from a single facial input, which then feeds into a transformer-based reconstructor that produces a comprehensive 3D Gaussian splats representation. Previous methods for monocular 3D face reconstruction often lack full view coverage or view consistency due to insufficient multi-view supervision. We address this by creating a high-quality synthetic head dataset that enables consistent supervision across viewpoints. To bridge the domain gap between synthetic training data and real-world images, we propose a simple yet effective technique that ensures the view generation process maintains fidelity to the input by learning to reconstruct the input image alongside the view generation. Despite being trained exclusively on synthetic data, our method demonstrates remarkable generalization to real-world images. Through extensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations, we show that FaceLift outperforms state-of-the-art 3D face reconstruction methods on identity preservation, detail recovery, and rendering quality.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Recent works on dynamic 3D neural field reconstruction assume the input from
synchronized multi-view videos whose poses are known. The input constraints are
often not satisfied in real-world setups, making the approach impractical. We
show that unsynchronized videos from unknown poses can generate dynamic neural
fields as long as the videos capture human motion. Humans are one of the most
common dynamic subjects captured in videos, and their shapes and poses can be
estimated using state-of-the-art libraries. While noisy, the estimated human
shape and pose parameters provide a decent initialization point to start the
highly non-convex and under-constrained problem of training a consistent
dynamic neural representation. Given the shape and pose parameters of humans in
individual frames, we formulate methods to calculate the time offsets between
videos, followed by camera pose estimations that analyze the 3D joint
positions. Then, we train the dynamic neural fields employing multiresolution
grids while we concurrently refine both time offsets and camera poses. The
setup still involves optimizing many parameters; therefore, we introduce a
robust progressive learning strategy to stabilize the process. Experiments show
that our approach achieves accurate spatio-temporal calibration and
high-quality scene reconstruction in challenging conditions.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from single-person, static-camera Panoptic scenes to three-person smartphone recordings in Mobile-Stage and two-person EgoBody scenes containing a moving head-mounted camera alongside static cameras. v2 also evaluates mixed-frame-rate inputs. The documented Panoptic sampling, training budget, and test-time optimization remain.

P2.justification: Figure 5 becomes a multi-dataset calibration display, and new Figures 7, 9, and 10 show Mobile-Stage and EgoBody results. Tables 1 and 3 gain dataset groupings and additional results, while Table 2 gains the mixed-FPS row. Existing Panoptic visual comparisons are retained as Figures 8, 11, and 12 rather than replaced.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantive 'Camera calibration with human' subsection covering CameraHMR, Virtual Correspondence, moving-person calibration, person-reidentification calibration, and HSfM. It acknowledges shared human-based calibration ideas and distinguishes synchronization, camera-motion, and reconstruction assumptions. This materially expands positioning beyond v1's human-pose and NeRF discussions.

T1.justification: The stated problem assumptions now explicitly include known cross-view person correspondences and permit unequal frame rates, replacing v1's equal-rate restriction. The mathematical formulation and Procrustes/alignment algorithms otherwise remain substantively unchanged after renumbering and relocation; no new proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 validates the approach only on static, single-person Panoptic scenes. v2 substantially strengthens evidence beyond that setting through multi-person smartphone reconstruction, initialization with sparse and moving cameras, and mixed-rate testing. Unexplained Panoptic offset changes and Appendix C's overstatement of EgoBody refinement weaken reporting, but the validation and positioning gains outweigh these limited problems. arxiv_record.abstract:
Approximately 200 million individuals around the world suffer from varying
degrees of visual impairment, making it crucial to leverage AI technology to
offer walking assistance for these people. With the recent progress of
vision-language models (VLMs), applying VLMs to offer walking guidance has
become popular. However, the existing methods of walking guidance are mainly
based on self-curated question-answering datasets that are not publicly
accessible, without a standardized benchmark for training or evaluation.
Moreover, walking assistance often requires real-time streaming video analysis
and the generation of concise yet informative reminders, making VLMs struggle
due to excessive responses and low efficiency in inferences. In this paper, we
introduce the first large-scale dataset dedicated to walking assistance,
comprising 12,000 video-annotation pairs, to provide a unified benchmark for
training and evaluating systems to help visually-impaired individuals walk.
Furthermore, a WalkVLM model is proposed, which employs chain of thought for
hierarchical planning to generate concise but informative reminders and
utilizes temporal-aware adaptive prediction to reduce the temporal redundancy
of reminders. Finally, we have established a solid benchmark for blind walking
task and verified the advantages of WalkVLM in stream video processing for this
task compared to other VLMs. Our dataset and code are available at
https://walkvlm2024.github.io.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain WAD and timely, concise walking guidance through hierarchical reasoning and adaptive triggering. v4 removes the repeated claim that WAD is unbiased and explicitly claims the first large-scale dataset dedicated to walking assistance. These are limited changes to the dataset's claimed properties and novelty.

C2.justification: The original geographic, camera and linguistic biases and generalization/efficiency limitations are retained in the appendix. v4 adds specific limitations involving event prioritization, obstacle/direction errors and fine-grained recognition. It also discusses interaction with existing walking aids, respondents' concerns about redundant or inaccurate guidance, and interprets the new walking trial as evidence of practical assistance.

D1.justification: The appendix supplies annotation interfaces, category thresholds, normalization/inference/judging prompts, temporal labeling instructions and task-specific test counts. These are substantial new disclosures, not proof of changed implementations or splits. The abstract changes code/data availability from promised to stated available; external availability was not verified.

E1.justification: The 12k-example WAD dataset and reminder/QA tasks remain. v4 additionally evaluates annotation suitability through 34 visually impaired respondents and actual walking assistance with three visually impaired participants (Sections 3.4 and 5.4), substantially extending target-population and interactive deployment coverage.

E2.justification: Relative to v1 Table 2, v4 Table 3 adds LLaVa-7B and WAD-fine-tuned DeepSeek-VL-7B, MiniCPM-V2.6 and Qwen2-VL alongside the original baselines. The subjective comparison also replaces three baseline configurations with fine-tuned versions. DeepSeek becoming DeepSeek-VL is a naming change, while the TRF comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v4 adds explicitly WAD-fine-tuned comparison controls and new survey and walking-study protocols. The walking trial counts manual reminders with and without WalkVLM, always testing WalkVLM first. Section 5.4 also changes the reported subjective-evaluation panel from nine annotators to eight; this establishes a reporting revision, not that every retained result was rerun.

E4.justification: The three original component ablations and their scores are unchanged. However, v4 adds a field case study testing whether WalkVLM reduces manual assistance, supplementary hierarchical-reasoning and streaming-inference cases, and category/text-length analyses (Table 6; Figures 15–21). These substantially broaden analysis beyond the original offline component tests and examples.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or formal significance tests. Added participant counts and outcome percentages concern study design and results. The walking trial's description of a significant reduction is not accompanied by statistical testing.

E6.justification: v4 adds baseline results, 88.24% positive survey responses, and manual-reminder counts of 24/22/28 with WalkVLM versus 35/33/37 without it. Subjective results also change. Existing TF-IDF, ROUGE, TRF and ablation values remain. WalkVLM's GPT scores change from 0.447/0.521 to 1.103/4.168; the pattern suggests rescaling against GPT-4o, not demonstrated performance gains, and the normalization is insufficiently explained.

M1.justification: Both versions retain MiniCPM-V2.6 with LoRA, perception–comprehension–decision reasoning, POLM object-location priors and the ConvNext3D/history-state TAP module. arxiv_record.abstract: The increasing demand to process long and high-resolution videos significantly burdens Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) due to the enormous number of visual tokens. Existing token reduction methods primarily prune tokens based on importance metrics, such as cumulative attention scores. However, even important tokens may exhibit high redundancy caused by similarity among adjacent video frames and repetitive visual elements. To address this limitation, we propose FrameFusion, a novel token reduction approach integrating similarity-based merging with importance-based pruning. We conduct a thorough study on token similarity characteristics, revealing three key insights: (1) spatially corresponding visual tokens between adjacent frames have higher cosine similarities compared to other token pairs; (2) high token similarities prominently decrease in deeper model layers; and (3) token similarity rankings are highly consistent across different layers. Guided by these observations, FrameFusion computes token similarities exclusively between corresponding visual tokens from adjacent frames, applies token merging at initial successive layers followed by pruning in deeper layers, and adopts a cascaded merging strategy to further enhance efficiency. We evaluate FrameFusion comprehensively across six diverse LVLMs, ranging from 2B to 72B parameters, using five video benchmarks encompassing video retrieval, question-answering, and spatial-temporal understanding tasks. Experiments show that FrameFusion reduces visual tokens by 70%, achieving 1.6-3.6x end-to-end speedups, with an average performance impact of less than 3%. Our code is available at: https://github.com/thu-nics/FrameFusion.

arxiv_record.abstract: No published work on visual question answering (VQA) accounts for ambiguity regarding where the content described in the question is located in the image. To fill this gap, we introduce VQ-FocusAmbiguity, the first VQA dataset that visually grounds each plausible image region a question could refer to when arriving at valid answers. We next analyze and compare our dataset to existing datasets to reveal its unique properties. Finally, we benchmark modern models for two novel tasks related to acknowledging focus ambiguity: recognizing whether a visual question has focus ambiguity and locating all plausible focus regions within the image. Results show that the dataset is challenging for modern models. To facilitate future progress on these tasks, we publicly share the dataset with an evaluation server at https://vizwiz.org/tasks-and-datasets/focus-ambiguity-in-visual-questions.
arxiv_record.authors: Chongyan Chen, Yu-Yun Tseng, Zhuoheng Li, Anush Venkatesh, Danna Gurari

arxiv_record.abstract: Clothed avatar generation has wide applications in virtual and augmented reality, filmmaking, and more. Previous methods have achieved success in generating diverse digital avatars, however, generating avatars with disentangled components (\eg, body, hair, and clothes) has long been a challenge. In this paper, we propose LayerAvatar, the first feed-forward diffusion-based method for generating component-disentangled clothed avatars. To achieve this, we first propose a layered UV feature plane representation, where components are distributed in different layers of the Gaussian-based UV feature plane with corresponding semantic labels. This representation supports high-resolution and real-time rendering, as well as expressive animation including controllable gestures and facial expressions. Based on the well-designed representation, we train a single-stage diffusion model and introduce constrain terms to address the severe occlusion problem of the innermost human body layer. Extensive experiments demonstrate the impressive performances of our method in generating disentangled clothed avatars, and we further explore its applications in component transfer. The project page is available at: https://olivia23333.github.io/LayerAvatar/
arxiv_record.authors: Weitian Zhang, Yichao Yan, Sijing Wu, Manwen Liao, Xiaokang Yang
arxiv_record.title: Disentangled Clothed Avatar Generation with Layered Representation

native_poster_event.abstract: Clothed avatar generation has wide applications in virtual and augmented reality, filmmaking, and more. While existing methods have made progress in creating animatable digital avatars, generating avatars with disentangled components (e.g., body, hair, and clothes) has long been a challenge. In this paper, we propose LayerAvatar, a novel feed-forward diffusion-based method capable of generating high-quality component-disentangled clothed avatars in seconds. We propose a layered UV feature plane representation, where components are distributed in different layers of the Gaussian-based UV feature plane with corresponding semantic labels. This representation can be effectively learned with current feed-forward generation pipelines, facilitating component disentanglement and enhancing details of generated avatars. Based on the well-designed representation, we train a single-stage diffusion model and introduce constrain terms to mitigate the severe occlusion issue of the innermost human body layer. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performances of our method in generating highly detailed and disentangled clothed avatars. In addition, we explore its applications in component transfer.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Motion-controllable image animation is a fundamental task with a wide range
of potential applications. Recent works have made progress in controlling
camera or object motion via various motion representations, while they still
struggle to support collaborative camera and object motion control with
adaptive control granularity. To this end, we introduce 3D-aware motion
representation and propose an image animation framework, called
Perception-as-Control, to achieve fine-grained collaborative motion control.
Specifically, we construct 3D-aware motion representation from a reference
image, manipulate it based on interpreted user instructions, and perceive it
from different viewpoints. In this way, camera and object motions are
transformed into intuitive and consistent visual changes. Then, our framework
leverages the perception results as motion control signals, enabling it to
support various motion-related video synthesis tasks in a unified and flexible
way. Experiments demonstrate the superiority of the proposed approach. For more
details and qualitative results, please refer to our anonymous project webpage:
https://chen-yingjie.github.io/projects/Perception-as-Control.
arxiv_record.authors: Yingjie Chen, Yifang Men, Yuan Yao, Miaomiao Cui, Liefeng Bo

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations linking spatial alignment, depth, the world envelope, and staged training to the ablation outcomes (Section 4.3). It revises reported hardware from eight A100 GPUs to one and adds integration, training, and application diagrams in Appendices B–D. E2.justification: V1 discusses competitors but presents no evaluated head-to-head comparisons. V2 evaluates CameraCtrl, reproduced CameraCtrl*, MotionCtrl, and their ++ adaptations for camera control (Table 1), and Motion-I2V, MOFA-Video, and the ++ adaptations for object control (Table 2). Figures 5–6 add qualitative baseline comparisons.

E3.justification: V2 introduces quantitative evaluation on 1K test clips from each dataset, six quality/controllability metrics, frame-count comparison variants, and controlled ablation protocols. Section 4.1 also revises reported training sizes from approximately 6K/35K to 61K/352K RealEstate/WebVid clips. The PDFs do not establish whether these size revisions reflect expanded training or corrected reporting.

E4.justification: V2 adds representation ablations comparing point offsets, point positions, 3D spheres, and spheres plus the world envelope, and compares one-, two-, and three-stage training (Tables 3–4, Figure 7, Appendix C). M1.justification: The central representation, U-Net/ReferenceNet framework, loss, and three-stage training procedure are retained. arxiv_record.abstract: Recent video generation models have shown promising results in producing high-quality video clips lasting several seconds. However, these models face challenges in generating long sequences that convey clear and informative events, limiting their ability to support coherent narrations. In this paper, we present a large-scale cooking video dataset designed to advance long-form narrative generation in the cooking domain. We validate the quality of our proposed dataset in terms of visual fidelity and textual caption accuracy using state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and video generation models, respectively. We further introduce a Long Narrative Video Director to enhance both visual and semantic coherence in generated videos and emphasize the role of aligning visual embeddings to achieve improved overall video quality. Our method demonstrates substantial improvements in generating visually detailed and semantically aligned keyframes, supported by finetuning techniques that integrate text and image embeddings within the video generation process. Project page: https://videoauteur.github.io/

arxiv_record.abstract:
Recent advances in monocular depth estimation methods (MDE) and their
improved accuracy open new possibilities for their applications. In this paper,
we investigate how monocular depth estimates can be used for relative pose
estimation. In particular, we are interested in answering the question whether
using MDEs improves results over traditional point-based methods. We propose a
novel framework for estimating the relative pose of two cameras from point
correspondences with associated monocular depths. Since depth predictions are
typically defined up to an unknown scale or even both unknown scale and shift
parameters, our solvers jointly estimate the scale or both the scale and shift
parameters along with the relative pose. We derive efficient solvers
considering different types of depths for three camera configurations: (1) two
calibrated cameras, (2) two cameras with an unknown shared focal length, and
(3) two cameras with unknown different focal lengths. Our new solvers
outperform state-of-the-art depth-aware solvers in terms of speed and accuracy.
In extensive real experiments on multiple datasets and with various MDEs, we
discuss which depth-aware solvers are preferable in which situation. The code
will be made publicly available.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contribution on jointly estimating scale, shift and pose with state-of-the-art accuracy. v2 broadens the central contribution to determining when depth information and different estimation strategies help, explicitly emphasizing scale-only alternatives, RANSAC choices and efficiency against competing affine-depth solvers. The three camera configurations remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantial conditional interpretation: when shift modelling is unnecessary, when reprojection refinement can help with reliable indoor depths, and why hybrid RANSAC trades computation for accuracy. It also tentatively attributes declining accuracy at larger iteration budgets to physically implausible scale/focal solutions that current checks admit. Existing coplanarity and pure-translation limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 documents Mast3r's 500 coarse/200 fine refinement iterations, its distinct CPU/GPU hardware, and exclusions from runtime measurements. Conversely, v1's statement that source code is available, accompanied by a URL, becomes only a promise of future public release in v2. This changes the documented access information without establishing the repository's actual status.

E1.justification: v2 adds ScanNet RGB-D evaluation for calibrated, shared-focal and different-focal cases (Tables 10, 12 and 15), while retaining Phototourism and ETH3D. Conversely, v1's synthetic evaluations covering controlled image/depth noise and pure-rotation scenarios disappear, including Appendix B.1.

E2.justification: v2 adds MadPose's affine-depth solvers as direct comparators for all three camera configurations and Mast3r's nonlinear optimization for focal-length comparisons. The existing P3P, Rel3PT, 3p3d, 4p4d and standard point-based solvers remain. These additions substantially strengthen comparison against competing estimation approaches.

E3.justification: The primary evaluation moves from GC-RANSAC without local optimization to PoseLib with local optimization; PoseLib already appeared in v1's appendix, but its stated threshold changes from 1 to 2 pixels. Phototourism changes from nine scenes/43,678 pairs to five scenes/24,750 pairs. v2 also adds hybrid protocols and iteration-budget sweeps, introduces RoMA/Mast3r matching, revises depth sources from eleven to five, and replaces separate real-data rotation/translation summaries with combined maximum pose error.

E4.justification: v1's numerical-stability and controlled noise-sensitivity studies are removed. v2 adds systematic comparisons of Sampson versus reprojection refinement, shift/scale modelling assumptions, iteration-dependent speed–accuracy tradeoffs, and Mast3r matches combined with MoGe depth. The inverse-depth comparison and selected fast-versus-GB results are retained, rather than newly introduced analyses.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 2 reports error distributions using medians and 25th/75th-percentile boxes; these statistical spread displays disappear with the synthetic experiments. Neither version reports seed-based uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests for the main benchmark results.

E6.justification: v2 substantially replaces and expands the benchmark results. For example, its new Phototourism SP+LG/MoGe comparison reports 40.42 mAA at 23.41 ms for 3PTs00f1,2 versus 38.89 at 44.03 ms for 4PTsuvf1,2 (Table 5). These are new within-version comparisons, not demonstrated gains over v1 under identical settings. Supplementary Tables 6–7 retain selected v1 DA V2 results unchanged.

M1.justification: The core geometric solver formulations remain. v2 extends their estimation pipeline with reprojection-error scoring and refinement, with or without shift, and integration into hybrid RANSAC. The zero-shift configurations already appear in v1's solver tables; their expanded explanation and testing do not establish an entirely new solver family.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled RePoseD and extensively rewrites its abstract, introduction, contributions and experimental narrative. A dedicated Related Work section is introduced, method sections are consolidated, and inverse-depth material is moved into a separately organized supplement. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond added experiments.

P2.justification: v1's stability and noise figures are replaced by a pipeline illustration and speed–accuracy plots. The solver-configuration tables are merged, and benchmark tables are extensively redesigned around matchers and optimization variants, with much denser supplementary displays. Selected unchanged DA V2 results are extracted into compact supplementary tables.

R1.justification: The new Related Work section substantially revises positioning, especially by acknowledging Yu et al.'s concurrent MadPose work as solving the same affine-depth formulation. v2 distinguishes its contribution through solver efficiency, additional parameter configurations and conditional disagreement about shift modelling. It also expands discussion of DUSt3R/Mast3r and depth-assisted reconstruction research.

T1.justification: Most affine- and inverse-depth reasoning is retained or relocated. Limited mathematical revisions include replacing the calibrated 3PTs00 worked example with explicit shared-focal 3PTs00f constraints and removing an extra scale factor from the four-correspondence focal-length distance constraint. The configuration table also revises reported focal-solver solution counts.

improvement.justification: Direct MadPose comparisons, systematic optimization and parameter-modelling controls, and ScanNet evaluation substantially strengthen the evidence for when depth-based estimation helps. Together with clearer positioning and more conditional conclusions, these address important limitations of v1's comparative argument. Removing synthetic stability/noise evidence and replacing the code URL with a future-release promise weaken verification, but the expanded controlled comparisons provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Despite the new RePoseD title, both PDFs describe the same underlying research, with matching solver formulations, camera configurations and retained results. Both main texts and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: Section 4 and supplementary Section 7 report original evaluations on Phototourism, ETH3D and ScanNet, including solver, matching and optimization comparisons.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix B report original synthetic experiments and pose/focal-length evaluations on Phototourism and ETH3D.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Traditional animation production decomposes visual elements into discrete
layers to enable independent processing for sketching, refining, coloring, and
in-betweening. Existing anime generation video methods typically treat
animation as a distinct data domain different from real-world videos, lacking
fine-grained control at the layer level. To bridge this gap, we introduce
LayerAnimate, a novel video diffusion framework with layer-aware architecture
that empowers the manipulation of layers through layer-level controls. The
development of a layer-aware framework faces a significant data scarcity
challenge due to the commercial sensitivity of professional animation assets.
To address the limitation, we propose a data curation pipeline featuring
Automated Element Segmentation and Motion-based Hierarchical Merging. Through
quantitative and qualitative comparisons, and user study, we demonstrate that
LayerAnimate outperforms current methods in terms of animation quality, control
precision, and usability, making it an effective tool for both professional
animators and amateur enthusiasts. This framework opens up new possibilities
for layer-level animation applications and creative flexibility. Our code is
available at https://layeranimate.github.io.

C1.justification: The introduction and conclusion expand the central contribution from independent layer manipulation with motion scores or sketches to flexible composition of heterogeneous controls, including trajectories, across layers. The contribution statement and principal demonstrations now foreground simultaneous composite control, substantially broadening the claimed capability beyond the terminology change.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations of control informativeness, complementary heatmap/offset representations, and the benefits of increasing layer capacity and motion information. It removes v1's explanation of weaker sketch guidance and its explicit limitation concerning control of elements absent from the initial I2V frame. Resolution/duration constraints and possible real-world transfer remain in Appendix E. Improved training-data segmentation does not itself establish that the omitted inference limitation is resolved.

D1.justification: v3 documents four-frame key-frame spacing, CoTracker3 tracking on a 60-by-60 grid, an 80% masklet-consistency threshold, control encoders, and padded-layer masking. It specifies 10% mask dropout and 20/40/40 modality-selection probabilities, and changes reported hardware from 16 to 32 A100 GPUs. Conversely, v1's explicit first/last-half allocation recipe for interpolation is no longer described. Both retain the same project-code link.

E1.justification: The four animation tasks in v1 expand to six through trajectory-conditioned I2V and trajectory-conditioned interpolation. v3 also demonstrates simultaneous heterogeneous controls across layers in Figure 6. The animation domain remains unchanged; the increased clip count is a setting change rather than additional domain coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds CogVideoX to I2V and interpolation, and AniDoc to sketch-conditioned I2V. New trajectory comparisons evaluate DragAnything, Tora, and Framer. SEINE, DynamiCrafter, LVCD, and ToonCrafter remain quantitative comparators, although SEINE disappears from the main qualitative comparison figure.

E3.justification: The reported corpus grows from 563K to 665K clips, training changes from 50,000 to 30,000 steps, and batch size increases from 32 to 96. The static threshold changes from 0.05 to 0.1 and the motion-score upper bound from 20 to 30. Sketch extraction changes from Anime2Sketch to Chan et al.'s extractor. v3 explicitly excludes motion scores from headline I2V/interpolation comparisons and specifies matched control inputs. Appendix B adds trajectory MSE evaluation. Both retain a 1K evaluation sample, without establishing identical membership.

E4.justification: v3 Table 2 adds layer-capacity tests and heatmap-versus-offset-versus-hybrid trajectory ablations. Motion assignment is examined through progressive motion-information conditions for both I2V and interpolation, replacing v1's simpler removal test. Appendix Figure 8 adds a motion-score sensitivity example. Conversely, v1's attention-fusion ablation, visual component-failure analysis, shot-filtering analysis, and sketch-style comparison are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Both provide point estimates and user-vote proportions; the changed values do not constitute a change in uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces LayerAnimate's reported results: I2V FVD changes from 98.86 to 87.96, interpolation from 55.69 to 59.64, and sketch-conditioned I2V from 40.64 to 26.64. Changed training and conditioning prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains or losses. v3 adds trajectory results, including appendix MSE values of 46.58 for I2V and 24.40 for interpolation. Ablation results, qualitative examples, and user-vote distributions also change.

M1.justification: v3 replaces first-frame-only segmentation propagation with iterative key-frame segmentation that incorporates newly appearing elements. It adds trajectory conditioning through a hybrid heatmap/offset representation and trains with different control modalities selected independently across layers. These substantially extend v1's motion-score and sketch controls. The motion-coherence filtering stage is also omitted from the specified pipeline; the underlying layer fusion and motion-based assignment mechanisms remain recognizable.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, curation motivation, and method exposition undergo substantial rewriting. Section 4 is reorganized around frame decomposition, layer controlling, and feature fusion; the application narrative becomes composite control. Terminology changes throughout from layer-specific to layer-level, and the surviving limitations move into a substantially reorganized supplement.

P2.justification: The teaser, curation pipeline, architecture schematic, and qualitative comparison are substantially redesigned. Table 1 gains a six-task structure, Table 2 is rebuilt, Table 3 is added, and the user-study display expands to six charts. The merging tree moves from v1 Figure 2 to v3 appendix Figure 7; a trimmed version of v1 Figure 7 becomes appendix Figure 9. Several earlier appendix displays are removed and a motion-score sensitivity display is added.

R1.justification: The existing diffusion and controllable-generation survey remains largely intact. v3 adds CoTracker3, MIMO, DragAnything, and Tora citations, discussing trajectory control and contrasting animation decomposition with depth-based approaches. PySceneDetect and Anime2Sketch citations disappear. Framer's publication update is bibliographic; its new experimental participation is assessed under E2.

T1.justification: v3 Section 3.1 introduces explicit mask-set subtraction and union-update definitions in Equations 1–2 for iterative segmentation. This is a limited addition of formal algorithmic definitions. The diffusion denoising objective is retained with revised conditioning notation, and neither version provides theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the evidence for controllability through layer-capacity and representation ablations, direct trajectory-error measurements, and broader comparisons with explicitly matched control inputs. These address weaknesses in v1's validation, while detailed control-generation and training procedures improve reproducibility. Removing the attention ablation and the initial-frame limitation reduces completeness, but the stronger experimental design and targeted validation provide a substantial net improvement. The judgment does not depend on treating changed-protocol scores as direct performance gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LayerAnimate and contain readable main texts, figures, tables, equations, and supplementary material. Retained components and relocated material can be matched reliably despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: v3 reports original six-task benchmark results, expanded ablations, a 20-participant user study, and appendix trajectory-error measurements and motion-score experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original four-task benchmark results, component ablations, a 20-participant user study, and qualitative experiments, including appendix analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract:
In spite of recent progress, image diffusion models still produce artifacts.
A common solution is to leverage the feedback provided by quality assessment
systems or human annotators to optimize the model, where images are generally
rated in their entirety. In this work, we believe problem-solving starts with
identification, yielding the request that the model should be aware of not just
the presence of defects in an image, but their specific locations. Motivated by
this, we propose DiffDoctor, a two-stage pipeline to assist image diffusion
models in generating fewer artifacts. Concretely, the first stage targets
developing a robust artifact detector, for which we collect a dataset of over
1M flawed synthesized images and set up an efficient human-in-the-loop
annotation process, incorporating a carefully designed class-balance strategy.
The learned artifact detector is then involved in the second stage to optimize
the diffusion model by providing pixel-level feedback. Extensive experiments on
text-to-image diffusion models demonstrate the effectiveness of our artifact
detector as well as the soundness of our diagnose-then-treat design.

Yiyang Wang, Xi Chen, Xiaogang Xu, Sihui Ji, Yu Liu, Yujun Shen,
  Hengshuang Zhao

arxiv_record.abstract: We introduce Orchid, a unified latent diffusion model that learns a joint appearance-geometry prior to generate color, depth, and surface normal images in a single diffusion process. This unified approach is more efficient and coherent than current pipelines that use separate models for appearance and geometry. Orchid is versatile - it directly generates color, depth, and normal images from text, supports joint monocular depth and normal estimation with color-conditioned finetuning, and seamlessly inpaints large 3D regions by sampling from the joint distribution. It leverages a novel Variational Autoencoder (VAE) that jointly encodes RGB, relative depth, and surface normals into a shared latent space, combined with a latent diffusion model that denoises these latents. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that Orchid delivers competitive performance against SOTA task-specific methods for geometry prediction, even surpassing them in normal-prediction accuracy and depth-normal consistency. It also inpaints color-depth-normal images jointly, with more qualitative realism than existing multi-step methods.
arxiv_record.authors: Akshay Krishnan, Xinchen Yan, Vincent Casser, Abhijit Kundu
arxiv_record.comments: Accepted to ICCV 2025. Project webpage: https://orchid3d.github.io
